 [\alpha(\alpha+c\chi)q+\chi(\chi-c\alpha)q^3]}
 {(\alpha^2+\chi^2)^2}.
 \tag{OPB5}
\]
For completeness, the bracket never vanishes. Its two coefficients
$A=\alpha(\alpha+c\chi)$ and $B=\chi(\chi-c\alpha)$ are real;
$q^2$ is nonreal, so $A+Bq^2=0$ would force $A=B=0$.
If $\chi=0$, then $A=\alpha^2>0$. If $\chi\ne0$ and $B=0$,
then $\chi=c\alpha$ and $A=(1+c^2)\alpha^2>0$.
Thus no allowed $(\alpha,\chi)$ makes both coefficients zero.
Also $q^3\ne q$. Consequently all four boundary constants vanish
precisely on the two distinct phase lines
\[
             \chi=0\qquad\hbox{or}\qquad\alpha+c\chi=0.
 \tag{OPB6}
\]
These are exactly the exceptional phase values in the earlier PZ7
\cite{PeriodZeroOriginal}. To verify the identification with that source,
put $X_0=(\delta+i\gamma)^2$, $Y_0=(\delta-i\gamma)^2$,
$T_0=X_0/Y_0$, $A_e=(2T_0-1)/(3(T_0-1))$ and
$B_e=(2-T_0)/(3(T_0-1))$. Then
\[
 \chi=0\ \Longleftrightarrow\ a/\bar a=1,\qquad
 \alpha+c\chi=0\ \Longleftrightarrow\
 \frac a{\bar a}=\frac{c-i}{c+i}
       =\frac{2X_0-Y_0}{2Y_0-X_0}=\frac{A_e}{B_e}.
 \tag{OPB6a}
\]
The first equivalence is $a-\bar a=2i\chi$.
For the second, cross multiplication with $a=\alpha+i\chi$ gives
$\alpha=-c\chi$. The middle equality follows from
$X_0=-\beta/2+2i\delta\gamma$ and
$Y_0=-\beta/2-2i\delta\gamma$. All denominators are nonzero,
since $\delta\gamma>0$ and $c>0$.
Away from those lines each $n_j=\operatorname{ord}_{\xi=0}f_j(\xi,0)$
is zero and the total order is $v=0$. The leading moment there is
the product of the four explicit nonzero values OPB5.

\subsection{An exact coefficient calculation retaining the complete curve}
Introduce the multiplication matrix of the centered root in its original
coefficient order, and the original quadratic coefficient matrix,
\[
 T=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&0&-\eta\\1&0&0&0\\0&1&0&-\beta\\0&0&1&0\end{pmatrix},
 \quad
 Q=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&1&0\\0&-1&0&\beta\\1&0&-\beta&0\\
                    0&\beta&0&\eta-\beta^2\end{pmatrix}.
 \tag{OPB7}
\]
Thus $T^4+\beta T^2+\eta I=0$. Direct evaluation at all four roots gives
\[
 V\sum_{m\ge0}\frac{T^me_0}{m!}\xi^m=(e^{w_a\xi})_a,
 \qquad Q_0(Vp)=4i\delta\gamma\,p^{\mathsf T}Qp.
 \tag{OPB8}
\]
The first identity is the convergent matrix exponential evaluated at
each eigenvalue, with its original coefficient vectors. To verify the
second, write $p(w)=p_0+p_1w+p_2w^2+p_3w^3$ and expand
$p(w)p(-w)$. The coefficients of $w^2,w^4,w^6$ are
$2p_0p_2-p_1^2$, $p_2^2-2p_1p_3$, and $-p_3^2$.
The differences of those powers between $w_1$ and $w_2$ are
$4i\delta\gamma$, $-4i\delta\gamma\beta$, and
$4i\delta\gamma(\beta^2-\eta)$, proving every entry of $Q$.

Write $\mathcal R(z)=\sum_{n\ge0}R_nz^n$ with the literal PCL2
coefficients, and define the coefficients of its entire inverse by
\[
 I_0=J_\infty^{-1},\qquad
 I_n=-J_\infty^{-1}\sum_{k=1}^nR_k I_{n-k},\quad
 G_n=\sum_{k=0}^n I_k\operatorname{diag}(q,q^2,q^3,q^4)R_{n-k}.
 \tag{OPB9}
\]
Multiplication of the two convergent series proves the inverse recursion
and gives every coefficient of the original conjugated matrix.
In particular
\[
 R_1=\begin{pmatrix}
 0&\beta^3/27-\beta\eta/3&0&-11\beta^4/324+\beta^2\eta/3-\eta^2/2\\
 -\beta^2/9+\eta&0&7\beta^3/81-2\beta\eta/3&0\\
 0&-\beta^2/6+\eta&0&4\beta^3/27-\beta\eta\\
 \beta/3&0&-2\beta^2/9+\eta&0
 \end{pmatrix}.
 \tag{OPB10}
\]
All second and later $R_n$ are the explicit finite sums PCL2; they are
not free parameters. For any coefficient matrices $B_n$ used below, put
\[
 \mathcal C_{m,n}(B)=
 \sum_{k=0}^n\sum_{h=0}^m
 \frac{(B_k T^he_0)^{\mathsf T}Q(B_{n-k}T^{m-h}e_0)}{h!(m-h)!}.
 \tag{OPB11}
\]
Equations OPB8--9 prove the full convergent identity
$f_j(\xi,z)=4i\delta\gamma e^\xi
\sum_{m,n\ge0}\mathcal C_{m,n}(B)\xi^mz^n$
when $B_n$ is the appropriate exact coefficient conjugation.
The factor $4i\delta\gamma e^\xi$ is retained in every result below;
neither the original roots nor the original norm is changed.

\subsection{The real-unit phase: order sixteen and its four-factor unfolding}
On $\chi=0$, the nonzero scalar $\alpha$ cancels with its inverse
inside the specified conjugated map OPB2, so $B_n=G_n$ exactly.
The even and odd coefficient blocks of $G_0$ act by
\[
 \begin{split}
 (p_0,p_2)&\longmapsto
 \bigl(qp_0+\tfrac\beta3(q^3-q)p_2,\,q^3p_2\bigr),\\
 (p_1,p_3)&\longmapsto
 \bigl(q^2p_1+\tfrac{2\beta}3(q^4-q^2)p_3,\,q^4p_3\bigr).
 \end{split}\tag{OPB12}
\]
Substituting $e_0,T e_0,T^2e_0/2,T^3e_0/6,T^4e_0/24$
in OPB11 yields
\[
 \mathcal C_{0,0}=\mathcal C_{1,0}=\mathcal C_{2,0}
 =\mathcal C_{3,0}=0,\quad
 A_j:=\mathcal C_{4,0}=\frac{\beta(q^6-q^4)}{36}.
 \tag{OPB13}
\]
One can see the fourth coefficient explicitly without series elimination:
the even-square contribution, divided by $w_1^2-w_2^2$, is
$\beta(-q^6/12-q^4/4)$, and the subtracted odd-square contribution
is $\beta(-q^6/9-2q^4/9)$. Their difference is OPB13.
Since $q^2\ne1$ and $\beta>0$, each $A_j\ne0$. It follows that
\[
 n_1=n_2=n_3=n_4=4,\quad v=16,\quad
 f_j^{(4)}(0,0)=\frac83i\delta\gamma\beta(q^6-q^4),\quad
 \boxed{\mu_{16}(0)=16!\,5\left(\frac{\delta\gamma\beta}{9}\right)^4>0.}
 \tag{OPB14}
\]
Indeed $\prod_{j=1}^4(q_j^6-q_j^4)=5$, since $q_j^6-q_j^4
=q_j^{-1}(q_j^2-1)$, the $q_j^2$ permute the four nontrivial fifth
roots, and $\prod(q_j-1)=5$. Multiplication of the four complete
Taylor series gives the factorial and the leading moment displayed.

The first mixed coefficients, computed from the same original $R_1,R_2$
through OPB9--11, are
\[
 \begin{split}
 C_j:=\mathcal C_{1,1}
 &=\frac{\beta^2q^3(q-1)(2q^2+2q+1)}9,\\
 D_j:=\mathcal C_{0,2}
 &=-\frac{\beta^2q^4(\beta^2-9\eta)(q-1)(q^2+3q+1)}{81}.
 \end{split}\tag{OPB15}
\]
This reproduces the existing real-unit inverse-period coefficient while
also computing its full coupling to the exponential-curve coordinate.
Neither coefficient vanishes: the roots of $2q^2+2q+1$ have modulus
$1/\sqrt2$; the roots of $q^2+3q+1$ are real and negative;
$\beta^2<4\eta<9\eta$; and a nontrivial fifth root is neither real
nor $1$. PCL22--23 with the literal $t(\xi)$ give
\[
 f_j(\xi,-z)=e^{2\xi}f_j(-\xi,z).
 \tag{OPB16}
\]
For the proof, opposite-root permutation sends $t(\xi)$ to
$e^\xi t(-\xi)$, commutes with $U$, and preserves $Q_0$.
Consequently $\mathcal C_{m,n}=0$ when $m+n$ is odd. The complete
local expansion is thus
\[
 f_j(\xi,z)=4i\delta\gamma e^\xi
 \left(A_j\xi^4+C_jz\xi+D_jz^2+
       \sum_{\substack{m,n\ge0\\m+3n>4\\(m,n)\ne(0,2)}}
           \mathcal C_{m,n}(G)\xi^mz^n\right).
 \tag{OPB17}
\]
Every coefficient in this convergent remainder is defined by the finite
formula OPB11; coefficients of odd total degree vanish as just proved.

Here is the exact branch consequence. There is one holomorphic branch
$\xi_j(z)$ and three holomorphic branches on the actual three-sheeted
parameter $z=w^3$ satisfying
\[
 \begin{split}
 \xi_j(z)&=-D_jC_j^{-1}z+O(z^3),\\
 \xi_{j,\ell}(w)&=h_{j,\ell}w+O(w^3),\qquad
 h_{j,\ell}^3=-C_j/A_j,\quad \ell=1,2,3.
 \end{split}\tag{OPB18}
\]
To prove the first claim, substitute $\xi=zh$ into the full analytic
series, divide by $z^2$, and extend at $z=0$. Its value there is
$D_j+C_jh$, with nonzero derivative $C_j$. For the other branches
substitute $\xi=wh,z=w^3$ and divide by $w^4$. The extension at zero
is $A_jh^4+C_jh$; its derivatives at its three nonzero roots equal
$-3C_j\ne0$. The roots are distinct because $-C_j/A_j\ne0$.
Both extended equations are even in their parameter by OPB16, so their
unique holomorphic solutions $h$ are even, proving the stated errors.
For existence and uniqueness, in either equation $F(h,t)=0$ at a simple
root $(h_0,0)$, the map $h\mapsto h-F(h,t)/F_h(h_0,0)$ is, on a
sufficiently small closed disk about $h_0$, a contraction with derivative
of modulus at most $1/2$ and maps that disk into itself. Iteration
converges uniformly for small $t$, yielding the holomorphic solution;
the contraction proves uniqueness. Finally, on a fixed small circle in
$\xi$, the limit function has exactly its order-four zero inside.
Uniform convergence in $z$ preserves the number of zeros by the argument
principle, and the four branches just constructed account for them all.
These are zeros in the exponential-curve variable near the coefficient
boundary, not an assertion that $f_j(0,z)$ vanishes for a finite period.

\subsection{The second phase: order eight with its exact mixed coefficient form}
On $\alpha+c\chi=0$ we necessarily have $\chi\ne0$. The original
unit interpolates as $\chi(w^2+\beta/3)/(2\delta\gamma)$.
Define its coefficient multiplication matrix
\[
 W=T^2+\tfrac\beta3 I=
 \begin{pmatrix}
 \beta/3&0&-\eta&0\\0&\beta/3&0&-\eta\\
 1&0&-2\beta/3&0\\0&1&0&-2\beta/3
 \end{pmatrix},\qquad H_n=W^{-1}G_nW.
 \tag{OPB19}
\]
The cancelled scalar is exactly $\chi/(2\delta\gamma)$ in the
original conjugation and its inverse, with no other unit change.
The eigenvalue product of $W$ in each opposite-root pair is
$N=\eta-2\beta^2/9>\eta/9>0$, so $\det W=N^2$ and $W$ is
invertible. Equations OPB8--11 apply with $B_n=H_n$.
Put
\[
 X=\beta^4-27\beta^2\eta+81\eta^2,\quad
 Y=3\beta^4-27\beta^2\eta+81\eta^2,\quad
 K=2\beta^2-9\eta.
 \tag{OPB20}
\]
The boundary coefficients are
\[
 \mathcal C_{0,0}(H)=\mathcal C_{1,0}(H)=0,\qquad
 A'_j:=\mathcal C_{2,0}(H)
 =-\frac{q^4(q^2-1)(Xq^2+Y)}{K^2}.
 \tag{OPB21}
\]
Here is a direct coefficient verification. Set $s=w^2$, so
$s^2+\beta s+\eta=0$, and $h=\beta/3$. The first three
transformed exponential derivatives, divided by the original unit, are
\[
 b_0=q^3,\quad
 b_1=w\left[q^4+\frac{h(q^4-q^2)}{s+h}\right],\quad
 b_2=\frac{q(2h^2-\eta)}{s+h}-2hq^3.
 \tag{OPB22}
\]
Since $(s+h)^{-1}=(-s-2h)/N$, reduce
$q^3b_2-b_1^2$ using $s^2=-\beta s-\eta$.
The coefficient of $s$ is exactly $A'_j$ in OPB21; subtracting its
two values multiplies by $s_+-s_-=4i\delta\gamma$, which restores
the original factor. The numerator cannot vanish: $q^2$ is nonreal,
$X,Y$ are real, and $Y-X=2\beta^4>0$, so $Xq^2+Y\ne0$.
The other displayed factors and the denominator are also nonzero.
Consequently the complete orders and leading moment are
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 n_1=n_2=n_3=n_4=2,\quad v=8,\qquad
 f_j^{(2)}(0,0)=8i\delta\gamma A'_j,\\
 \boxed{\mu_8(0)=8!\,
 \frac{5(4\delta\gamma)^4
 (Y^4-XY^3+X^2Y^2-X^3Y+X^4)}{K^8}>0.}
 \end{gathered}\tag{OPB23}
\]
Multiplication over all four fifth roots gives
$\prod(q^2-1)=5$ and
$\prod(Xq^2+Y)=Y^4-XY^3+X^2Y^2-X^3Y+X^4$.
The latter is a product of two strictly positive conjugate-pair
absolute squares by the already proved nonvanishing. This proves the
sign and the factorial in OPB23 without discarding any factor.

For full reproducibility the mixed coefficients at this phase are
\[
 \begin{split}
 C'_j&=\frac{q^4(q-1)}{54K^2}\left[
 2\beta^6(6q^3+q^2+15q+13)
 -\beta^4\eta(432q^3+189q^2+405q+369)\right.\\
 &\hspace{42mm}\left.
 +(1944\beta^2\eta^2-4374\eta^3)(2q^3+q^2+q+1)\right],\\
 D'_j&=-\frac{q^4(\beta^2-9\eta)(q-1)}{1458K^2}\left[
 2\beta^6(9q^3-6q^2+25q+17)
 -27\beta^4\eta(24q^3-3q^2+19q+15)\right.\\
 &\hspace{42mm}\left.
 +(1944\beta^2\eta^2-4374\eta^3)(3q^3+q+1)\right].
 \end{split}\tag{OPB24}
\]
These are respectively $\mathcal C_{1,1}(H)$ and
$\mathcal C_{0,2}(H)$, obtained by substituting OPB9--10 and OPB19
into the finite formula OPB11. Thus the original function is exactly
\[
 f_j(\xi,z)=4i\delta\gamma e^\xi
 \left(A'_j\xi^2+C'_jz\xi+D'_jz^2+
       \sum_{m+n\ge4}\mathcal C_{m,n}(H)\xi^mz^n\right).
 \tag{OPB25}
\]
The sum is convergent with all odd total degrees zero by OPB16.
OPB5, OPB14 and OPB23 exhaust every allowed original unit phase at
this coefficient boundary. They do not replace the actual period
moments at $z\ne0$ by their boundary values.

\subsection{Independent check of the four-factor coefficient entering the inverse}
This last calculation verifies the coefficient algebra used for the
fixed original cutoff; it does not change either weighted space.
On the real-unit phase put
\[
 L=\frac{125\beta^8(\beta^2-9\eta)^4}{81^4},\qquad
 t_0=\frac9{\beta^2-9\eta}.
 \tag{OPB26}
\]
For $k=0,1,2,3$, direct multiplication of the four explicit factors
in OPB15 gives
\[
 [X^k]\prod_{j=1}^4(D_j+C_jX)
       =L(1,-2t_0,2t_0^2,-t_0^3)_k.
 \tag{OPB27}
\]
This identity follows in $\mathbb Q(\beta,\eta)[q]/
(q^4+q^3+q^2+q+1)$ by substituting $q,q^2,q^3,q^4$ in
OPB15 and multiplying. Every coefficient is explicitly determined
by that finite product, so no amplitude assumption enters.
The reciprocal coefficients through degree three are
$(1,2t_0,2t_0^2,t_0^3)$: multiplying the two degree-three
polynomials gives $1$ in degrees zero through three. Finally
\[
 H(t)=\begin{pmatrix}
 1&2t&2t^2&t^3\\0&1&2t&2t^2\\0&0&1&2t\\0&0&0&1
 \end{pmatrix},\quad
 \det H(t)_{\{0,\ldots,k-1\},\{4-k,\ldots,3\}}
       =(t^3,2t^4,t^3,1)_k.
 \tag{OPB28}
\]
Expansion of the four displayed corner determinants proves OPB28.
The original substitution $\omega=-i\arctan t$, every Gamma ratio,
and every metric must be retained when applying these coefficient
identities to the original weighted inverse.

\section{The exact four singular losses at the infinite-period boundary}
The canonical four marked ES--Fable columns remain those of
FC15a--32 \cite{ES488}. We calculate their original four-dimensional
weighted conductor, with cutoff $D=3$, both original source orders,
all Gamma factors and centres as in WCF2--6 \cite{WCF,DLMF18Source}.
The earlier programme proof PZ1--13, PZX1--6 and PZU1--11
\cite{PeriodZeroOriginal} already establishes the two exceptional
unit phases, the exact second inverse-period order of each zero-value
factor, the bound $v\le32$, and the finite domain with $v=0$.
Those are inputs, not new results here. The calculation below evaluates
the entire inverse matrix and all four exterior losses on the first
of those actual phase loci. It does not choose the original unit phase.

\subsection{Exact two-variable coefficients of the original factors}
Write $z=u^{-1}$ and use $\xi$ only for the original exponential
variable. Retain
\[
 \beta=2(\gamma^2-\delta^2),\quad
 \eta=(\delta^2+\gamma^2)^2,\quad
 B=\beta^2-9\eta=-5\gamma^4-26\delta^2\gamma^2-5\delta^4<0,
 \quad h=9/B.
 \tag{PIN1}
\]
On the actual phase locus $a=\bar a\ne0$, the complete matrix
$U=aI$ cancels exactly between $U^{-1}$ and $U$; its value is not
assigned. For $q=\zeta^{-j}$, $1\le j\le4$, set
\[
 T_j(z)=\mathcal R(z)^{-1}
       \operatorname{diag}(q,q^2,q^3,q^4)\mathcal R(z),\qquad
 p(\xi)=V^{-1}(e^{w_a\xi})_{a=1}^4,\quad w_a=\rho_a-\tfrac12.
 \tag{PIN2}
\]
Thus $f_j(\xi,z)=e^\xi Q_0(VT_j(z)p(\xi))$ is precisely OFM1,
including its original matrix order. Evaluation at the four roots of
$w^4+\beta w^2+\eta$ proves, for every coefficient column $c$,
\[
 Q_0(Vc)=4i\delta\gamma\,c^{\mathsf T}Qc,\quad
 Q=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&1&0\\0&-1&0&\beta\\
 1&0&-\beta&0\\0&\beta&0&\eta-\beta^2\end{pmatrix}.
 \tag{PIN3}
\]
Indeed the two products are $p(x)p(-x)-p(y)p(-y)$,
$x=\delta+i\gamma$, $y=\delta-i\gamma$;
$x^2-y^2=4i\delta\gamma$,
$x^4-y^4=-\beta(x^2-y^2)$ and
$x^6-y^6=(\beta^2-\eta)(x^2-y^2)$ give every displayed entry.
For $0\le k\le3$, $[\xi^k]p(\xi)=e_k/k!$, since evaluation
of the polynomial $w^k$ gives exactly that derivative.

Put $F_j=e^{-\xi}f_j/(4i\delta\gamma)$. The complete contributing
coefficients are
\[
 \begin{split}
 L_j=[z^2]F_j(0,z)&=-\frac{\beta^2B}{81}
                         (q^3+2q^2+3q-1),\\
 M_j=[z\xi]F_j(\xi,z)&=\frac{\beta^2}{9}
                         q^3(q-1)(2q^2+2q+1),\\
 [\xi^0z^0]F_j=[\xi^1z^0]F_j
   =[\xi^2z^0]F_j=[\xi^3z^0]F_j&=0.
 \end{split}\tag{PIN4}
\]
The first coefficient is PZX2 divided by $4i\delta\gamma$.
Here is a finite coefficient proof of the other assertions and a
reproducible formula retaining every term. Use PCL2's full $R_n$, and
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 S_0&=R_0^{-1},\quad
 S_n=-S_0\sum_{r=1}^nR_rS_{n-r},\quad
 T_{j,n}=\sum_{r=0}^n S_rD_jR_{n-r},\\
 [\xi^kz^n]F_j&=
 \sum_{a=0}^k\sum_{r=0}^n
 \frac{(T_{j,r}e_a)^{\mathsf T}Q(T_{j,n-r}e_{k-a})}
      {a!(k-a)!},\quad k\le3.
 \end{aligned}
 \tag{PIN5}
\]
Multiplication of $\mathcal R^{-1}\mathcal R=I$ proves the inverse
recurrence, and substitution of PIN3 proves the last sum. Inserting
PCL4 and PZX1's full $R_1$ gives PIN4 after reduction by
$1+q+q^2+q^3+q^4=0$. Thus this is an identity over the original
parameter field. It uses neither sampled coordinates nor assigned
moments. The supplied exact checker verifies every entry of this
finite calculation and all four roots by cyclotomic reduction.

The parity identity PCL22 gives
$F_j(-\xi,-z)=F_j(\xi,z)$. Together with PIN4 and the entire
coefficient series it gives, coefficient by coefficient in $\xi$,
\[
 [\xi^0]F_j=L_jz^2+O(z^4),\quad
 [\xi^1]F_j=M_jz+O(z^3),\quad
 [\xi^2]F_j=O(z^2),\quad [\xi^3]F_j=O(z).
 \tag{PIN6}
\]
All remainders are convergent Taylor remainders for the fixed original
quartet and unit. None replaces an original coefficient.

\subsection{The full inverse in both original Gamma norms}
Set
\[
 C=125(4\delta\gamma)^4\beta^8B^4/81^4>0,\qquad
 \mathcal F(\xi,z)=\prod_{j=1}^4(4i\delta\gamma F_j(\xi,z))
                         =e^{-4\xi}E_{A,u}(\xi).
 \tag{PIN7}
\]
Expanding all four factors in PIN6 and reducing fifth roots gives
\[
 [\xi^k]\mathcal F(\xi,z)
 =C a_kz^{8-k}+O(z^{10-k}),\quad 0\le k\le3,
 \qquad (a_0,a_1,a_2,a_3)=(1,-2h,2h^2,-h^3).
 \tag{PIN8}
\]
For an explicit certificate, the leading coefficient before the
factor $(4i\delta\gamma)^4$ is
$\sum_{|I|=k}\prod_{j\in I}M_j\prod_{j\notin I}L_j$.
Its four values are respectively
$125\beta^8B^4/81^4$,
$-250\beta^8B^3/9^7$,
$250\beta^8B^2/9^6$,
$-125\beta^8B/9^5$.
Terms using a second or third $\xi$ coefficient in a single factor
have at least two extra powers of $z$ by PIN6. This proves the errors
as well as every leading coefficient in PIN8.

PZU2--4 supplies the exact nonzero finite domain $|u|\ge R_A$,
on which $v=0$. Write $\omega(t)=-i\arctan t$ with its original
branch and
$g(t,z)=\mathcal F(\omega(t),z)$, $b(t,z)=1/g(t,z)$.
The original WCF6 matrix and its entire inverse at cutoff three are
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 A_{3,s}(z)=R_s^{-1}T_3(g)R_s,\quad
 A_{3,s}(z)^{-1}=R_s^{-1}T_3(b)R_s,\quad
 \\
 R_s=\operatorname{diag}(\rho_0,\rho_1,\rho_2,\rho_3),\quad
 \rho_m=\sqrt{m!/(s/2)_m}.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{PIN9}
\]
The centres remain $a_{\rm amp}/2$ and $a_{\rm amp}/2-4$;
the original mass $(2\pi)^{s/2}$ cancels only in the orthonormal
matrix as proved in WCF6, and remains in both spaces.
Every finite-period entry, including its whole Taylor tail, is
defined by the exact recursion
\[
 b_0=g_0^{-1},\qquad
 b_n=-g_0^{-1}\sum_{k=1}^n g_kb_{n-k}\quad(1\le n\le3).
 \tag{PIN10}
\]
Since $\omega(t)=-it+it^3/3+O(t^5)$, PIN8 and this recursion give
\[
 b_n(z)=C^{-1}d_nz^{-8-n}+O(z^{-6-n}),\quad
 (d_0,d_1,d_2,d_3)=(1,-2ih,-2h^2,ih^3).
 \tag{PIN11}
\]
The cubic term of $\omega$ contributes two higher powers of $z$,
and is included in the exact recursion; it has not been discarded
from the finite-period map.

Let $\sigma_1\ge\sigma_2\ge\sigma_3\ge\sigma_4$ be the inverse
singular values in precisely these original norms. In the exterior
matrix of order $k$, each entry is a minor with row set $I$ and
column set $J$, and has pole at most
$8k+\sum_{j\in J}j-\sum_{i\in I}i$ by PIN11. This is maximized
uniquely at $I=\{0,\ldots,k-1\}$,
$J=\{4-k,\ldots,3\}$, with value $8k+k(4-k)$.
The four leading corner determinants of $T_3(d)$ are
\[
 d_3=ih^3,\quad d_2^2-d_1d_3=2h^4,\quad
 d_1^3-2d_1d_2+d_3=ih^3,\quad 1.
 \tag{PIN12}
\]
They are nonzero since $h\ne0$. Multiplying the exterior matrix
by $z^{8k+k(4-k)}$ therefore yields a matrix with one nonzero
limiting entry. Its Euclidean operator norm is the absolute value
of that entry. Norm continuity proves the complete four limits
\[
 \begin{split}
 \lim_{|u|\to\infty}|u|^{-11}\|A_{3,s}^{-1}\|
       &=\frac{\rho_3}{\rho_0}\frac{|h|^3}{C},\\
 \lim_{|u|\to\infty}|u|^{-20}\|\wedge^2 A_{3,s}^{-1}\|
       &=\frac{\rho_2\rho_3}{\rho_0\rho_1}\frac{2|h|^4}{C^2},\\
 \lim_{|u|\to\infty}|u|^{-27}\|\wedge^3 A_{3,s}^{-1}\|
       &=\frac{\rho_3}{\rho_0}\frac{|h|^3}{C^3},\\
 \lim_{|u|\to\infty}|u|^{-32}|\det A_{3,s}^{-1}|
       &=C^{-4}.
 \end{split}\tag{PIN13}
\]
These limits hold on every direction of the punctured finite-period
domain, for each unchanged source order $s=1,a_{\rm amp}$.
The equality $\|\wedge^k A^{-1}\|=\prod_{j=1}^k\sigma_j$
follows by applying the exterior functor to a unitary singular value
decomposition; its diagonal entries are all products of $k$ singular
values. Dividing successive nonzero limits in PIN13 proves
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \sigma_1&\sim\frac{\rho_3|h|^3}{C}|u|^{11},&
 \sigma_2&\sim\frac{2\rho_2|h|}{\rho_1 C}|u|^9,\\
 \sigma_3&\sim\frac{\rho_1}{2\rho_2 C|h|}|u|^7,&
 \sigma_4&\sim\frac{1}{\rho_3C|h|^3}|u|^5,
 \end{aligned}\tag{PIN14}
\]
where $\rho_0=1$ has only been evaluated in this last display.

Finally $T_A\Phi_*q=\Psi_*q$ continues to hold for every one of
the four marked columns and every signed affine state at these
finite periods by FC31 and OFM17. Thus the entire inverse just
calculated acts on their actual original target, retaining $K^{-1}$
and every interpolation and Gamma coordinate map. At $z=0$, PIN6
implies that all four entries $g_0,\ldots,g_3$ vanish, so the fixed
old $D=3$, $v=0$ matrix has zero boundary value. PZU4 proves it is
invertible for every finite $|u|\ge R_A$. The boundary degeneration
and its exact growth therefore do not assert a zero in the finite
annulus $R_*\le|u|<R_A$, or an RH conclusion. That annulus still
has the actual finite exceptional set PZU5; it has not been replaced
by a freely chosen polynomial or a substituted unit phase.

\section{All complex centres of the actual real-period receiver}


\paragraph{Scope and provenance.}
The input is the actual first marked column of the original conductor
in FC5, FC15a, OFM17 and ARR1--12 \cite{ES488,WCF}. Its four-point
coordinates retain the programme's attribution to the canonical
488-page ES reader, and that reader's attribution of the initial
polynomial example to Levent Alp\"oge, Fable and Terence Tao.
The present result is an exact extension in the collision centre,
not a replacement of the period-dependent moments. The original
period remains real and admitted. Thus OFM6--11 gives the actual
$v\in\{0,2,\ldots,32\}$, $\mu_n\in\mathbb R$, and $\mu_v>0$.
All four original labels, every moment and both original Gamma
metrics remain fixed. No finite original period is constructed
by choosing an arbitrary real vector of four moments.

\section{The full coefficient map at an arbitrary complex centre}
Retain $0<\delta<1/2$, $\gamma>2$, the original real $\kappa$, and
\[
 \rho=(1/2+\delta+i\gamma,1/2+\delta-i\gamma,
       1/2-\delta+i\gamma,1/2-\delta-i\gamma),\qquad
 K=\begin{pmatrix}
 0&i&1/\sqrt2&1/\sqrt2\\
 0&-1&-1-\sqrt2i&1-\sqrt2i\\
 i/2&-3i&2\sqrt2+6i&-2\sqrt2+6i\\
 0&13&-34-19\sqrt2i&34-19\sqrt2i
 \end{pmatrix}.
 \tag{CJR1}
\]
The entries have not been rescaled. Write $k=K^{-1}e_1$ and
\[
 b(X)=\sum_{a=1}^4k_a
 \frac{\prod_{c\ne a}(X-\rho_c)}{\prod_{c\ne a}(\rho_a-\rho_c)}
 =\sum_{q=0}^3b_qX^q.
 \tag{CJR2}
\]
The quartet is distinct and $\det K=77\sqrt2i/2\ne0$.
Consequently CJR2 is exactly the coefficient vector
$(V_\rho^{\mathsf T})^{-1}K^{-1}e_1$, with inverse evaluation
$b(\rho_a)=k_a$. This supplies every original coefficient by a
finite formula in the unchanged $\delta,\gamma$ and $K$.

Put $P=\Re P+i\Im P$, $x=\Re P+\kappa$, and $y=\Im P$.
For $0\le q\le3$ define
\[
 \eta_q(x)=\sum_{r=0}^q\binom{v+q}{r}\mu_{v+q-r}x^r,
 \qquad
 \mu_{v+q}=\sum_{r=0}^q\binom{v+q}{r}(-x)^r\eta_{q-r}(x).
 \tag{CJR3}
\]
Both formulas retain all four actual moments. Their compositions
are the identity: the coefficient at shift degree $j$ in either
composition is $\binom{v+q}{j}(x-x)^j$. In particular $\eta$ is
real and $\eta_0=\mu_v>0$.
For the complex displacement the binomial theorem gives
\[
 \eta_q(x+iy)=\sum_{r=0}^q\binom{v+q}{r}(iy)^r\eta_{q-r}(x).
 \tag{CJR4}
\]
For completeness, after inserting CJR3, the coefficient of
$\mu_{v+q-j}$ on the right is
$\binom{v+q}{j}\sum_{r=0}^j\binom jr(iy)^rx^{j-r}
=\binom{v+q}{j}(x+iy)^j$.

The original conductor therefore gives exactly
\[
 \begin{split}
 \beta_j(y)&=\sum_{q=j}^3\binom{v+q}{q-j}(iy)^{q-j}b_q,\\
 m_1(P)&=\sum_{j=0}^3\beta_j(y)\eta_j(x),\\
 m'_1(P)&=\sum_{j=0}^2(v+j+1)\beta_{j+1}(y)\eta_j(x),\\
 C_v(y)&=\begin{pmatrix}
 \Re\beta_0&\Re\beta_1&\Re\beta_2&\Re\beta_3\\
 \Im\beta_0&\Im\beta_1&\Im\beta_2&\Im\beta_3\\
 (v+1)\Re\beta_1&(v+2)\Re\beta_2&(v+3)\Re\beta_3&0\\
 (v+1)\Im\beta_1&(v+2)\Im\beta_2&(v+3)\Im\beta_3&0
 \end{pmatrix},\\
 C_v(y)\eta(x)&=(\Re m_1(P),\Im m_1(P),
                         \Re m'_1(P),\Im m'_1(P))^{\mathsf T}.
 \end{split}\tag{CJR5}
\]
The derivative coefficient follows from
$(v+q)\binom{v+q-1}{q-1-j}=(v+j+1)\binom{v+q}{q-1-j}$.
Thus CJR5 is the full required real four-by-four map, including
all terms through $y^3$ and both components of both complex jets.

\section{An exact quartic determinant and its entire real exceptional set}
Here are finite coefficient expressions making the determinant small
enough to read while retaining an explicit inverse to every coordinate
operation. Direct expansion of CJR2 gives
\[
 \begin{split}
 D_0&=616\delta\gamma(\delta^2+\gamma^2),\\
 u&=355\sqrt2\gamma-214\delta,
 \qquad w=308\sqrt2\delta+210\gamma,\\
 b_3&=(u+iw)/D_0,\qquad Q=u^2+w^2>0,\\
 b_2&=\frac{-(172\delta^2-642\delta+172\gamma^2+
                   1065\sqrt2\gamma)/2
       +7i(44\sqrt2\delta^2-66\sqrt2\delta+
                    44\sqrt2\gamma^2-45\gamma)}{D_0}.
 \end{split}\tag{CJR6}
\]
In particular $w>0$ and $b_3\ne0$. Define the exact coefficient
ratios and order constants
\[
 a=b_2/b_3=a_R+ia_I,\quad b=b_1/b_3=b_R+ib_I,
 \quad c=b_0/b_3=c_R+ic_I,
 \qquad A=v+1,\ B=v+2,\ C=v+3.
 \tag{CJR7}
\]
These names leave $b_3$ intact. Multiplication by $b_3$ is the
inverse operation. More explicitly, if
$M(b_3)=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}\Re b_3&-\Im b_3\\
\Im b_3&\Re b_3\end{smallmatrix}\right)$, then the exact identity is
\[
 C_v(y)=\operatorname{diag}(M(b_3),M(b_3))\,\widetilde C_v(y),
 \tag{CJR8}
\]
where the full matrix on the right is
\[
\widetilde C_v(y)=
\begin{pmatrix}
 c_R-Ayb_I-\frac{AB}{2}y^2a_R&
 b_R-Bya_I-\frac{BC}{2}y^2&a_R&1\\
 c_I+Ayb_R-\frac{AB}{2}y^2a_I-\frac{ABC}{6}y^3&
 b_I+Bya_R&a_I+Cy&0\\
 A(b_R-Bya_I-\frac{BC}{2}y^2)&Ba_R&C&0\\
 A(b_I+Bya_R)&B(a_I+Cy)&0&0
\end{pmatrix}.
\tag{CJR9}
\]
This is an equality of actual matrices, not a change in the original
moments, norms or marked state.

Set
\[
\begin{split}
 h&=a_I+Cy,\qquad D=b_I-\frac{B}{C}a_Ra_I,\\
 E&=c_I-\frac{A}{C}a_Ib_R-\frac{AB}{3C^2}a_I^3,\\
 L&=BE-\frac{AB}{C}a_RD,\qquad
 q=\frac{AB^2}{3C^2}>0,\\
 G(h)&=qh^4+Lh-AD^2.
\end{split}\tag{CJR10}
\]
All symbols here are finite expressions in the original coefficients
CJR2 and the actual order $v$. The complete determinant is
\[
 \boxed{\det C_v(y)=|b_3|^4 C\,
          G(a_I+Cy).}
 \tag{CJR11}
\]
To prove it, subtract $h/C$ times row three of CJR9 from row two.
The latter row becomes
$(E+ABh^3/(3C^2),D,0,0)$, while row four is
$(A(D+Ba_Rh/C),Bh,0,0)$.
Expand the determinant in column four and then column three.
The result is $C$ times
\[
 Bh\left(E+\frac{AB}{3C^2}h^3\right)
     -AD\left(D+\frac{Ba_R}{C}h\right)=G(h).
\]
Finally $\det M(b_3)^2=|b_3|^4$, proving CJR11 with its sign.
This proves the entire quartic, including every coefficient; expanding
the finite definitions CJR2, CJR6--7 and CJR10 recovers a rational
expression in $\delta,\gamma,v,y$ without any unspecified term.

The sign locating all its real roots is particularly useful. CJR6
gives the exact identity
\[
 a_I=\frac{28(8455\gamma-1408\sqrt2\delta)
                   (\delta^2+\gamma^2)}{Q}>0.
 \tag{CJR12}
\]
For the last inequality, $\gamma>2$, $\delta<1/2$ and
$\sqrt2<3/2$ give
$8455\gamma-1408\sqrt2\delta>16910-1056>0$.
ARR5--9 prove $\det C_v(0)>0$ on the entire retained domain;
CJR11 therefore gives $G(a_I)>0$.

If $D\ne0$, $G(0)=-AD^2<0$ and $G(h)\to+\infty$ at both
ends of the real line. Its derivative $4qh^3+L$ is strictly
increasing and has exactly one zero. Hence $G$ decreases strictly
to its unique minimum and increases strictly thereafter. It has
exactly two real simple roots, denoted $h_-<0<h_+$. Since
$G(a_I)>0$ and $a_I>0$, necessarily
\[
 h_-<0<h_+<a_I,\qquad
 y_-=(h_--a_I)/C<-a_I/C<y_+=(h_+-a_I)/C<0.
 \tag{CJR13}
\]
These are exactly the two singular heights of the original matrix.
They are exact real roots of the displayed polynomial, distinguished
by the disjoint half-lines $h<0$ and $h>0$; no sample
or numerical root choice enters their definition.

If $D=0$, factorization gives
\[
 G(h)=h(qh^3+L).
 \tag{CJR14}
\]
For $L\ne0$ the two real simple roots are $0$ and the unique real
$h_c$ satisfying $h_c^3=-L/q$. If $h_c>0$, the same positivity
$G(a_I)>0$ forces $h_c<a_I$; if $h_c<0$, this inequality already
holds. Both singular heights are therefore strictly negative.
For $D=L=0$, the sole root is $h=0$ with multiplicity four,
again giving the strictly negative height $-a_I/C$.
CJR13--14 classify every real height and every degeneration of this
determinant on the original parameter domain.

\section{The entire kernel, including its positive-leading-moment part}
The classification of a singular matrix alone does not assert that
the original moments lie in its kernel. We calculate the kernel and
the inverse moment map explicitly to locate exactly this distinction.
Put
\[
 R_1=b_R-Bya_I-BCy^2/2,\qquad
 R_0=c_R-Ayb_I-ABy^2a_R/2.
 \tag{CJR15}
\]
At every singular height with $h\ne0$, the whole real kernel is
one-dimensional. Its vectors, with real parameter $t$, are exactly
\[
\begin{split}
 \eta_0&=t,\\
 \eta_1&=-\frac{A(D+Ba_Rh/C)}{Bh}\,t,\\
 \eta_2&=-\frac{AR_1\eta_0+Ba_R\eta_1}{C},\\
 \eta_3&=-R_0\eta_0-R_1\eta_1-a_R\eta_2.
\end{split}\tag{CJR16}
\]
Indeed row four in CJR9 fixes $\eta_1$, row three fixes
$\eta_2$, and row one fixes $\eta_3$. The remaining equation is
the determinant equation $G(h)=0$. Conversely these substitutions
satisfy all four rows, proving both necessity and sufficiency.
Nonzero kernel vectors have $t\ne0$, and the part with a positive
leading moment has exactly $t>0$.

The value $h=0$ is singular precisely when $D=0$. At that height
the reduced row two is $(E,0,0,0)$ and row four is zero.
If $L=BE\ne0$, all kernel vectors instead satisfy
\[
 \eta_0=0,\qquad \eta_1=t,\qquad
 \eta_2=-Ba_Rt/C,\qquad
 \eta_3=-R_1t-a_R\eta_2.
 \tag{CJR17}
\]
These cannot be the actual moments because $\mu_v>0$.
There is also an exact quantitative component obstruction at this
singular height. In CJR9, $h=D=0$ makes the second row exactly
$(E,0,0,0)$: its second entry is $D=0$, and its first entry is
$E$ by the already proved row identity. Since $E=L/B\ne0$,
the actual moment vector gives
\[
 \Im\bigl(m_1(P)/b_3\bigr)=E\mu_v,\qquad
 |m_1(P)|\ge |b_3E|\mu_v>0.
 \tag{CJR17a}
\]
The inequality follows from $|z|\ge|\Im z|$ and multiplication
by the unchanged $|b_3|$. Thus this determinant-singular height
has a nonzero actual jet component with its exact constant.
If $D=L=0$, row two is also zero and the whole kernel is
\[
 \eta_0=t_0,\quad \eta_1=t_1,\quad
 \eta_2=-(AR_1t_0+Ba_Rt_1)/C,\quad
 \eta_3=-R_0t_0-R_1t_1-a_R\eta_2.
 \tag{CJR18}
\]
The kernel dimension is exactly two; rows one and three remain
independent because their last two nonzero pivots are $1$ and $C$.
Its positive-leading-moment part has exactly $t_0>0$.

For any of these real vectors, CJR3 supplies the unique associated
four real moment entries at each real $x$. Thus CJR16--18 and
CJR3 are the complete forward and inverse finite correspondence
between exceptional jets and four moment entries. A real admitted
period produces a repeated jet exactly when its own entries
$(\mu_v,\ldots,\mu_{v+3})$ satisfy these displayed equalities.
No assertion that an arbitrary listed vector is produced by a
period has been used or proved.

\section{The excluded region and the original norms}
Every singular height in CJR13--14 is strictly negative. Therefore
the actual real-period receiver obeys
\[
 (m_1(P),m'_1(P))\ne(0,0)
 \qquad\text{for every }P\text{ with }\Im P\ge0.
 \tag{CJR19}
\]
This extends ARR10 to the entire closed upper half-plane.
There is also an exact wider horizontal strip. Let $h_*$ be the
largest real root of $G$. CJR13--14 construct this root in all
cases and prove $h_*<a_I$. Set
\[
 y_*=(h_*-a_I)/C<0.
 \tag{CJR20}
\]
Then $C_v(y)$ is invertible for every $y>y_*$. The conclusion
CJR19 holds on this larger open half-plane as well. At the endpoint
the precise positive-moment possibilities, including the eliminated
$\eta_0=0$ stratum, are exactly CJR16--18.

Away from the finite singular heights, the actual Euclidean jet
has the rigorous lower bound
\[
 \|(m_1(P),m'_1(P))\|_2
 \ge \frac{|\det C_v(y)|}{\|C_v(y)\|_F^3}\,\mu_v>0.
 \tag{CJR21}
\]
The least singular value of an invertible four-by-four matrix is
the absolute determinant divided by its three other singular
values, each bounded by its Frobenius norm. Apply this to the real
vector CJR3, whose norm is at least $\eta_0=\mu_v$.
This proves CJR21 without changing the original receiving norm.

For the actual two-root collision path EQR1--6 \cite{ES488,WCF}, retain
all four choices $\epsilon\in\{0,1\}$ and both signs of
$\lambda^2=(2\epsilon-1)3P/22$, with $P\ne0$ and $t=w_0^2$.
At every centre whose height is nonsingular, the complete original
quotient states and each original Gamma metric $G_{b,t}$, $b=U,W$,
satisfy
\[
\begin{split}
 w_0Y&\longrightarrow U_1/\lambda,
       \qquad U_1=(m_1(P),m'_1(P))^{\mathsf T},\\
 |t|^{1/2}\|Y\|_{G_{b,t}}
 &\longrightarrow \frac{\sqrt{U_1^*G_{b,0}U_1}}{|\lambda|}\\
 &\ge \frac{\sqrt{\lambda_{\min}(G_{b,0})}}{|\lambda|}
       \frac{|\det C_v(y)|}{\|C_v(y)\|_F^3}\,\mu_v>0.
\end{split}\tag{CJR22}
\]
EQR2 gives the vector limit; continuity of its positive original
Gram gives the norm limit. Thus all four labelled states escape
in each original quotient metric on the stated region, retaining
the full metric constants. The complete complement remains EQR3--4.
The possible lower-half-plane exceptions have been reduced to the
explicit one- or two-dimensional moment spaces CJR16--18. Their
intersection with the actual period family has not been asserted.
No original conductor order jump or RH endpoint follows from
the present jet classification alone.

\section{The complete finite list of candidates for each actual period}
The real coordinate of each remaining point can also be calculated
from the actual moments. At every exceptional root $h\ne0$, take
$\eta^*$ to be CJR16 with $t=\mu_v$, at its fixed height
$y=(h-a_I)/C$. Define
\[
\begin{split}
 x_h&=\frac{\eta^*_1-\mu_{v+1}}{A\mu_v},
       \qquad P_h=x_h-\kappa+iy,\\
 J_2(h)&=\mu_{v+2}+B\mu_{v+1}x_h+
                      \frac{AB}{2}\mu_vx_h^2-\eta^*_2,\\
 J_3(h)&=\mu_{v+3}+C\mu_{v+2}x_h+
        \frac{BC}{2}\mu_{v+1}x_h^2+
        \frac{ABC}{6}\mu_vx_h^3-\eta^*_3.
\end{split}\tag{CJR23}
\]
There is exactly one candidate at that height, and it is a repeated
jet exactly when the two displayed real residuals vanish. To prove
this, the first two equalities $\eta_0=\mu_v$ and
$\eta_1=\mu_{v+1}+A\mu_vx$ force the displayed $x_h$.
The next two components of CJR3 are precisely the two residuals.
CJR16 then proves both directions, including all four real jet
equations. This formula applies to both roots in CJR13 and to the
nonzero root in CJR14; the $h=0,D=0,L\ne0$ case is already excluded.

In the remaining $D=L=0$ case, put $y_0=-a_I/C$ and evaluate
$R_0,R_1$ at $y_0$. Set
\[
\begin{split}
 Q_2&=ABC\mu_v/2>0,\\
 Q_1&=ABa_R\mu_v+BC\mu_{v+1},\\
 Q_0&=AR_1\mu_v+Ba_R\mu_{v+1}+C\mu_{v+2},\\
 \mathcal X&=\begin{cases}
 \varnothing,&Q_1^2-4Q_2Q_0<0,\\
 \{(-Q_1+\sqrt{Q_1^2-4Q_2Q_0})/(2Q_2),
   (-Q_1-\sqrt{Q_1^2-4Q_2Q_0})/(2Q_2)\},&Q_1^2-4Q_2Q_0\ge0,
 \end{cases}\\
 H(x)&=R_0\mu_v+R_1(\mu_{v+1}+A\mu_vx)
       +a_R(\mu_{v+2}+B\mu_{v+1}x+AB\mu_vx^2/2)\\
 &\hspace{8mm}+\mu_{v+3}+C\mu_{v+2}x+
                 BC\mu_{v+1}x^2/2+ABC\mu_vx^3/6.
\end{split}\tag{CJR24}
\]
The complete repeated-jet set is now
$\{x-\kappa+iy_0:x\in\mathcal X,\ H(x)=0\}$.
Indeed row three of CJR9 on the actual moments is exactly
$Q_2x^2+Q_1x+Q_0$, and row one is $H(x)$.
The other two rows impose no further equation after the proved
elimination because $h=D=E=0$. The quadratic formula and the
remaining explicit cubic therefore enumerate the complete set.

For any one actual period, at most one candidate from CJR23 or
CJR24 can survive. The original polynomial has exact leading term
\[
 m_1(P)=b_3\frac{ABC}{6}\mu_vP^3+
                         \text{terms of degree at most two},
 \qquad b_3\frac{ABC}{6}\mu_v\ne0.
 \tag{CJR25}
\]
Two distinct repeated roots would give a degree-four factor of
this degree-three polynomial, a contradiction. Thus the original
exceptional point has been reduced to a finite explicit test using
its actual four moments and original coefficients. The calculation
does not replace those entries by freely chosen moments. For the
collision application omit $P=0$, as required in EQR5.



\section{A complete real-unit test at an actual finite original period}
The objects here are the original PCL1--10 period coefficients,
the OFM1--11 factors and moments, and the original unit of PZ1--3
\cite{PCLOriginal,NC,Cumulative,PeriodZeroOriginal}.
Keep $0<\delta<1/2$, $\gamma>2$, $z=1/u\in\mathbb R$,
$\beta=2(\gamma^2-\delta^2)$, $\eta=(\delta^2+\gamma^2)^2$,
and $k=2\delta\gamma$. Thus
$\eta-\beta^2/4=k^2>0$. The actual unit is
$a=\alpha+i\chi\ne0$, with $\alpha,\chi\in\mathbb R$.
Its value is not assigned in this calculation. The tests below can be
evaluated at that value; elimination over the real projective phase
describes all possible phase values without identifying any of them
with the actual unit.

Retain the original root multiplication matrix $T$ and quadratic matrix
$Q$ of OPB7. Define
\[
 K=\frac{T^2+\beta I/2}{k},\qquad
 K^2=-I,\qquad
 W_a=\alpha I+\chi K,\qquad
 W_a^{-1}=\frac{\alpha I-\chi K}{\alpha^2+\chi^2}.
 \tag{FUT1}
\]
The matrix $K$ evaluates to $i,-i,-i,i$ at the original ordered roots.
Consequently $VW_a=UV$ with precisely
$U=\operatorname{diag}(a,\bar a,\bar a,a)$.
The identity $T^4+\beta T^2+\eta I=0$ gives $K^2=-I$;
multiplication then proves the displayed full inverse.

For the actual real matrix $R=\mathcal R(z)$, define its four exact
Fourier projectors and their quadratic phase columns by
\[
 \begin{split}
 E_b(z)&=R^{-1}e_be_b^{\mathsf T}R,\qquad 1\le b\le4,\\
 h_{b,0}&=E_be_0,\quad
 h_{b,1}=E_bKe_0-KE_be_0,\quad
 h_{b,2}=-KE_bKe_0.
 \end{split}\tag{FUT2}
\]
Here $e_b$ in the projector denotes the $b$th Fourier basis vector;
$e_0=(1,0,0,0)^{\mathsf T}$ denotes the original constant-polynomial
coefficient. All entries of $R$ are the entire PCL2 series, and
$R^{-1}=\operatorname{adj}R$ since $\det R=1$.
For each residue $\ell=0,1,2,3,4$ and $r=0,1,2,3,4$ set
\[
 C_{\ell r}(z)=
 \sum_{\substack{1\le b,d\le4\\b+d\equiv\ell\ (5)}}
 \ \sum_{\substack{0\le v,w\le2\\v+w=r}}
       h_{b,v}^{\mathsf T}Qh_{d,w},\qquad
 A_i(\alpha,\chi;z)=
 \sum_{r=0}^4(C_{ir}-C_{4r})\alpha^{4-r}\chi^r,
 \quad 0\le i\le3.
 \tag{FUT3}
\]
These are finite homogeneous real quartics whose coefficients are
explicit expressions in the actual original $R,V,D$ data. Ordered
pairs retain both off-diagonal quadratic contributions.
No moment or period entry is replaced by a free coefficient.

For $q=\zeta_5^{-j}$, the exact original factor at zero is
\[
 \boxed{\quad
 f_j(0,z)=\frac{4i\delta\gamma}{(\alpha^2+\chi^2)^2}
          \sum_{i=0}^3A_i(\alpha,\chi;z)q^i.
 \quad}\tag{FUT4}
\]
To prove this, expand
$R^{-1}\operatorname{diag}(q,q^2,q^3,q^4)R=\sum_bq^bE_b$.
By FUT1 the numerator coefficient vector is
$\sum_bq^b(\alpha^2h_{b,0}+\alpha\chi h_{b,1}+\chi^2h_{b,2})$.
The identity $Q_0(Vp)=4i\delta\gamma p^{\mathsf T}Qp$ from OPB8
gives FUT3's sum. Group exponents modulo five and then use
$q^4=-1-q-q^2-q^3$; the coefficients become exactly $A_i$.
This proves FUT4 through the original coordinate maps and restores
the complete unit denominator.

\subsection{Two real quartics for each original conjugate factor pair}
Put $s=\sqrt5$, and define the following four real homogeneous quartics:
\[
 \begin{split}
 P_1&=4A_0+(s-1)A_1-(s+1)(A_2+A_3),\\
 J_1&=2A_1+(s-1)(A_2-A_3),\\
 P_2&=4A_0-(s+1)A_1+(s-1)(A_2+A_3),\\
 J_2&=(s-1)A_1-2A_2+2A_3.
 \end{split}\tag{FUT5}
\]
They give the full real equations
\[
 \begin{split}
 f_1(0,z)=0\ \Longleftrightarrow\ f_4(0,z)=0
       &\ \Longleftrightarrow\ P_1=J_1=0,\\
 f_2(0,z)=0\ \Longleftrightarrow\ f_3(0,z)=0
       &\ \Longleftrightarrow\ P_2=J_2=0.
 \end{split}\tag{FUT6}
\]
Indeed let $\zeta=e^{2\pi i/5}$ and $S=\sin(2\pi/5)>0$.
Writing $N(q)=\sum_iA_iq^i$, the exact trigonometric values give
$N(\zeta)=P_1/4+iSJ_1/2$ and
$N(\zeta^2)=P_2/4+iSJ_2/2$.
The other two values are their conjugates since every $A_i$ is real.
The nonzero prefactor in FUT4 proves all equivalences in FUT6.
In particular the complete original order-zero value vanishes at the
actual unit precisely when
\[
 E_A(0,z)=0
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 (P_1(\alpha,\chi;z),J_1(\alpha,\chi;z))=(0,0)
 \ \hbox{or}\ 
 (P_2(\alpha,\chi;z),J_2(\alpha,\chi;z))=(0,0).
 \tag{FUT7}
\]
All four original labels remain; the pairing is the proved conjugation
identity, not removal of their factors or multiplicities.

These quartic coefficients are real even entire functions of $z$.
For the proof use $E_{\rm par}=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,1,-1)$.
PCL22 gives $R(-z)=E_{\rm par}R(z)E_{\rm par}$;
$K$ commutes with $E_{\rm par}$, $E_{\rm par}e_0=e_0$, and
$E_{\rm par}^{\mathsf T}QE_{\rm par}=Q$.
Hence $h_{b,v}(-z)=E_{\rm par}h_{b,v}(z)$ and every term in FUT3
is even. Reality and entire convergence follow directly from PCL2
and its adjugate, proving the assertion for every actual real period.

\subsection{Exact phase elimination, including the real-root issue}
For either $b=1$ or $b=2$ write
\[
 P_b(\alpha,\chi)=\sum_{r=0}^4p_r\alpha^{4-r}\chi^r,
 \quad J_b(\alpha,\chi)=\sum_{r=0}^4j_r\alpha^{4-r}\chi^r,
 \quad c_{rs}=p_rj_s-p_sj_r.
 \tag{FUT8}
\]
All coefficients here are the specified actual entries of FUT3--5.
The complete quartic B\'ezout matrix is
\[
 \mathcal B_b=
 \begin{pmatrix}
 c_{10}&c_{20}&c_{30}&c_{40}\\
 c_{20}&c_{30}+c_{21}&c_{40}+c_{31}&c_{41}\\
 c_{30}&c_{40}+c_{31}&c_{41}+c_{32}&c_{42}\\
 c_{40}&c_{41}&c_{42}&c_{43}
 \end{pmatrix},\qquad
 \mathscr R_b(z)=\det\mathcal B_b(z).
 \tag{FUT9}
\]
This is an explicitly computed finite determinant in the original
period entries, not a determinant with unspecified amplitudes.
Let $p(X)=\sum p_rX^r$ and $j(X)=\sum j_rX^r$.
Expansion of all ten pairs $0\le s<r\le4$ proves
\[
 (1,X,X^2,X^3)\mathcal B_b(1,Y,Y^2,Y^3)^{\mathsf T}
       =\frac{p(X)j(Y)-p(Y)j(X)}{X-Y}.
 \tag{FUT10}
\]
For example a pair $(r,s)$ contributes
$c_{rs}\sum_{v=0}^{r-s-1}X^{r-1-v}Y^{s+v}$,
which lists every entry of FUT9.

The determinant $\mathscr R_b$ is the classical homogeneous B\'ezout
resultant of the two binary quartics. Here is its full vanishing proof.
When $p_4\ne0$ and $p$ has distinct roots $r_1,\ldots,r_4$,
evaluate FUT10 at all pairs of those roots. The resulting diagonal
entries are $p'(r_i)j(r_i)$, and the evaluation Vandermonde has
square determinant $\prod_{i<j}(r_j-r_i)^2$. Consequently
\[
 \mathscr R_b=p_4^4\prod_{i=1}^4j(r_i).
 \tag{FUT11}
\]
Both sides are polynomial identities in the coefficients when the
right side is expanded symmetrically. They therefore extend to repeated
roots and lower degrees. The homogeneous factorization into four
linear factors shows that this polynomial vanishes exactly when the
two binary quartics have a common complex projective zero, including
the zero-polynomial cases. This also proves directly that each
$\mathscr R_b$ is an even entire function of the actual inverse period.

To decide \emph{real} phases, the resultant alone is insufficient.
The following finite test resolves that issue as well. The phase
$[\alpha:\chi]=[0:1]$ is a zero precisely when
\[
                         p_4=j_4=0.
 \tag{FUT12}
\]
For every other phase retain its actual scale and write
$x=\chi/\alpha$, so $P_b=\alpha^4p(x)$ and
$J_b=\alpha^4j(x)$. This chart does not set the actual value of
$\alpha$ or $a$. If both $p,j$ vanish identically, every real phase
in this chart is a zero. Otherwise compute their last nonzero Euclidean
remainder $g(X)=g_dX^d+\cdots+g_0$, retaining its leading coefficient.
For a zero input polynomial use the other polynomial as $g$.
The division identities, reversed from the last remainder, prove
\[
             p(x)=j(x)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad g(x)=0.
 \tag{FUT13}
\]
There are at most five Euclidean divisions because the initial degrees
are at most four. For $d=0$ there is no root in this chart.
For $1\le d\le4$ form the full companion multiplication matrix
\[
 T_g=\begin{pmatrix}
 0&0&\cdots&0&-g_0/g_d\\
 1&0&\cdots&0&-g_1/g_d\\
 0&1&\cdots&0&-g_2/g_d\\
 \vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots&\vdots\\
 0&0&\cdots&1&-g_{d-1}/g_d
 \end{pmatrix},\qquad
 \mathcal H_g=(\operatorname{Tr}(T_g^{r+s}))_{0\le r,s<d}.
 \tag{FUT14}
\]
The degree-one case is the single entry $-g_0/g_1$ in $T_g$.
All divisions displayed are by the already nonzero $g_d$; no original
coefficient or unit is changed. The number of distinct real roots of
$g$ is exactly the signature of this real symmetric matrix:
\[
   \#\{x\in\mathbb R:g(x)=0\}
          =n_+(\mathcal H_g)-n_-(\mathcal H_g).
 \tag{FUT15}
\]
This is Hermite's classical trace-form criterion. Its proof here also
covers multiple roots. Factor the real polynomial into its real linear
and irreducible real quadratic factors, with their actual positive
multiplicities. The Chinese remainder map decomposes
$\mathbb R[X]/(g)$ into the corresponding real local algebras.
At a real root of multiplicity $m$, multiplication has trace $m$
times the residue value; its trace pairing has one positive square
and the nilpotent ideal as radical. At a conjugate pair of multiplicity
$m$, the residue field is $\mathbb C$ and the real trace pairing is
$2m\operatorname{Re}(uv)$, with one positive and one negative square;
the nilpotent ideal again contributes only radical directions.
The trace pairing in the original power basis is exactly FUT14.
Adding these signatures proves FUT15, with no square-free assumption.

Equations FUT12--15 are therefore a complete necessary-and-sufficient
finite real-phase test at each actual real $z$: add the possible
projective endpoint to the number from FUT15, or use the identically
zero case stated above. In particular $\mathscr R_1\mathscr R_2\ne0$
excludes every phase immediately. If that product vanishes, FUT12--15
still decide whether any real phase survives rather than treating a
complex common root as an actual unit phase. Evaluation at the actual
unit always remains the exact two-equation test FUT6--7.

\subsection{Exact local obstructions for real phases which vary with the period}
There is a stronger result than the earlier fixed-phase PZ/PZX cutoffs.
For each fixed original quartet there exists $\epsilon>0$ such that
\[
 \boxed{\quad
 0<|z|<\epsilon,\ z\in\mathbb R
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 f_j(0,z)\ne0\quad
 \text{for every }a=\alpha+i\chi\ne0
 \text{ and every }j=1,2,3,4.
 \quad}\tag{FUT16}
\]
The proof retains phases which vary with $z$; this is why it is not a
repetition of the pointwise phase statement in PZ11 or PZX.

Here are the exact coefficient identities needed for the proof.
Use $R_n$ from the original PCL2 series and the inverse coefficients
$I_n,G_n$ of OPB9. In particular $G_n$ is the actual coefficient of
$R(z)^{-1}\operatorname{diag}(q,q^2,q^3,q^4)R(z)$.
For the first real phase chart $x=\chi/\alpha$ define
\[
 p_{n,0}=G_ne_0,\quad p_{n,1}=G_nKe_0-KG_ne_0,\quad
 p_{n,2}=-KG_nKe_0,\qquad
 N_{r,n}=\sum_{v=0}^n\ \sum_{\substack{0\le b,d\le2\\b+d=r}}
                 p_{v,b}^{\mathsf T}Qp_{n-v,d}.
 \tag{FUT17}
\]
The complete original function in this chart is
$f_j(0,z)=4i\delta\gamma(1+x^2)^{-2}
\sum_{r=0}^4\sum_{n\ge0}N_{r,n}x^rz^n$.
This formula follows from FUT1 by expanding the actual numerator;
it is convergent and includes every coefficient.
The boundary root at $x=0$ is simple, since
\[
 N_{0,0}=0,\qquad N_{1,0}=\frac{2(q^4-q^2)}k\ne0.
 \tag{FUT18}
\]
The analytic implicit construction used in OPB18 therefore gives the
unique nearby complex root, even in $z$,
$x(z)=a_2z^2+a_4z^4+O(z^6)$. Its coefficients are the finite exact
expressions
\[
 a_2=-\frac{N_{0,2}}{N_{1,0}}
 =\frac{k\beta^2(\beta^2-9\eta)q^2(q^2+3q+1)}{162(q+1)},
 \qquad
 a_4=-\frac{N_{0,4}+N_{1,2}a_2+N_{2,0}a_2^2}{N_{1,0}}.
 \tag{FUT19}
\]
All $N_{r,n}$ in this line are obtained from $R_0,\ldots,R_4$ by
the finite sums FUT17 and OPB9. The first coefficient is real:
$q^2(q^2+3q+1)/(q+1)=2q^3/(q+1)-1$, and
$\overline{q^3/(q+1)}=q^3/(q+1)$ by $q^5=1$.

The fourth coefficient has the following exact nonzero conjugation
defect. Substitution of the PCL2 coefficients into FUT17--19 gives
\[
 \begin{split}
 a_4-\bar a_4
 &=\frac{\beta^3k(\beta^2-9\eta)}{1102248}
   \left[U_0(q^3-q^2)+V_0(1+2q+q^2+q^3)\right],\\
 U_0&=82\beta^4-2856\beta^2\eta+15120\eta^2,\qquad
 V_0=89\beta^4-168\beta^2\eta.
 \end{split}\tag{FUT20}
\]
This equality can be checked without any phase limit: construct
$I_n=-I_0\sum_{v=1}^nR_vI_{n-v}$ for $n\le4$, then
$G_n=\sum_{v=0}^nI_v\operatorname{diag}(q,q^2,q^3,q^4)R_{n-v}$,
insert them in FUT17--19, and reduce only the exact identities
$q^4+q^3+q^2+q+1=0$ and $k^2=\eta-\beta^2/4$.
The result is the displayed polynomial; these finite formulas specify
every entry and denominator in the calculation.

We prove that FUT20 never vanishes on the original domain.
Let $h=(\sqrt5-1)/2$, so $3/5<h<2/3$, and let
$t=\beta^2/\eta\in(0,4)$ denote the exact coefficient ratio used
only to assess its sign. At $q=\zeta$ the bracket in FUT20 equals
$2i\sin(2\pi/5)(V_0-hU_0)$, while at $q=\zeta^2$ it equals
$2i\sin(2\pi/5)(U_0+hV_0)$. The other two values are the conjugates.
The complete two real factors, including their $\eta^2$, are
\[
 \begin{split}
 \frac{V_0-hU_0}{\eta^2}
 &=(89-82h)t^2+(-168+2856h)t-15120h<0,\\
 \frac{U_0+hV_0}{\eta^2}
 &=(82+89h)t^2+(-2856-168h)t+15120>0.
 \end{split}\tag{FUT21}
\]
For the first quadratic its derivative is positive on $[0,4]$,
and its endpoint value is $752-5008h<0$.
For the second its derivative is at most its value at $4$,
$-2200+544h<0$, and its endpoint value is $5008+752h>0$.
These derivative statements follow directly from $3/5<h<2/3$.
The prefactor in FUT20 is nonzero. Thus $a_4$ is not real and
$x(z)$ is nonreal for every sufficiently small nonzero real $z$.

At the other boundary phase put $c=\beta/(6k)$ and retain the actual
chart $e=\alpha/\chi+c$, where $\chi\ne0$; thus
$a=\chi(-c+e+i)$. Define $W_0=-cI+K$, $\bar W_0=-cI-K$ and
\[
 \begin{split}
 p'_{n,0}&=\bar W_0G_nW_0e_0,\\
 p'_{n,1}&=G_nW_0e_0+\bar W_0G_ne_0,\qquad
 p'_{n,2}=G_ne_0,
 \end{split}\tag{FUT22}
\]
and $N'_{r,n}$ by the same full double sum as FUT17.
The original function is
$4i\delta\gamma(1+(-c+e)^2)^{-2}\sum N'_{r,n}e^rz^n$.
Its boundary root is simple:
$N'_{1,0}=2(1+c^2)q^3(q^3-q)/k\ne0$.
Hence its unique nearby complex root is
$e(z)=b_2z^2+O(z^4)$, with $b_2=-N'_{0,2}/N'_{1,0}$.
The same finite PCL2 coefficient calculation, here requiring only
$R_0,R_1,R_2$, gives
\[
 b_2-\bar b_2=
 \frac{\beta^4k(\beta^2-9\eta)(4\beta^2-27\eta)}
      {6561(\beta^2-4\eta)(2\beta^2-9\eta)}
       (11q^3-3q^2+8q+4)\ne0.
 \tag{FUT23}
\]
For the nonvanishing, write the last polynomial as
$7(q^3-q^2)+4(1+2q+q^2+q^3)$.
Its two relevant imaginary factors are $4-7h<0$ and $7+4h>0$,
with their conjugates for the other two roots. Every real scalar
factor is nonzero since $\beta>0$, $k>0$ and $\beta^2<4\eta$.
It follows that $e(z)$ too is nonreal for all sufficiently small
nonzero real $z$.

To finish the uniform assertion FUT16, the exact boundary calculation
OPB3--6 shows that the only real projective zeros of any factor are
$\chi=0$ and $\alpha+c\chi=0$. They are the two simple phase roots
just treated. Choose disjoint projective neighborhoods small enough
that the corresponding complex analytic zero is unique for each of
the four factors. FUT20--23 exclude real zeros in those neighborhoods
for small nonzero real $z$. On the complement, compactness of the
real projective line and continuity of the original phase quotient
give a strictly positive minimum of all four boundary absolute values.
The PCL2 entire series converges uniformly there for $z$ in a small
closed disk, so all four values remain nonzero on that complement.
Take the minimum of these finitely many positive radii.
This proves FUT16 uniformly over every actual unit phase and scale.
It also verifies the five-orbit condition there directly. If the
$j$th conjugated quadric were proportional to the original $Q_0$,
evaluation at $\boldsymbol1$ would give $f_j(0,z)=0$, since
$Q_0(\boldsymbol1)=0$. This contradicts FUT16 for every $j=1,2,3,4$.
Two distinct orbit members could be proportional only if conjugating
by the inverse of one of their powers made a nontrivial orbit member
proportional to $Q_0$, which was just excluded. The original invertible
period matrices therefore give five distinct quadric factors on this
region. The original conductor has $v=0$ there; no missing bound is
assumed and no RH conclusion is inferred.

\subsection{Every real-unit factor is genuinely nonquadratic in the inverse period}
The first nonzero real-unit period coefficient is the existing PZX
coefficient OPB15. Its next even coefficient is also nonzero for every
original quartet and all four factors. This supplies an exact input
for the independent entire-function analysis, without claiming that
any resulting complex zero is in the admitted five-orbit domain.

For the complete real-unit function, set
$d_j(z)=f_j(0,z)/(4i\delta\gamma)$; this is only an explicitly
restored nonzero scalar in the coefficient formula. All its coefficients
are $[z^n]d_j=\sum_{v=0}^n(G_ve_0)^{\mathsf T}Q(G_{n-v}e_0)$,
with the original $G_n$ above. For $\zeta=e^{2\pi i/5}$, substitution
of $R_0,\ldots,R_4$ gives the following exact imaginary parts:
\[
 \begin{split}
 \operatorname{Im}\left(
   \frac{-1653372\,[z^4]d_1}{\beta(\beta^2-9\eta)}\right)
 &=\eta^3\sin(2\pi/5)F_1(t),\\
 \operatorname{Im}\left(
   \frac{1653372\,[z^4]d_2}{\beta(\beta^2-9\eta)}\right)
 &=\eta^3\sin(2\pi/5)F_2(t),
 \end{split}\tag{FUT24}
\]
where $t=\beta^2/\eta$, $h=(\sqrt5-1)/2$, and the full polynomials are
\[
 \begin{split}
 F_1(t)&=(169+48h)t^3-(2583+378h)t^2
                 +(11340-2835h)t+25515h,\\
 F_2(t)&=(48-169h)t^3+(-378+2583h)t^2
                 -(2835+11340h)t+25515.
 \end{split}\tag{FUT25}
\]
Their exact degree-three Bernstein coefficients on $[0,4]$ are
\[
 \begin{split}
 B_1&=(25515h,\ 15120+21735h,\ 16464+15939h,\ 14848+11199h),\\
 B_2&=(25515,\ 21735-15120h,\ 15939-16464h,\ 11199-14848h),\\
 F_j(t)&=\sum_{r=0}^3(B_j)_r\binom3r(t/4)^r(1-t/4)^{3-r}.
 \end{split}\tag{FUT26}
\]
Expansion verifies these identities. Every entry of $B_1$ is positive.
Every entry of $B_2$ is positive already with $h<2/3$; the last three
are greater respectively than $11655$, $4963$, and $3901/3$.
The Bernstein basis is nonnegative and sums to one, so both $F_j$
are strictly positive throughout $[0,4]$.
FUT24 therefore proves $[z^4]d_1,[z^4]d_2\ne0$.
The exact original conjugation gives $d_{5-j}(z)=\overline{d_j(z)}$
for real $z$, and hence the same result for $j=3,4$.
All four real-unit factors have both a nonzero second and a nonzero
fourth inverse-period coefficient. No sampled value is used in this
nonvanishing proof.

\section{The actual period receiver excludes every repeated complex root near infinite period}


\paragraph{Original objects and provenance.}
This calculation applies the complete CJR receiver \cite{ComplexReceiver061} to
the actual moment family calculated in PIN1--14 \cite{PeriodInverse061}.
The period matrix and all its coefficients are the original PCL1--10
\cite{PCLOriginal}; the finite-period domain is PZU1--4 \cite{PeriodZeroOriginal}.
The marked matrix and quartet remain FC5 and FC15a, with the
canonical ES reader and its human-source attributions retained in
the cumulative source \cite{ES488,WCF}. The source and target norms below
are exactly ECC24--26 and EQR1--6, including the Gamma masses,
centres and both source orders \cite{ES488,WCF}. No free moment
vector is substituted for a period.

Throughout, $0<\delta<1/2$, $\gamma>2$, and the actual nonzero
unit is on the phase $a=\bar a\ne0$. Its value is retained:
$U=aI$ cancels with its own inverse in the original conjugation.
Write $z=u^{-1}$ and retain the exact constants
\[
 \beta=2(\gamma^2-\delta^2),\quad
 \eta=(\delta^2+\gamma^2)^2,\quad
 B=\beta^2-9\eta=-5\gamma^4-26\delta^2\gamma^2-5\delta^4<0,
 \quad h=9/B,
 \quad C=\frac{125(4\delta\gamma)^4\beta^8B^4}{81^4}>0.
 \tag{PRD1}
\]
The letter $C$ here is PIN7's scalar, not CJR's order constant.
The exponential variable is $\xi$; it is distinct from $z$.

\section{The actual entire coefficients and their first two terms}
Here is a complete source of every coefficient used below. Let
$\mathcal R(z)=\sum_{n\ge0}R_nz^n$ have precisely the entries
\[
 (R_n)_{a r}=
 \sum_{\substack{p,l\ge0\\2p+4l=5n+r+1-a}}
 \frac{\beta^p\eta^l}{3^p p!l!}
 (-5)^{p+l-n}(a/5)_{p+l-n},
 \quad 1\le a\le4,\quad0\le r\le3.
 \tag{PRD2}
\]
All sums at a fixed $n$ are finite. PCL2--5 prove convergence
for every complex $z$, $\det\mathcal R=1$, and the entire
inverse $\operatorname{adj}\mathcal R$. In particular, with
$S_0=R_0^{-1}$,
\[
 S_n=-S_0\sum_{r=1}^nR_rS_{n-r},\qquad
 T_{j,n}=\sum_{r=0}^nS_rD_jR_{n-r},\quad
 D_j=\operatorname{diag}(\zeta^{-j},\zeta^{-2j},
                           \zeta^{-3j},\zeta^{-4j}),
 \tag{PRD3}
\]
where $\zeta=e^{2\pi i/5}$ and every $j=1,2,3,4$ is retained.
Let $Q$ be the complete matrix PIN3 and define, for $0\le k\le3$,
\[
 F_{j,k,n}=
 \sum_{a=0}^k\sum_{r=0}^n
 \frac{(T_{j,r}e_a)^{\mathsf T}Q(T_{j,n-r}e_{k-a})}
 {a!(k-a)!}.
 \tag{PRD4}
\]
These are exactly $[\xi^kz^n]e^{-\xi}f_j(\xi,z)/(4i\delta\gamma)$
by PIN3--5. Thus every coefficient of the four actual moment
functions used here is the convergent, fully specified sum
\[
\begin{split}
 \nu_m(z)&=\partial_\xi^m(e^{-4\xi}E_A(\xi,z))\big|_{\xi=0},\\
 [z^N]\nu_m(z)&=m!(4i\delta\gamma)^4
 \sum_{\substack{k_1+\cdots+k_4=m\\n_1+\cdots+n_4=N}}
          \prod_{j=1}^4F_{j,k_j,n_j},\qquad0\le m\le3,\\
 \mu_m(z)&=\sum_{r=0}^m\binom mr4^{m-r}\nu_r(z).
\end{split}\tag{PRD5}
\]
There are no independent amplitudes in these expressions.
The last line is exactly $E_A=e^{4\xi}\prod_j(4i\delta\gamma F_j)$.

PIN6--8, including their parity proof, give
\[
 \nu_0=Cz^8+O(z^{10}),\quad
 \nu_1=-2Chz^7+O(z^9),\quad
 \nu_2=4Ch^2z^6+O(z^8),\quad
 \nu_3=-6Ch^3z^5+O(z^7).
 \tag{PRD6}
\]
Every remainder is the convergent Taylor tail from PRD2--5.
Consequently the functions $M_m(z)=z^{m-8}\mu_m(z)$ have
removable singularities at zero and are entire. Their exact first
two Taylor coefficients are
\[
\begin{array}{c|rrrr}
 m&0&1&2&3\\\hline
 M_m(0)&C&-2Ch&4Ch^2&-6Ch^3\\
 M'_m(0)&0&4C&-16Ch&48Ch^2
\end{array}.
\tag{PRD7}
\]
For example $\mu_2=\nu_2+8\nu_1+16\nu_0$ and
$\mu_3=\nu_3+12\nu_2+48\nu_1+64\nu_0$ give the last
two columns. Parity in PRD6 supplies the absence of every other
term that could contribute to this table.

\section{The full cubic, its discriminant and a convergent-coefficient radius}
Keep $b(X)=\sum_{q=0}^3b_qX^q$ from the literal interpolation
CJR1--2; in particular
\[
 b_3=\frac{355\sqrt2\gamma-214\delta+
                   i(308\sqrt2\delta+210\gamma)}
                   {616\delta\gamma(\delta^2+\gamma^2)}\ne0.
 \tag{PRD8}
\]
Let $\kappa=a_{\rm amp}/2-4-1/2$ as in ECC22--27.
For precision the unchanged PZU radius on this phase is
\[
 d_j(z)=f_j(0,z)=\sum_{n\ge1}d_{j,2n}z^{2n},\quad
 d_{j,2}=4i\delta\gamma L_j\ne0,\quad
 C_j=\sum_{n\ge1}|d_{j,2+2n}|,\quad
 R_A=\max\{R_*,1,\max_j(2C_j/|d_{j,2}|)^{1/2}\}.
 \tag{PRD8a}
\]
Here $L_j$ is exactly PIN4 and $R_*$ is the original proved
five-orbit radius. The coefficients are PRD2--4 at $k=0$.
PZU1--4 proves their convergence and $v=0$ at every finite
$|u|\ge R_A$. The actual first receiver polynomial is
\[
 m_1(P,z)=\sum_{q=0}^3b_q\sum_{r=0}^q
          \binom qr\mu_{q-r}(z)(P+\kappa)^r.
 \tag{PRD9}
\]
For $z\ne0$ introduce the invertible coordinate map
$X=z(P+\kappa)$, with inverse $P=X/z-\kappa$, and define
\[
 H(X,z)=z^{-5}m_1(X/z-\kappa,z)=\sum_{r=0}^3A_r(z)X^r,
 \quad
 A_r(z)=\sum_{q=r}^3\binom qr b_qz^{3-q}M_{q-r}(z).
 \tag{PRD10}
\]
This identity keeps the entire original $m_1=z^5H$; it does
not replace its original scalar or coordinate. Each $A_r$ is
entire by PRD7. Their boundary polynomial and first derivative are
\[
\begin{split}
 H(X,0)&=Cb_3p(X),\qquad
 p(X)=X^3-6hX^2+12h^2X-6h^3=(X-2h)^3+2h^3,\\
 \partial_zH(X,0)&=C(b_2+12b_3)(X-2h)^2
       =\left(4+\frac{b_2}{3b_3}\right)\partial_XH(X,0).
\end{split}\tag{PRD11}
\]
Substitution of all eight entries of PRD7 into PRD10 proves
both complete coefficient identities.

For the actual polynomial $H$, define its full discriminant
by the finite expression
\[
 \Delta(z)=A_2^2A_1^2-4A_3A_1^3-4A_2^3A_0
                    -27A_3^2A_0^2+18A_3A_2A_1A_0
             =\sum_{n\ge0}\Delta_nz^n.
 \tag{PRD12}
\]
The polynomial $p$ has discriminant $-108h^6$, as follows
by translating it to $Y^3+2h^3$ and substituting its coefficients
in PRD12. Its leading coefficient is one. Therefore
\[
 \Delta_0=-108C^4b_3^4h^6\ne0,\qquad \Delta_1=0,
 \qquad
 \operatorname{Disc}_P m_1(P,z)=z^{26}\Delta(z).
 \tag{PRD13}
\]
For the middle equality, PRD11 says that the first-order
coefficient variation is exactly that of the translation
$Cb_3p(X+(4+b_2/(3b_3))z)$; a translation does not change
root differences or the leading coefficient. Thus its discriminant
has zero first derivative. Equivalently, substitution of PRD7
into the five monomials of PRD12 gives zero directly.
For the final equality, the discriminant of a cubic with leading
coefficient $a_3$ and roots $r_j$ is
$a_3^4\prod_{j<k}(r_j-r_k)^2$; this equals PRD12 by expansion.
Multiplication of a cubic by $z^5$ gives a factor $z^{20}$,
and substituting $X=z(P+\kappa)$ gives a factor $z^6$.
This proves the exponent $26$, including all original constants.

Here is a positive, explicitly specified radius using the complete
actual coefficient tails, not an unspecified sufficiently-small
parameter. Set
\[
 T_\Delta=\sum_{n\ge2}|\Delta_n|<\infty,\quad
 r_\Delta=\begin{cases}
 1,&T_\Delta=0,\\
 \min\{1,(|\Delta_0|/(2T_\Delta))^{1/2}\},&T_\Delta>0,
 \end{cases}
 \qquad r_D=\min\{R_A^{-1},r_\Delta\}>0.
 \tag{PRD14}
\]
Convergence follows because PRD10--12 are entire power series;
absolute convergence at a larger radius also proves convergence
of the displayed coefficient sum. PRD2--5, PRD10 and PRD12
specify every term by finite exact convolutions. For $|z|\le r_D$,
\[
 |\Delta(z)-\Delta_0|\le T_\Delta|z|^2
       \le|\Delta_0|/2,
 \qquad
 |\operatorname{Disc}_Pm_1|\ge54C^4|b_3|^4|h|^6|z|^{26}>0
 \quad(z\ne0).
 \tag{PRD15}
\]
Also the leading coefficient of $m_1$ is $b_3\mu_0(z)\ne0$
by PZU4. Thus for every actual finite period $|u|\ge r_D^{-1}$
on this unit phase the original receiver has exactly three simple
complex roots. In particular
\[
 (m_1(P,z),\partial_Pm_1(P,z))\ne(0,0)
              \quad\text{for every }P\in\C.
 \tag{PRD16}
\]
This evaluates and excludes every actual CJR23--25 candidate in
this period domain. It uses the actual family PRD5 throughout.

\section{All three moving roots as exact convergent functions}
Write $\varrho=2^{1/3}>0$, $\omega_\ell=e^{2\pi i\ell/3}$ and
\[
 X_\ell=h(2-\varrho\omega_\ell),\quad 0\le\ell\le2,
 \qquad d=\sqrt3\varrho|h|,
 \quad m=\min_\ell|X_\ell|>0,
 \quad \epsilon=\tfrac14\min\{d,m\},
 \quad R=\max_\ell|X_\ell|+\epsilon.
 \tag{PRD17}
\]
The three $X_\ell$ are exactly the distinct roots of $p$, every
pair has distance $d$, and none is zero because $\varrho<2$.
Let $a_{r,n}=[z^n]A_r(z)$ from PRD10 and put
\[
 T_r=\sum_{n\ge1}|a_{r,n}|<\infty,\quad
 T_H=\sum_{r=0}^3T_rR^r,\quad
 L_H=|Cb_3|\epsilon(d-\epsilon)^2>0,
 \quad
 r_H=\begin{cases}1,&T_H=0,\\
 \min\{1,L_H/(2T_H)\},&T_H>0,
 \end{cases}
 \quad r_{\rm root}=\min\{r_D,r_H,m/(4(1+|\kappa|)),1\}>0.
 \tag{PRD18}
\]
On $\Gamma_\ell=\{X:|X-X_\ell|=\epsilon\}$ the other two
root distances are at least $d-\epsilon$, hence
$|H(X,0)|\ge L_H$. For $|z|\le r_{\rm root}$,
$|H(X,z)-H(X,0)|\le T_H|z|\le L_H/2$ on every contour.
Thus no polynomial in the interpolation
$H(X,0)+t(H(X,z)-H(X,0))$, $0\le t\le1$, vanishes there.
Its number of zeros inside each circle, with multiplicity, is one.
For a direct proof of this polynomial form of Rouch\'e's count,
factor each polynomial over $\C$: the integral of its logarithmic
derivative divided by $2\pi i$ is the sum of the circle integrals
of $(X-r_j)^{-1}$, hence the integer number of roots inside.
The integral depends continuously on $t$ since the denominator
never vanishes on the circle. It is therefore constant and equals
one at $t=0$. This proves the claimed count and simplicity without
an assumed root-selection rule.

The unique root in each circle is the exact holomorphic function
\[
 \mathcal X_\ell(z)=\frac1{2\pi i}
       \int_{\Gamma_\ell}
             X\frac{\partial_XH(X,z)}{H(X,z)}\,dX,
 \qquad
 P_\ell(z)=\mathcal X_\ell(z)/z-\kappa
                    \quad(0<|z|<r_{\rm root}).
 \tag{PRD19}
\]
Factorization and the same circle integral show that the first
integral equals the single root, including its multiplicity one.
Uniform nonvanishing of the denominator permits integration of
the convergent local $z$ power series, proving holomorphy.
These are all three original receiver roots. Moreover
$|\mathcal X_\ell(z)|\ge3m/4$ and $|\kappa z|\le m/4$,
so $P_\ell(z)\ne0$, as required for the EQR collision path.

The full Taylor series is determined recursively, not only its
limiting point. If $\mathcal X_\ell=X_\ell+\sum_{n\ge1}x_{\ell,n}z^n$,
then
\[
 x_{\ell,n}=-\frac{[z^n]H(X_\ell+
                     \sum_{j=1}^{n-1}x_{\ell,j}z^j,z)}
                    {Cb_3p'(X_\ell)},\quad
 p'(X_\ell)=3(X_\ell-2h)^2\ne0,
 \quad x_{\ell,1}=-4-\frac{b_2}{3b_3}.
 \tag{PRD20}
\]
The coefficient of the newly inserted $x_{\ell,n}$ is exactly
$\partial_XH(X_\ell,0)$; the contour construction proves convergence
of this recursively specified series on $|z|<r_{\rm root}$.
In original coordinates this gives all three expansions
\[
 P_\ell(z)=\frac{h(2-2^{1/3}\omega_\ell)}z
       -\kappa-4-\frac{b_2}{3b_3}+O(z),\qquad
 \partial_Pm_1(P_\ell(z),z)
       =Cb_3p'(X_\ell)z^6+O(z^7).
 \tag{PRD21}
\]
The derivative equality follows from the exact PRD10 chain rule.
Every leading constant is nonzero and retains the original quartet.

\section{The four collisions in both complete original Gamma norms}
Fix any of these finite actual periods and a centre $P\ne0$.
PRD16 makes $U_1=(m_1(P,z),m'_1(P,z))^{\mathsf T}\ne0$.
The EQR1--6 calculation therefore applies to all four retained
choices $\epsilon_c\in\{0,1\}$ and both signs of
$\lambda^2=(2\epsilon_c-1)3P/22$. For the collision parameter
$t=w_0^2$, it gives in each unchanged original metric
\[
 w_0Y\longrightarrow U_1/\lambda,\qquad
 |t|^{1/2}\|Y\|_{G_{b,t}}
       \longrightarrow\frac{\sqrt{U_1^*G_{b,0}U_1}}{|\lambda|}>0,
                \quad b=U,W.
 \tag{PRD22}
\]
Thus the bounded-jet alternatives EQR7--10 are excluded for every
complex centre throughout the evaluated period domain.

At the three actual moving roots, there is a further complete
evaluation of both original metric constants. Write
\[
 b_\Gamma=s/2,\quad M_\Gamma=(2\pi)^{s/2},\quad
 k_j=(b_\Gamma)_j/j!,\quad
 L_0=a_{\rm amp}/2+b_2/(3b_3),\quad
 d_\ell=p'(X_\ell),
 \qquad s\in\{1,a_{\rm amp}\}.
 \tag{PRD23}
\]
Both source orders are retained, as are the centres
$a_{\rm amp}/2$ and $a_{\rm amp}/2-4$.
At $P=P_\ell(z)$, the exact constant in PRD22 is
\[
 \mathcal E_{b,\ell}(z)=
 \sqrt{\frac{22}{3|P_\ell(z)|}}\,
 |\partial_Pm_1(P_\ell(z),z)|\,
                  \sqrt{(G_{b,0})_{22}}.
 \tag{PRD24}
\]
Here index $22$ denotes the derivative coordinate of the two-by-two
Gram. This formula is exact for every retained sign and either
collision-root choice; $|\lambda|=\sqrt{3|P|/22}$.

We calculate its period behaviour from the full ECC24--26
covariance factors, not a substituted metric. At $v=0$ their
actual coefficients satisfy, directly from PRD6,
\[
 g_0=Cz^8+O(z^{10}),\quad
 g_1=2iChz^7+O(z^9),\quad
 g_2=-2Ch^2z^6+O(z^8),\quad
 g_3=-iCh^3z^5+O(z^7).
 \tag{PRD25}
\]
Let $e(P)=(1,P,P^2,P^3)$, let $Q_U,Q_W$ be the exact
covariance factors in ECC26, and put
$J_b=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}e(P)\\e'(P)\end{smallmatrix}\right)
Q_bQ_b^*
\left(\begin{smallmatrix}e(P)\\e'(P)\end{smallmatrix}\right)^*$,
$G_{b,0}=J_b^{-1}$.
For the source, multiplication by the complete upper triangular
$B_F$ in ECC25 gives the four entries of $e(P)Q_U$, after their
unchanged column factors $M_\Gamma^{-1/2}k_j^{-1/2}$, as
\[
\begin{split}
 c_0&=g_0,\qquad c_1=g_1-i(P-1/2)g_0,\\
 c_2&=g_2-b_\Gamma g_0/2-i(P-1/2)g_1
                                      -(P-1/2)^2g_0/2,\\
 c_3&=g_3-b_\Gamma g_1/2
       -i(P-1/2)(g_2-(3b_\Gamma+2)g_0/6)\\
    &\hspace{10mm}-(P-1/2)^2g_1/2+i(P-1/2)^3g_0/6.
\end{split}\tag{PRD26}
\]
The derivative row is the derivative of these same expressions
with $z$ fixed. Since
$z(P_\ell-1/2)=X_\ell-zL_0+O(z^2)$ by PRD21,
the entire two-row limit is
\[
 z^{-6}\begin{pmatrix}e(P_\ell)Q_U\\e'(P_\ell)Q_U\end{pmatrix}
 \longrightarrow
 \frac{Cd_\ell}{6\sqrt{M_\Gamma}}
 \begin{pmatrix}
 0&0&-k_2^{-1/2}&-iL_0k_3^{-1/2}\\
 0&0&0&i k_3^{-1/2}
 \end{pmatrix}.
 \tag{PRD27}
\]
To see the cancellation explicitly, the leading $z^5$ term in
$c_3$ is $iCp(X_\ell)z^5/6=0$; its next term is
$-iCd_\ell L_0z^6/6$. The leading $c_2$ is
$-C(X_\ell-2h)^2z^6/2=-Cd_\ell z^6/6$.
The derivative of $c_3$ has leading $iCd_\ell z^6/6$;
all other derivative entries have higher order. PRD25 proves
that the omitted actual Taylor tails enter only at those higher
orders, establishing every entry of PRD27.
The limiting two rows are independent. Taking their full Gram
and its inverse therefore gives
\[
 |z|^{12}(G_{U,0})_{22}\longrightarrow
 \frac{36M_\Gamma(k_3+k_2|L_0|^2)}{C^2|d_\ell|^2}.
 \tag{PRD28}
\]
For example the unscaled two-by-two Gram in PRD27 has entries
$k_2^{-1}+|L_0|^2k_3^{-1}$, $-L_0k_3^{-1}$,
$-\bar L_0k_3^{-1}$ and $k_3^{-1}$; its determinant is
$(k_2k_3)^{-1}$. This proves the displayed inverse entry and
retains every Gamma factor.

For the target $Q_W$ is independent of the period. Write $q_j$
for its row with index $j=0,1,2,3$. Polynomial expansion gives
$\|e(P)Q_W\|^2\sim|P|^6\|q_3\|^2$, while the determinant
of its two-row Gram is the squared exterior norm and satisfies
\[
 \det J_W\sim |P|^8\|q_3\wedge q_2\|^2,
 \quad
 |P|^2(G_{W,0})_{22}\longrightarrow
       \frac{\|q_3\|^2}{\|q_3\wedge q_2\|^2}
       =2M_\Gamma b_\Gamma(b_\Gamma+1).
 \tag{PRD29}
\]
Indeed the leading wedge is
$P^3q_3\wedge2Pq_2+P^2q_2\wedge3P^2q_3
=-P^4q_3\wedge q_2$.
The last two rows of the complete ECC26 factor are upper triangular;
their diagonal magnitudes are respectively
$[2M_\Gamma b_\Gamma(b_\Gamma+1)]^{-1/2}$ and
$[6M_\Gamma b_\Gamma(b_\Gamma+1)(b_\Gamma+2)]^{-1/2}$.
Their off-diagonal term affects neither the wedge nor the ratio,
proving the last equality rather than omitting that entry.

Combining PRD21, PRD24, PRD28 and PRD29 proves the two actual
positive period limits, for each $\ell$ and each original $s$:
\[
\begin{split}
 \lim_{z\to0}|z|^{-1/2}\mathcal E_{U,\ell}(z)
 &=6|b_3|\sqrt{\frac{22M_\Gamma(k_3+k_2|L_0|^2)}{3|X_\ell|}},\\
 \lim_{z\to0}|z|^{-15/2}\mathcal E_{W,\ell}(z)
 &=C|b_3||d_\ell|
     \sqrt{\frac{44M_\Gamma b_\Gamma(b_\Gamma+1)}
                         {3|X_\ell|^3}}.
\end{split}\tag{PRD30}
\]
These are iterated limits: first the EQR collision parameter tends
to zero at its fixed actual finite period; then the period tends
to infinity on the constructed branch. No simultaneous-limit
interchange or uniform collision assertion is assumed.
In particular the first marked receiver column can vanish at
each of its three moving simple roots, but its derivative there
remains nonzero and all four collision states escape in both
original quotient norms. Their full complements remain EQR3--4.
The result proves absence of repeated receiver roots on the
specified finite-period region. It does not assert an original
conductor order jump or an RH endpoint.


\section{A certified finite geometric period with an order-one conductor symbol}
\label{sec:finite-period-zero}

This section constructs a finite complex period of the complete PCL
coefficient family \cite{PCLOriginal} at which the original symbol changes order.
It uses the original four factors, the original exponential variable and
the original Gamma metrics \cite{WCF}. The quartet parameters in this
construction are specified geometric parameters. They are not asserted
to be zeros of the Riemann zeta function. The statement concerns this
coefficient family and its exact ES return; it is not an arithmetic RH
conclusion. The ES marking and human provenance remain FC1--15a and
\cite{ES488}.

\subsection{The full convergent functions and the exact point}
Fix
\[
 \delta=\frac14,\quad\gamma=3,\quad
 \beta=\frac{143}{8},\quad\eta=\frac{21025}{256},\quad
 w=(\delta+i\gamma,\delta-i\gamma,-\delta+i\gamma,-\delta-i\gamma),
 \quad\rho_a=\frac12+w_a.
 \tag{FPZ1}
\]
The unit is on its nonzero real phase $a=\bar a\ne0$. Its magnitude is
unchanged: $U=aI$ cancels with $U^{-1}$ in PCL8. Put
$V_{ar}=w_a^r$ for $0\le r\le3$, $\zeta=e^{2\pi i/5}$ and
$D_j=\operatorname{diag}(\zeta^{-j},\zeta^{-2j},\zeta^{-3j},\zeta^{-4j})$.
Retain every coefficient of the original period:
\[
 \mathcal R(z)=\sum_{n\ge0}R_nz^n,\qquad
 (R_n)_{ar}=\sum_{\substack{p,h\ge0\\2p+4h=5n+r+1-a}}
 \frac{(\beta/3)^p\eta^h}{p!h!}(-5)^{p+h-n}(a/5)_{p+h-n}.
 \tag{FPZ2}
\]
This is precisely PCL2, with row index $1\le a\le4$. The exact
conjugation PCL7--9, including all branch powers and Gamma ray factors,
gives
\[
 \begin{split}
 M_j(z)&=V\mathcal R(z)^{-1}D_j\mathcal R(z)V^{-1},\\
 t(\xi)&=(e^{\rho_a\xi})_{a=1}^4,\quad Q_0(t)=t_1t_4-t_2t_3,\\
 f_j(\xi,z)&=Q_0(M_j(z)t(\xi)),\quad d_j(z)=f_j(0,z),\\
 E_A(\xi,z)&=\prod_{j=1}^4f_j(\xi,z),\quad
 \mu_n(z)=\partial_\xi^n E_A(0,z).
 \end{split}\tag{FPZ3}
\]
No coefficient of $A_z$, including its off-diagonal coefficients, is
discarded by this identity.

The following two terminating decimals specify exact rational numbers:
\[
 \begin{split}
 c_R&=0.011136978231486808477778740306233906621055400363647396688725562781,\\
 c_I&=0.0078780133477760021239711966284294386302928222474756316845213852718,\\
 c&=c_R+ic_I,\qquad r=10^{-14},\qquad
 \mathbb D=\{z:|z-c|<r\}.
 \end{split}\tag{FPZ4}
\]
There is exactly one zero $z_*$ of $d_1$ in $\mathbb D$, counted with
multiplicity. It is simple. Equations FPZ2--4 and this unique-root
condition define the point exactly, rather than specifying it by an
unverified floating-point approximation. The proof follows below.

\subsection{An explicit bound for every omitted series coefficient}
Set $K=11/2$, $C_R=4K^3$ and $T_R=6K^5/5$. Then
$K^2\ge5\beta/3$, $K^4\ge5\eta$ and $K\ge1$. For each term in
FPZ2 let $m=p+h$ and $L=m-n\ge0$. Since $0<a/5<1$,
$(a/5)_L\le L!$. Also
\[
 \frac{n!L!}{p!h!}=\frac{\binom mp}{\binom mn}\le2^m,
 \qquad 2m\le5n+3,\qquad 2^m\le4\,6^n.
 \tag{FPZ5}
\]
The defining constraint gives $K^{2p+4h}\le K^{5n+3}$, and there
are at most $2n+2$ contributing pairs. Multiplying these inequalities
with $5^L=5^{m-n}$ proves the uniform entrywise estimate
\[
 |(R_n)_{ar}|\le C_R(2n+2)\frac{T_R^n}{n!}.
 \tag{FPZ6}
\]
It proves absolute convergence on every bounded disk, including that
of the derivative series; it also bounds every tail actually used here.
Let $N=400$, and let $\rho$ be an outward upper bound for the modulus
on the rectangle $|\Re(z-c)|\le r$, $|\Im(z-c)|\le r$.
With $w=T_R\rho$, the entrywise tails satisfy
\[
 \begin{split}
 \left|\mathcal R-\sum_{n=0}^N R_nz^n\right|_{ar}
 &\le\tau_0=
 \frac{C_R(2N+4)w^{N+1}}{(N+1)!(1-2w/(N+2))},\\
 \left|\mathcal R'-\sum_{n=1}^N nR_nz^{n-1}\right|_{ar}
 &\le\tau_1=
 \frac{C_R(2N+4)(N+1)T_Rw^N}
 {(N+1)!(1-3w/(N+1))}.
 \end{split}\tag{FPZ7}
\]
For the first tail the ratio of successive majorant terms is at most
$2w/(N+2)$. For the derivative tail that ratio is
$w(n+2)/(n(n+1))\le3w/(N+1)$ for $n\ge N+1$.
Both denominators are positive. Summing the resulting geometric
majorants proves FPZ7, including the full infinite remainder.

\subsection{The enclosing calculation and the zero count}
The reproducible calculation is
\texttt{certify\_finite\_period\_zero.py}, with its full ball output in
\texttt{FINITE\_PERIOD\_ZERO\_CERTIFICATE.json}.
It uses Python-FLINT 0.9.0, 768-bit precision and one worker.
The inclusion-preserving arithmetic and outward radius operations are
those of Fredrik Johansson's Arb \cite{human:arb2016}, sections
``Features and example applications'', ``Radii and magnitude bounds''
and ``Precision and bounds''. The original author TeX was read at
those loci; the matrix-tail and zero-count proofs here are the present
calculation, not claims attributed to that software paper.

All rational coefficients in FPZ2 are evaluated as enclosing balls.
Simultaneous Horner evaluation encloses $\mathcal R,\mathcal R'$;
the two tails in FPZ7 are then added to every real and imaginary part.
In particular the complete run proves
\[
 \rho<0.013642,\qquad \tau_0<6.44\cdot10^{-98},\qquad
 \tau_1<2.92\cdot10^{-93}.
 \tag{FPZ8}
\]
The inverse is an enclosing matrix inverse. The independent companion
review also verifies $\|I-B\mathcal R(z)\|_\infty<1.73\cdot10^{-9}$
on the entire rectangle, with $B$ the exact dyadic midpoint of the
computed centre inverse. Thus a convergent Neumann series proves local
invertibility independently of PCL5. This is a certificate for the
full matrix, not for the truncated polynomial alone.

The derivative used in the calculation is exactly
\[
 M'_j=V\bigl(\mathcal R^{-1}D_j\mathcal R'
 -\mathcal R^{-1}\mathcal R'\mathcal R^{-1}D_j\mathcal R\bigr)V^{-1}.
 \tag{FPZ9}
