\]
For example, if $y=M_j\mathbf1$ and $y'=M'_j\mathbf1$, then
$d'_j=y'_1y_4+y_1y'_4-y'_2y_3-y_2y'_3$.
The original symbol derivative uses $M_j(\rho_a)_a$, retaining
the original $1/2$ in every $\rho_a$.
On the closed rectangle the certified strict bounds are
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 |d_1(c)|<5\cdot10^{-63},\quad |d'_1(c)|>434,\quad
 \sup|d'_1(z)-d'_1(c)|<8,\\
 \Im\partial_\xi f_1(0,z)>3.68,\qquad
 -0.24<\Re d_2(z)<-0.22,\\
 -2.43<\Re d_3(z)<-2.41,\qquad
 -3.36<\Re d_4(z)<-3.34.
 \end{gathered}\tag{FPZ10}
\]
For $|z-c|=r$, integration of the derivative along the straight
segment from $c$ proves
\[
 |d_1(z)-d'_1(c)(z-c)|
 \le |d_1(c)|+8r<434r<|d'_1(c)(z-c)|.
 \tag{FPZ11}
\]
The homotopy between the two holomorphic functions has no boundary
zero. Its contour integral of the logarithmic derivative is continuous
and integer-valued: isolated zeros locally have the form
$(z-z_0)^m h(z)$ with $h(z_0)\ne0$, so each contributes its
integer multiplicity to that integral. The count is therefore constant.
The linear function has one zero, proving the unique simple zero asserted
after FPZ4. For any two distinct points $z_1,z_2$ in the convex
rectangle, the same segment integration gives
\[
 |d_1(z_1)-d_1(z_2)-d'_1(c)(z_1-z_2)|\le8|z_1-z_2|,
 \qquad |d_1(z_1)-d_1(z_2)|>426|z_1-z_2|.
\]
Thus $d_1$ is injective on the entire rectangle. The other three factors
have no zero anywhere in that rectangle by FPZ10. Therefore $\mu_0$
also has exactly one simple zero in the rectangle as well as in the disk.

At that zero define, with every original factor retained,
\[
 m_*:=\mu_1(z_*)=\partial_\xi f_1(0,z_*)\prod_{j=2}^4d_j(z_*),\quad
 \alpha_*:=\mu'_0(z_*)=d'_1(z_*)\prod_{j=2}^4d_j(z_*).
 \tag{FPZ12}
\]
The enclosing calculation proves $|m_*|>13.80$ and
$|\alpha_*|>1524$. Consequently
\[
 \operatorname{ord}_{\xi=0}E_A(\xi,z_*)=1,\qquad
 \mu_0(z)=\alpha_*(z-z_*)+O((z-z_*)^2),\qquad
 u_*:=z_*^{-1}\in
 [59.8455390191\pm8.74\cdot10^{-11}]
 +i[-42.333202544\pm4.75\cdot10^{-10}].
 \tag{FPZ13}
\]
These are enclosures of the exact constructed point, not replacements
for its definition. The finite period and any local logarithm branch
remain those of PCL1 and PCL7.

\subsection{The five distinct original quadrics at this finite period}
Let $H$ be the full original period matrix at $u_*$ and put
$Q_j(X)=Q_0(H^{-1}D^{-j}X)$ for $j\in\mathbb Z/5\mathbb Z$.
Every $Q_j$ is an invertible linear pullback of the rank-four quadratic
$Q_0$. Such a quadratic cannot factor into two linear forms, since a
product of two linear forms has symmetric matrix rank at most two.
Hence each $Q_j$ is irreducible.

The action $X\mapsto D^{-1}X$ on their projective classes has order
five. Every orbit length divides five. An association between any two
distinct indexed quadrics would therefore make this orbit have length
one. It would give $Q_1=\lambda Q_0(H^{-1}\,\cdot)$ for a nonzero
scalar $\lambda$. But $Q_0(t(\xi))=0$ for every $\xi$, because
$\rho_1+\rho_4=\rho_2+\rho_3=1$. Substitution would imply
$f_1(\xi,z_*)=0$ identically, contradicting FPZ10. Thus
\[
 Q_0(H^{-1}\,\cdot),Q_1,Q_2,Q_3,Q_4
 \text{ are five pairwise nonassociated irreducible quadrics.}
 \tag{FPZ14}
\]
This proves the required five-orbit property at the actual constructed
point. It does not infer any separately imposed coordinate-section
coprimality or large-period radius from the orbit property.

\subsection{The exact fixed-space rank loss in every original degree}
Fix $a_{\rm amp}=4\ell+1\ge9$ and $s\in\{1,a_{\rm amp}\}$.
Retain $c_0=a_{\rm amp}/2$, $c_1=c_0-4$, the complete measure
$dm_s$ in FC28, and $\rho_n=\sqrt{n!/(s/2)_n}$ in WCF2.
For every $D\ge0$ consider the \emph{fixed} old $v=0$ spaces
$\mathcal P_D\to\mathcal P_D$ with these exact two norms.
Their matrix, also at the singular parameter, is
\[
 B_{D,s}(z)=\operatorname{diag}(\rho_0,\ldots,\rho_D)^{-1}
 T_D(g(z))\operatorname{diag}(\rho_0,\ldots,\rho_D),\quad
 g(t,z)=e^{-4\omega(t)}E_A(\omega(t),z),\quad
 \omega(t)=-i\arctan t.
 \tag{FPZ15}
\]
WCF3--6 prove this identity in the original orthonormal frames.
In particular $g_0=\mu_0$ and at $z_*$,
\[
 g_{0,*}=0,\quad g_{1,*}=-im_*,\quad
 g_{2,*}=4m_*-\mu_2(z_*)/2,\quad
 g_{3,*}=i\bigl(\mu_3(z_*)/6-2\mu_2(z_*)+25m_*/3\bigr).
 \tag{FPZ16}
\]
The Taylor coefficients of $\omega=-it+it^3/3+O(t^5)$ prove all
four formulas. Every higher coefficient is given by the convergent
FPZ2--3 composition in FPZ15. Explicitly, for every $n$ set
$y_{j,k}=M_j(z_*)(\rho_a^k)_a$; then
\[
 f_{j,n}=\sum_{k=0}^n\binom nk
 (y_{j,k,1}y_{j,n-k,4}-y_{j,k,2}y_{j,n-k,3}),\quad
 \mu_n(z_*)=\sum_{n_1+\cdots+n_4=n}
 \frac{n!}{n_1!\cdots n_4!}\prod_{j=1}^4 f_{j,n_j}.
 \tag{FPZ17}
\]
Here $f_{1,0}=0$ exactly. Thus no moment needed in any degree is
an unspecified independent input.

For $D\ge1$, at $z_*$ the first column and last row of FPZ15
vanish. Removing them leaves an upper triangular $D$ by $D$ matrix
with diagonal $g_{1,*}\rho_j/\rho_{j-1}$, $1\le j\le D$.
Its determinant is $g_{1,*}^D\rho_D\ne0$. Consequently
\[
 \operatorname{rank}B_{D,s}(z_*)=D,\quad
 \ker B_{D,s}(z_*)=\mathbb C\phi_{0,s,c_0},\quad
 \operatorname{im}B_{D,s}(z_*)=\mathcal P_{D-1},\quad
 \det B_{D,s}(z)=\mu_0(z)^{D+1}.
 \tag{FPZ18}
\]
For $D=0$ the rank is zero and the same kernel and determinant
statements hold. The actual new order is $v=1$; its WCF map is instead
$\mathcal P_{D+1}/\mathcal P_0\to\mathcal P_D$ and is invertible,
with diagonal $(-im_*)\rho_{j+1}/\rho_j$. This gives the exact
map between the fixed-space degeneration and the order-adjusted
quotient, retaining both domains.

\subsection{All inverse exterior poles in the exact original metrics}
Let $n=D+1$, $1\le r\le n$, $\tau=z-z_*$, and
$B_*=B_{D,s}(z_*)$. In a sufficiently small punctured disk FPZ11--13
give $v=0$ and $B_{D,s}(z)$ is invertible. In singular-value order,
the identity
\[
 \|\bigwedge^r B_{D,s}(z)^{-1}\|
 =\frac{\|\bigwedge^{n-r}B_{D,s}(z)\|}
 {|\det B_{D,s}(z)|}
 \tag{FPZ19}
\]
follows by cancelling the product of all $n$ singular values; it also
holds for $r=n$ with the zeroth exterior norm equal to one.
All exterior norms in the numerator converge by continuity of their
matrix entries and the operator norm. FPZ18 makes their limits positive.
Thus the complete leading asymptotes are
\[
 \boxed{\displaystyle
 \lim_{z\to z_*}|z-z_*|^{D+1}
 \|\bigwedge^r B_{D,s}(z)^{-1}\|
 =\frac{\|\bigwedge^{D+1-r}B_*\|}{|\alpha_*|^{D+1}}>0.}
 \tag{FPZ20}
\]
There is one inverse singular value with pole $D+1$ and $D$ inverse
singular values with finite positive limits. Indeed FPZ18 leaves exactly
$D$ positive forward singular values; their product tends to
$|g_{1,*}|^D\rho_D$, while their product with the remaining singular
value is $|\mu_0|^{D+1}$. In particular
\[
 \lim_{z\to z_*}|z-z_*|^{D+1}\|B_{D,s}(z)^{-1}\|
 =\frac{\rho_D|m_*|^D}{|\alpha_*|^{D+1}}.
 \tag{FPZ21}
\]
No mass or center has changed: the common $M_s$ cancels only when
expressing the map in its two original orthonormal frames.

For the requested four-dimensional return, $D=3$, the three nonzero
forward singular values are exactly those of
\[
 C_s=\begin{pmatrix}
 g_{1,*}\rho_1&g_{2,*}\rho_2&g_{3,*}\rho_3\\
 0&g_{1,*}\rho_2/\rho_1&g_{2,*}\rho_3/\rho_1\\
 0&0&g_{1,*}\rho_3/\rho_2
 \end{pmatrix}.
 \tag{FPZ22}
\]
This matrix, FPZ12, FPZ16--17 and FPZ2--4 specify every constant
without free coefficients. If $\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\ge\lambda_3>0$
are the roots of $\det(\lambda I-C_s^*C_s)$, the four constants in
FPZ20, in exterior ranks $1,2,3,4$, are respectively
\[
 \frac1{|\alpha_*|^4}
 \left(\rho_3|m_*|^3,\sqrt{\lambda_1\lambda_2},
                           \sqrt{\lambda_1},1\right).
 \tag{FPZ23}
\]
The singular values of the inverse have orders $(4,0,0,0)$.
All four exterior ranks have order four. This is the exact finite-period
mechanism entering the inverse-exterior expression of audit equation
(11). It prevents a bound uniform across this geometric parameter
disk on the fixed old spaces. It does not assert a failure of an estimate
whose period is fixed, whose quotient uses the actual order, or whose
arithmetic parameter set has not been mapped to this disk.

Finally $z-z_* =-(u-u_*)/(uu_*)$. Therefore the original-period version
of FPZ20 has the exact constant
\[
 \lim_{u\to u_*}|u-u_*|^{D+1}
 \|\bigwedge^r B_{D,s}(u^{-1})^{-1}\|
 =|u_*|^{2(D+1)}
 \frac{\|\bigwedge^{D+1-r}B_*\|}{|\alpha_*|^{D+1}}.
 \tag{FPZ24}
\]
Both coordinates and their exact conversion are retained. The remaining
arithmetic question is not answered by assigning this geometric point
to the zeta-zero locus; no such assignment is made here.

\subsection{A finite complex zero exists for every original quartet on this phase}
There is also a general existence result, using the new coefficient
calculation FUT24--26 below. For every original
$0<\delta<1/2$, $\gamma>2$ and real nonzero unit, each of the four
functions $d_j$ has a nonzero finite complex zero. Here is a complete
growth argument; it does not assert the five-orbit condition at every
zero obtained by this existence argument.

In FPZ5--6 choose instead
$K=\max\{1,(5\beta/3)^{1/2},(5\eta)^{1/4}\}$, retaining the actual
$\beta,\eta$. The same bound gives
\[
 |\mathcal R_{ar}(z)|\le 2C_R(1+T_R|z|)e^{T_R|z|}.
 \tag{FPZ25}
\]
PCL5 gives $\mathcal R^{-1}=\operatorname{adj}\mathcal R$.
Each adjugate entry is a sum of six triple products. Write
$v_V=\|V\|_\infty$, $v_I=\|V^{-1}\|_\infty$ and
$H(r)=2C_R(1+T_Rr)e^{T_Rr}$. Then
$\|\operatorname{adj}\mathcal R\|_\infty\le24H^3$ and
$\|\mathcal R\|_\infty\le4H$, so FPZ3 gives
$|d_j(z)|\le2(96v_Vv_I)^2H(|z|)^8$. In particular
$|d_j(z)|\le A(1+|z|)^8e^{B|z|}$ with the full constants
$A=2(96v_Vv_I)^2(2C_R)^8\max(1,T_R)^8$ and $B=8T_R$.
PCL parity, or FUT3's direct parity proof, makes $d_j$ even.
The earlier PZX coefficient and FUT24--26 prove that both its
second and fourth Taylor coefficients are nonzero.

If it had no nonzero zero, $F(z)=d_j(z)/z^2$ would be an entire
zero-free function with $F(0)\ne0$. The integral of $F'/F$ on the
simply connected complex plane defines an entire logarithm $h$ with
$F=e^h$. The growth bound implies
$\Re h(z)\le A_0+B|z|+8\log(1+|z|)$, with the compact disk
absorbed into $A_0$. Write $h(z)=\sum h_nz^n$ and let $M_R$ be
this upper bound on $|z|=R$. Fourier integration of the real part
and its mean-value identity gives, for $n\ge1$,
\[
 |h_n|\le\frac{2(M_R-\Re h(0))}{R^n}.
 \tag{FPZ26}
\]
Indeed subtract $M_R$ inside the nonconstant Fourier coefficient;
the integral of $M_R-\Re h$ is $2\pi(M_R-\Re h(0))$ and this
integrand is nonnegative. Letting $R\to\infty$ proves $h_n=0$
for every $n\ge2$. Hence $F=e^{h_0+h_1z}$. Evenness implies
$e^{2h_1z}=1$ for every $z$, whose derivative at zero gives
$h_1=0$. This would make $d_j$ a constant multiple of $z^2$,
contradicting its nonzero fourth coefficient. A nonzero finite zero
therefore exists for each original factor. FPZ4--14 additionally
construct one particular such zero and prove its precise symbol order
and orbit property; those additional conclusions came from the full
certificate, not from the growth argument alone.

\section{The complete four-label return at the finite singular period}


\paragraph{The actual singular period and the scope of this derivation.}
The companion finite-period certificate \cite{FinitePeriod064} uses
the original geometric family at $\delta=1/4$, $\gamma=3$ and
the actual real-unit phase. Its unique root is in the stated disk
of radius $10^{-14}$ about
$0.011136978231486808477778740306233906621055400363647396688725562781
+0.0078780133477760021239711966284294386302928222474756316845213852718i$
in the inverse period. The certified moment facts there are
$\mu_0=0$ and $\mu_1\ne0$, so the actual symbol order is one.
The interval proof belongs to that companion calculation; this note
independently derives the exact algebraic ES return at those coefficients.
In every formula the original $\mu_1,\mu_2,\mu_3$ and the quartet
remain intact. The proof also records the full parameter formulas
so none of their geometry is hidden by the numerical values.
The certificate concerns the geometric family; it does not identify
this quartet with zeta zeros or prove the arithmetic unit's phase.

The polynomial and marking below were checked directly against
the canonical version-69 ES reader, theorem
\texttt{explicit-four-time-Jacobian-collision} \cite{ES488}.
The original conductor and norms are FC20--32 and WCF \cite{ES488,WCF}.
This is a calculation in the fixed old spaces
$\mathcal P_3\longrightarrow\mathcal P_3$, whose image is
$\mathcal P_2$ at this period, followed by the exact actual-order
return. It does not silently identify those two presentations.

\section{Literal polynomial, marking and kernel}
Write $q=(a,y,z,w)$ in the original ES coordinates and retain
\[
\begin{aligned}
 P_0(q)&=a^3z+2a^2y-ia,\\
 P_2(q)&=-a^3y^2z-2ia^2yz+a^2w-2a^2y^3-10iay^2+3az+y,\\
 P_3(q)&=2a^3y^3z+6ia^2y^2z+2a^2wy+4a^2y^4
          +2iaw-4iay^3-2ayz+2iz+7y^2,\\
 P_4(q)&=2a^3y^4z+8ia^2y^3z+a^2wy^2+4a^2y^5
          +2iawy+7iay^4-10ay^2z-4iyz-w-3y^3,
 \qquad P=(P_0,P_2,P_3,P_4)^{\mathsf T}.
\end{aligned}\tag{FSR1}
\]
The original ordered columns are
\[
 K=\begin{pmatrix}
 0&i&1/\sqrt2&1/\sqrt2\\
 0&-1&-1-\sqrt2i&1-\sqrt2i\\
 i/2&-3i&2\sqrt2+6i&-2\sqrt2+6i\\
 0&13&-34-19\sqrt2i&34-19\sqrt2i
 \end{pmatrix},\qquad
 q_{\mathrm M}=Ke_{\mathrm M},\quad q_{\mathrm N}=Ke_{\mathrm N},
 \quad q_{\mathrm T}=Ke_{\mathrm T},\quad q_{\mathrm E}=Ke_{\mathrm E}.
 \tag{FSR2}
\]
Direct polynomial calculation, with $i^2=-1$ and the positive
$\sqrt2$, gives
\[
 \det K=77\sqrt2i/2,\qquad \det DP(q)=-2,\qquad
 P(q_j)=h_0=(0,0,-1,0)^{\mathsf T}=2iq_{\mathrm M}
       \quad(j=\mathrm M,\mathrm N,\mathrm T,\mathrm E).
 \tag{FSR3}
\]
For the first identity, expansion in the first column reduces
the determinant to $i/2$ times $30\sqrt2+94/\sqrt2=77\sqrt2$.
For the polynomial identity the companion checker differentiates
all sixteen entries of FSR1 and expands the determinant over
$\mathbb Q(i)$, giving exactly $-2$ with every nonconstant
coefficient zero. It separately substitutes all four complete
columns of FSR2. These are literal algebraic identities, not
numerical determinant evaluations.

Retain
$\rho=(1/2+\delta+i\gamma,1/2+\delta-i\gamma,
1/2-\delta+i\gamma,1/2-\delta-i\gamma)$ and
$(V_\rho)_{rj}=\rho_j^r$, $0\le r\le3$. Define the exact original
coefficient isomorphism
\[
 \Phi q=(V_\rho^{\mathsf T})^{-1}K^{-1}q,
 \qquad (\Phi^{-1}f)=K(f(\rho_j))_j.
 \tag{FSR4}
\]
The inverse follows by evaluating the interpolating cubic. The
quartet is distinct and
$\det V_\rho=-64\delta^2\gamma^2(\delta^2+\gamma^2)\ne0$.
The literal old conductor at the certified period is
\[
 T_A(c_0+c_1S+c_2S^2+c_3S^3)
  =\mu_1c_1+\mu_2c_2+\mu_3c_3
        +(2\mu_1c_2+3\mu_2c_3)S'+3\mu_1c_3S'^2.
 \tag{FSR5}
\]
This is the original Taylor formula, with its proved $\mu_0=0$;
it retains every surviving moment. Its kernel is exactly the
constants, its rank is three, and its image is all of
$\mathcal P_2$: successive leading coefficients are
$\mu_1,2\mu_1,3\mu_1$, all nonzero.

In the unchanged ES coordinates its complete kernel is therefore
\[
 \ker(T_A\Phi)=\C n,\qquad
 n=K\mathbf1=
 \begin{pmatrix}\sqrt2+i\\-1-2\sqrt2i\\19i/2\\13-38\sqrt2i\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad \Phi n=1.
 \tag{FSR6}
\]
Indeed $K^{-1}n=\mathbf1$, which evaluates the constant polynomial.
The four labelled target vectors $y_j=T_A\Phi q_j=T_A\ell_j$
satisfy exactly one relation,
\[
 y_{\mathrm M}+y_{\mathrm N}+y_{\mathrm T}+y_{\mathrm E}=0.
 \tag{FSR7}
\]
If $\sum_jc_jy_j=0$, FSR5 makes $\sum_jc_j\ell_j$ constant;
evaluation gives $c_{\mathrm M}=c_{\mathrm N}=c_{\mathrm T}=c_{\mathrm E}$.
In particular all four target vectors remain distinct. Thus the
rank loss preserves the four labels and identifies exactly their
constant label direction.

\section{The full obstruction to descent, on every kernel line}
Use the complete four-label projection and mean
\[
 E=I_4-\tfrac14\mathbf1\mathbf1^{\mathsf T},\qquad
 \pi(q)=EK^{-1}q,\qquad
 \tau(q)=\tfrac14\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}K^{-1}q.
 \tag{FSR8}
\]
Their exact inverse is $q=K(\pi(q)+\tau(q)\mathbf1)$.
No label has been removed: $\pi(q)$ lies in the full labelled
hyperplane $\mathbf1^\perp$. In particular
$\pi(q_j)=e_j-\mathbf1/4$ and $\tau(q_j)=1/4$ for all four marks.

For completeness write $P_j(q)=\sum_\alpha p_{j,\alpha}q^\alpha$
with precisely the displayed monomials of FSR1. The whole
polynomial obstruction is
\[
\begin{split}
 \mathcal O(q,\lambda)&=EK^{-1}\bigl(P(q+\lambda n)-P(q)\bigr)
                  =\sum_{r=1}^8\lambda^r EK^{-1}A_r(q),\\
 (A_r(q))_j&=\sum_\alpha p_{j,\alpha}
       \sum_{\substack{\theta\le\alpha\\|\theta|=r}}
           \binom\alpha\theta q^{\alpha-\theta}n^\theta .
\end{split}\tag{FSR9}
\]
The multi-index formula is the binomial theorem applied to each
original monomial, and specifies every coefficient with its sign.
The machine-readable companion retains all eight complete vector
coefficients as exact polynomials. Descent of $P$ to the quotient
would require this entire obstruction to be zero.

Its leading coefficient can be evaluated without any omitted term.
The only degree-eight monomial of FSR1 is $2a^3y^4z$ in the last
component. Thus, for every $q$,
\[
 A_8(q)=\Lambda\,e_w,\qquad
 \Lambda=2n_a^3n_y^4n_z\ne0,
 \qquad
 EK^{-1}e_w=\frac1{308}
 \begin{pmatrix}17+i\sqrt2\\-3+i\sqrt2\\-13-i\sqrt2\\-1-i\sqrt2\end{pmatrix}.
 \tag{FSR10}
\]
Here $e_w=(0,0,0,1)^{\mathsf T}$ is the fourth ambient ES
coordinate vector; it is not the marked point $Ke_{\mathrm E}$.
Every factor of $\Lambda$ is nonzero by FSR6 and the displayed
four-label vector is nonzero. Consequently $\mathcal O(q,\lambda)$
has degree exactly eight in $\lambda$ for every $q$. The nonlinear
map does not descend through any entire old conductor fibre.
Equivalently $\Phi P(q+\lambda n)-\Phi P(q)$ is not always
constant. This proves the obstruction for the exact original map.

The obstruction also has a nonzero component in the original conductor
image. Let
$b^{(w)}(S)=\Phi e_w$. Exact interpolation from FSR2 gives
\[
 K^{-1}e_w=
 (6/77,1/77,-(3+i\sqrt2)/154,(3-i\sqrt2)/154)^{\mathsf T},
 \qquad
 [S^3]b^{(w)}(S)=
 -\frac{7\gamma+i(2\delta+\sqrt2\gamma)}
          {616\delta\gamma(\delta^2+\gamma^2)}\ne0.
 \tag{FSR11}
\]
To check the coefficient, the centered quartic is
$w^4+2(\gamma^2-\delta^2)w^2+(\delta^2+\gamma^2)^2$.
Its derivatives at the four roots are $\pm8i\delta\gamma w$.
The interpolation leading coefficient is the sum of each prescribed
value divided by that derivative, yielding FSR11; shifting $w=S-1/2$
does not change a cubic's leading coefficient. Therefore
\[
 [\lambda^8S'^2]\,T_A\Phi\bigl(P(q+\lambda n)-P(q)\bigr)
       =3\mu_1\Lambda\,[S^3]b^{(w)}\ne0.
 \tag{FSR12}
\]
The exact actual $\mu_1$ appears in this component. No change of
norm or arbitrary conductor coefficient is used to detect it.

\section{The exact total return with the one lost scalar restored}
Put $J=T_A\Phi:\C^4\to\mathcal P_2$. We construct the entire
inverse of the augmented old quotient
\[
 \Theta(q)=(Jq,\tau(q))\in\mathcal P_2\oplus\C.
 \tag{FSR13}
\]
Let $Y(S')=Y_0+Y_1S'+Y_2S'^2$. Define
\[
\begin{split}
 c_3&=Y_2/(3\mu_1),\qquad
 c_2=(Y_1-3\mu_2c_3)/(2\mu_1),\qquad
 c_1=(Y_0-\mu_2c_2-\mu_3c_3)/\mu_1,\\
 \sigma_1&=1/2,\quad
 \sigma_2=1/4+\delta^2-\gamma^2,\quad
 \sigma_3=1/8+\tfrac32(\delta^2-\gamma^2),\\
 c_0&=-\sigma_1c_1-\sigma_2c_2-\sigma_3c_3,
 \qquad p_Y(S)=\sum_{j=0}^3c_jS^j,\\
 \Theta^{-1}(Y,t)&=K\bigl(p_Y(\rho_j)+t\bigr)_j.
\end{split}\tag{FSR14}
\]
The values $\sigma_j$ are the exact quartet averages
$\tfrac14\sum_a\rho_a^j$. FSR5 proves $T_Ap_Y=Y$, and the
chosen $c_0$ proves $\tfrac14\sum_ap_Y(\rho_a)=0$.
Thus $\Theta\Theta^{-1}=I$. Conversely $\Phi q-p_{Jq}$ is
constant by FSR5 and its average is $\tau(q)$, proving the other
composition. Every old coordinate has therefore been recovered.

The strongest total polynomial correspondence on these fixed spaces
is now the explicit conjugate
\[
 \widehat P(Y,t)=
 \left(JP\bigl(K(p_Y(\rho_j)+t)_j\bigr),\quad
       \tau P\bigl(K(p_Y(\rho_j)+t)_j\bigr)\right),
 \qquad \Theta P=\widehat P\Theta,
 \qquad\det D\widehat P=-2.
 \tag{FSR15}
\]
All entries are the finite formulas FSR1--2 and FSR14. The last
identity follows from conjugation by the same invertible linear
$\Theta$, so its two determinants cancel exactly. The first
component genuinely depends on $t$ to degree eight by FSR12;
the omitted scalar cannot be suppressed in this correspondence.

There is nevertheless an exact three-dimensional slice containing
all four marked points. Define
\[
 F_{1/4}(Y)=JP\bigl(\Theta^{-1}(Y,1/4)\bigr).
 \tag{FSR16}
\]
All four $y_j$ from FSR7 belong to this same affine slice, and
\[
 \Theta(q_j)=(y_j,1/4),\qquad
 \widehat P(y_j,1/4)=(2iy_{\mathrm M},i/2),\qquad
 F_{1/4}(y_j)=2iy_{\mathrm M}.
 \tag{FSR17}
\]
This is a specified slice map, with its missing output scalar
retained in FSR15. It is not an assertion of descent along the
old kernel fibres.

Its derivative at every marked point is also computable exactly.
Let $\ell=\tfrac14\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}K^{-1}$. The cofactor
identity in the coordinates FSR13 gives
\[
 \det DF_{1/4}(y_j)=-2\ell\,(DP(q_j))^{-1}n.
 \tag{FSR18}
\]
Indeed the desired determinant is the upper-left three-by-three
minor of $\Theta DP(q_j)\Theta^{-1}$; its complementary inverse
entry is $\ell(DP(q_j))^{-1}n$, and its full determinant is $-2$.
Evaluation gives the following complete table:
\[
\begin{array}{c|l}
 j&616\det DF_{1/4}(y_j)\\\hline
 \mathrm M&3580+8830i-4\sqrt2(549+1003i)\\
 \mathrm N&-80720-12413i-8\sqrt2(1247+746i)\\
 \mathrm T&-39134+21326i+\sqrt2(3107-124144i)\\
 \mathrm E&-108226+40740i+\sqrt2(-2587+216544i)
\end{array}\tag{FSR19}
\]
Each entry is nonzero since its imaginary part has a nonzero rational
coefficient in the basis $1,\sqrt2$. In particular these are four
distinct regular inputs with one common output. The first two
determinants differ, so this three-dimensional slice does not have
the constant Jacobian of the complete four-dimensional polynomial.
Every assertion here is an exact value at a named marked point;
no sampled value has been used as a global determinant proof.

\section{The complete original quotient metric and actual-order return}
The section $p_Y$ in FSR14 was chosen by the label mean; its metric
correction is retained explicitly. Use the original source centre
$c=a_{\rm amp}/2$, source order $s\in\{1,a_{\rm amp}\}$,
$b=s/2$ and mass $M=(2\pi)^{s/2}$. The original Gamma moments give
\[
 \frac{\langle1,p_Y\rangle_U}{M}
  =c_0+cc_1+(c^2-b)c_2+(c^3-3cb)c_3=:\chi(Y),
 \quad
 \|p_Y+t\|_U^2=
 \|p_Y\|_U^2-M|\chi(Y)|^2+M|t+\chi(Y)|^2.
 \tag{FSR20}
\]
The convention is $\langle f,g\rangle=\int\bar f g\,dm_s$.
For the first formula substitute $S=c+iy$; the unchanged measure
has mass $M$, zero odd moments and $\int y^2dm_s=Mb$ by WCF2.
The second follows by expanding the two squares. It retains all
cross terms between the lost constant coordinate and the chosen
section. The attained quotient norm is therefore exactly
$\|p_Y\|_U^2-M|\chi(Y)|^2$, with minimizing scalar $t=-\chi(Y)$.
The target is the inherited original $\mathcal P_2$ norm at centre
$a_{\rm amp}/2-4$, with its same mass and order. Thus the nonlinear
obstruction was not obtained by imposing a new metric on the quotient.

Finally the actual order-one four-column receiver has an exact
relation to this singular old receiver. Define
\[
 \Phi_1q=[S\Phi q]\in\mathcal P_4/\mathcal P_0,
 \qquad \Psi_1q=T_A(S\Phi q)\in\mathcal P_3.
 \tag{FSR21}
\]
Multiplication by $S$ is the displayed coefficient isomorphism
from $\mathcal P_3$ to these classes; division of their unique
representatives with zero constant coefficient gives its inverse.
The original $T_A$ in these corrected spaces is an isomorphism:
its four successive leading coefficients are
$\mu_1,2\mu_1,3\mu_1,4\mu_1$. In particular
\[
 [T_A]_{S,S^2,S^3,S^4}^{1,S',S'^2,S'^3}=
 \begin{pmatrix}
 \mu_1&\mu_2&\mu_3&\mu_4\\
 0&2\mu_1&3\mu_2&4\mu_3\\
 0&0&3\mu_1&6\mu_2\\
 0&0&0&4\mu_1
 \end{pmatrix},\qquad
 \det\Psi_1=\frac{24\mu_1^4}{(\det V_\rho)(\det K)}\ne0,
 \qquad \Phi_1n=[S],\qquad \Psi_1n=\mu_1.
 \tag{FSR22}
\]
These determinants use the coefficient basis $S,S^2,S^3,S^4$
in the source and $1,S',S'^2,S'^3$ in the target, exactly as stated;
the original quotient and target Gamma norms remain unchanged.

The exact correction between the two receiving maps is
\[
 \Psi_1q=S'Jq+T_{E_A'}\Phi q,\qquad
 T_{E_A'}f(S')=\sum_\nu a_\nu\beta_\nu f(S'+\beta_\nu).
 \tag{FSR23}
\]
Here $E_A(\xi)=\sum_\nu a_\nu e^{\beta_\nu\xi}$ is the entire
original collected conductor with all its amplitudes and exponents.
Expanding $(S'+\beta_\nu)f(S'+\beta_\nu)$ proves FSR23 term
by term. The correction has moments $\mu_{j+1}$ and nonzero
constant diagonal $\mu_1$, so it restores the lost direction
explicitly rather than hiding it. On the actual order-one spaces,
\[
 P_U^{(1)}=\Phi_1P\Phi_1^{-1},\qquad
 P_W^{(1)}=\Psi_1P\Psi_1^{-1},\qquad
 T_AP_U^{(1)}=P_W^{(1)}T_A.
 \tag{FSR24}
\]
Both compositions are legitimate isomorphism conjugations, and
their four marked inputs remain distinct. Equations FSR9--12,
FSR13--20 and FSR21--24 together give the complete relation:
the nonlinear polynomial fails to descend through the singular
old kernel, its old quotient has an exact return with one scalar
restored, and its actual-order return is intertwined by the same
original conductor with the full correction FSR23.


\section{Every original unit gives nonconstant factors and nonzero finite complex zeros}
Retain the complete original data of PCL1--10, OFM1--11 and FUT1--4
\cite{PCLOriginal,NC,Cumulative,PeriodZeroOriginal}. In particular
$0<\delta<1/2$, $\gamma>2$, $a=\alpha+i\chi\ne0$ with real
$\alpha,\chi$, $\beta=2(\gamma^2-\delta^2)>0$,
$\eta=(\delta^2+\gamma^2)^2$, and $k=2\delta\gamma>0$.
Write
\[
 F_j(z)=f_j(0,z)
 =Q_0\!\left(U^{-1}V\mathcal R(z)^{-1}D_5^{-j}
                  \mathcal R(z)V^{-1}U\boldsymbol1\right),
 \qquad j=1,2,3,4.
 \tag{ANP1}
\]
Here $z=1/u$ is the actual inverse original period, not the
exponential-curve variable. The functions in ANP1 are even entire.
We prove the following assertions for every allowed original unit:
\[
 \boxed{\quad
 ([z^2]F_j,[z^4]F_j)\ne(0,0),\qquad
 F_j\text{ has a zero }z_j\in\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}.
 \quad}\tag{ANP2}
\]
Thus there are no real unit phases for which all nonconstant
inverse-period coefficients vanish. This assertion does not select
the unit or any coefficient independently of its original period.

\subsection{The complete second and fourth coefficients with the original unit}
The following auxiliary coefficient variables retain an exact inverse
map to the unit and its denominator:
\[
 x=\frac\eta{\beta^2},\quad
 p=\alpha+\frac{\beta\chi}{2k},\quad b=\frac{\beta\chi}{k},
 \quad
 \alpha=p-b/2,\quad\chi=kb/\beta,\quad
 \alpha^2+\chi^2=p^2-pb+xb^2.
 \tag{ANP3}
\]
The allowed original domain gives $x>1/4$; in fact
$1/4<x<289/900$ because $0<\delta^2/\gamma^2<1/16$.
No original coordinate, unit scale, or denominator is discarded.
For $q=\zeta_5^{-j}$ define the polynomials $H_2(y,x,q)$ and
$H_4(y,x,q)$ by the full coefficient table at the end of this section:
$H_n=\sum_{r=0}^4h_{n,r}(x,q)y^r$.
The complete exact original coefficients are
\[
 \boxed{\quad
 [z^n]F_j(z)=
 \frac{4i\delta\gamma\,\beta^{5n/2-1}}
      {(\alpha^2+\chi^2)^2}
       \sum_{r=0}^4h_{n,r}(x,q)p^rb^{4-r},
       \qquad n=2,4.
 \quad}\tag{ANP4}
\]
For $b\ne0$ the numerator sum is $b^4H_n(p/b,x,q)$.
For $b=0$ it is $p^4h_{n,4}(x,q)$; this endpoint is retained
throughout. All four factors use their own original fifth root.

Here is a finite derivation of every table entry, also supplying an
independent way to reproduce the full coefficients. Use the PCL2
series, its inverse coefficients $I_n$, and the original $G_n$
defined in OPB9, through $n=4$. In the original coefficient basis put
\[
 T=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&0&-\eta\\1&0&0&0\\0&1&0&-\beta\\0&0&1&0\end{pmatrix},
 \quad W=pI+(b/\beta)T^2,\quad
 \bar W=(p-b)I-(b/\beta)T^2,
 \quad v_n=\bar W G_n W e_0.
 \tag{ANP5}
\]
The original unit is exactly multiplication by $W$, and
$\bar WW=(\alpha^2+\chi^2)I$, using
$T^4+\beta T^2+\eta I=0$. Thus
\[
 [z^n]F_j=
 \frac{4i\delta\gamma}{(\alpha^2+\chi^2)^2}
              \sum_{r=0}^n v_r^{\mathsf T}Qv_{n-r}.
 \tag{ANP6}
\]
This proves the table by finite multiplication, retaining every
ordered quadratic contribution and every original unit entry.
For the extracted power of $\beta$ in ANP4, a PCL2 entry has
the exact weighted degree $5n+r+1-a$ in the centered-root scale.
More explicitly, for $S=\operatorname{diag}(1,\beta^{1/2},\beta,\beta^{3/2})$,
its coefficient identity is
$R_n(\beta,\beta^2x)=\beta^{5n/2}S^{-1}R_n(1,x)S$.
The same identity holds for $G_n$; also
$T(\beta,\beta^2x)^2=\beta S^{-1}T(1,x)^2S$ and
$Q(\beta,\beta^2x)=\beta^{-1}S^{\mathsf T}Q(1,x)S$.
Inserting these identities into ANP6 gives exactly
$\beta^{5n/2-1}$ and the homogeneous quartic displayed in ANP4.
These are identities between the full matrices with their inverse
maps; the original $\beta,\eta,a$ are present on the left and
are restored with all their factors in ANP4.

\subsection{Exact elimination of simultaneous coefficient vanishing}
Write $H_n=\sum_{i=0}^3A_{n,i}(y,x)q^i$ using the table's
reduction modulo $q^4+q^3+q^2+q+1$. Put $s=\sqrt5$ and
\[
 P_n=4A_{n,0}+(s-1)A_{n,1}-(s+1)(A_{n,2}+A_{n,3}),
 \quad
 J_n=2A_{n,1}+(s-1)(A_{n,2}-A_{n,3}).
 \tag{ANP7}
\]
For real $x,y$ these are four times the real part and a nonzero
real multiple of the imaginary part at $q=e^{2\pi i/5}$,
as proved in FUT5--6. The same vanishing test applies at its conjugate.
Thus simultaneous coefficient vanishing for that original factor pair
would imply
$P_2=J_2=P_4=J_4=0$.

The complete degree-four resultant in $y$ is
\[
 \operatorname{Res}_y(P_2,J_2)
 =C(x-1/4)(x-1/9)^2\mathfrak F(x),\qquad
 C=-\frac{492160000000}{59049}
      +\frac{24448000000}{6561}\sqrt5,
 \tag{ANP8}
\]
where $\mathfrak F$ is monic of degree $19$ over $\mathbb Q(\sqrt5)$.
It is specified completely either by this exact determinant identity
and ANP7 or by its coefficient table below.
The identity is obtained by the eight-by-eight Sylvester determinant
of the two displayed quartics; exact polynomial division leaves the
degree-nineteen factor and the nonzero constant $C$ shown.
The factors $x-1/4$ and $x-1/9$ cannot vanish on the original domain.

The following small cofactor matrix makes the residual phase equation
an explicit consequence of $P_2=J_2=0$. Form the $6$ by $7$ matrix
$M$ whose rows are the coefficients in descending powers
$y^6,\ldots,y^0$ of
\[
               y^2P_2,\ yP_2,\ P_2,\ y^2J_2,\ yJ_2,\ J_2.
 \tag{ANP9}
\]
Let $M_{0:4}$ denote its first five columns, and put
\[
 A(x)=\det[M_{0:4}\mid M_5],\qquad
 B(x)=\det[M_{0:4}\mid M_6].
 \tag{ANP10}
\]
Their degrees are $14$ and $15$ respectively.
Laplace expansion along the last column gives the same coefficients
for the linear combination of the six row polynomials in both
determinants. The coefficients of $y^6,\ldots,y^2$ vanish because
the corresponding determinant has a repeated column. Hence
$A(x)y+B(x)$ is a polynomial combination of $P_2,J_2$.
In particular every common zero of those original quartics satisfies
$A(x)y+B(x)=0$, including specializations of $x$.

Here are finite exact certificates proving that this residual equation
never also makes $P_4$ vanish. They use the prime $101$ and the
homomorphism $\sqrt5\mapsto45$, since $45^2=5$ in $\mathbb F_{101}$.
All coefficient sequences below are in ascending powers of $x$.
The two tables together list degrees $0$ through $19$, with trailing
zeros displayed where the degree is smaller.

In these tables $\bar F,\bar A,\bar B$ are the exact reductions

identities
\[
 \bar A\,a=1\pmod{\bar F},\qquad
 Y=-\bar B a\pmod{\bar F},\qquad

 \tag{ANP11}

Here $P_4$ on the right is reduced by the same homomorphism.
Each identity is verified by multiplication and division by the
listed monic degree-nineteen polynomial. In particular both inverse

We spell out why this modular certificate proves the required
characteristic-zero assertion. Express every coefficient of
$\mathfrak F,A,B,P_4,J_4$ as $r+t\sqrt5$ with rational $r,t$.
Their denominators, and those of ANP8, are all prime to $101$;
this is checked directly from the displayed coefficient formulas
and the two determinants. Thus these data lie in a localization
$\mathcal O$ of $\mathbb Z[\sqrt5]$ at integers prime to $101$,
and the stated reduction is a well-defined ring homomorphism.
The leading constant $C$ reduces to $37\ne0$.
The polynomial $\mathfrak F$ is monic before and after reduction,
so $\mathcal O[x]/(\mathfrak F)$ is a free module of rank nineteen
in the unchanged power basis. Determinants of multiplication maps
in that basis commute with this reduction.

The first inverse in ANP11 makes multiplication by $\bar A$
invertible. Its multiplication determinant is therefore nonzero
modulo $101$, hence nonzero over $\mathbb Q(\sqrt5)$.
Consequently $A$ is invertible modulo $\mathfrak F$ in
characteristic zero. Now define the actual polynomial
\[
              H(x)=A(x)^4P_4(-B(x)/A(x),x).
 \tag{ANP12}
\]
It is polynomial because $P_4$ has degree at most four in its first
argument. Its reduction modulo $\bar F$ equals $\bar A^4 E$,
which is invertible by both inverse identities in ANP11.
Therefore its multiplication determinant is also nonzero in
characteristic zero. This proves
\[
          \gcd(A,\mathfrak F)=1,\qquad
          \gcd(H,\mathfrak F)=1
              \quad\text{over }\mathbb Q(\sqrt5).
 \tag{ANP13}
\]
No preservation of the leading degree of $H$ is needed in this
argument: both determinants act on the same free algebra of rank
nineteen defined by the monic $\mathfrak F$. The listed reductions
also preserve the actual degrees $14$ and $15$ of $A$ and $B$.

If $P_2=J_2=P_4=0$ at an original real $x>1/4$, ANP8 forces
$\mathfrak F(x)=0$, ANP10 forces $Ay+B=0$, and the first identity
in ANP13 ensures $A(x)\ne0$. Then $H(x)=0$, contradicting the
second identity in ANP13. This excludes simultaneous vanishing for
the first conjugate pair.

For completeness the other pair is covered by the exact coefficient
automorphism $\sigma:\sqrt5\mapsto-\sqrt5$.
If $\widetilde P_n,\widetilde J_n$ are the second-pair equations
in FUT5, direct substitution gives
$\sigma(P_n)=\widetilde P_n$ and
$\sigma(J_n)=(\sqrt5+1)\widetilde J_n/2$.
The scalar is nonzero. Applying $\sigma$ to the characteristic-zero
identities ANP8--13 therefore proves the same exclusion for that pair.
This uses an exact field automorphism after the modular nonvanishing
has been established, and does not assume that a second modular
specialization has any particular leading coefficient.

The phase endpoint $b=0$ was not present in the affine variable $y$.
The coefficient table gives
\[
 h_{2,4}(x,q)=
       -\frac{q^4(1-9x)(q-1)(q^2+3q+1)}{81}\ne0.
 \tag{ANP14}
\]
The roots of $q^2+3q+1$ are real and negative, whereas the four
nontrivial fifth roots are nonreal; the other factors are also nonzero.
Since $p=\alpha\ne0$ at this endpoint, ANP4 proves its second
coefficient is nonzero. This completes the first assertion of ANP2
for every original unit, including both endpoints of every phase chart.

\subsection{The second boundary phase also has a nonzero fourth coefficient}
The exact original boundary calculation OPB5--6 gives
$F_j(0)=0$ precisely on $\chi=0$ or $\alpha+\beta\chi/(6k)=0$.
The first is the endpoint $b=0$, whose nonzero second and fourth
coefficients are PZX1--6 and FUT24--26.
The second has $b\ne0$ and $p/b=1/3$ by ANP3.
Set $P=P_4(1/3,x)$, $J=J_4(1/3,x)$.
The exact coefficient table shows that both are divisible by
$x-1/9$. Write $P=(x-1/9)P_*$ and $J=(x-1/9)J_*$.
Their reduced coefficients and a complete B\'ezout identity are

\[

The table uses ascending powers, and its last two rows satisfy
$S\bar P_*+T\bar J_*=1$ exactly in $\mathbb F_{101}[x]$.
Both $P_*,J_*$ have degree five before and after reduction: their
reduced leading coefficients are $11$ and $14$, respectively.
All their rational coefficient denominators are prime to $101$.
Thus their degree-five resultant reduces to a nonzero resultant;
it is nonzero in characteristic zero. It follows that
$P_*,J_*$ have no common complex zero over $\mathbb Q(\sqrt5)$.
Since $x>1/4$, the removed factor does not vanish, so
$P_4(1/3,x)$ and $J_4(1/3,x)$ cannot both vanish.
The automorphism argument above gives the same result for the other
pair. Equation ANP4 restores the nonzero original unit denominator
and proves $[z^4]F_j\ne0$ on this second phase as well.
The already proved PZX order-two coefficient is nonzero there.
We have therefore proved on both complete boundary phase lines
\[
          F_j(0)=0,\qquad [z^2]F_j\ne0,
                     \qquad [z^4]F_j\ne0.
 \tag{ANP15}
\]

\subsection{Nonzero finite complex zeros for all original units}
The FPZ25 entire-function estimate applies to the original arbitrary
unit without a changed constant. In the matrix norm used there,
$\|U\|_\infty=|a|$ and $\|U^{-1}\|_\infty=|a|^{-1}$, since
all four diagonal entries have the same modulus. Their product is one.
With the same actual $v_V=\|V\|_\infty$, $v_I=\|V^{-1}\|_\infty$,
$C_R,T_R$ and $H(r)=2C_R(1+T_Rr)e^{T_Rr}$ as FPZ25, ANP1 gives
\[
 |F_j(z)|\le2(96v_Vv_I)^2H(|z|)^8
          \le A(1+|z|)^8e^{B|z|},
 \quad
 A=2(96v_Vv_I)^2(2C_R)^8\max(1,T_R)^8,\quad B=8T_R.
 \tag{ANP16}
\]
All phase entries remain in the actual function; the displayed
equality of norms only proves this uniform growth estimate.

Off the two phase lines in ANP15, the exact boundary value is nonzero.
If $F_j$ were zero-free, it would have an entire logarithm $h$,
obtained by integrating $F_j'/F_j$ on the simply connected plane.
The growth estimate bounds $\operatorname{Re}h$ on $|z|=R$ by
$M_R=A_0+BR+8\log(1+R)$. Its power-series coefficients satisfy
$|h_n|\le2(M_R-\operatorname{Re}h(0))/R^n$ by the Fourier and
mean-value calculation in FPZ26. Letting $R\to\infty$ gives
$h_n=0$ for $n\ge2$. Since $F_j$ is even, the identity
$e^{2h_1z}=1$ for every $z$ forces $h_1=0$ by differentiation.
Thus a zero-free $F_j$ would be constant. This contradicts the first
assertion of ANP2, already proved by complete coefficient elimination.
It therefore has a zero, and that zero is nonzero because $F_j(0)\ne0$.

On either boundary phase, the zero at the origin alone would not
prove a finite original-period zero. ANP15 resolves that point.
If there were no nonzero zero, then $F_j(z)/z^2$ would be an even
entire zero-free function with nonzero value at the origin and the
same type of growth bound. The preceding logarithm argument would
make it constant. That would contradict $[z^4]F_j\ne0$ in ANP15.
Hence a nonzero zero exists on those phases too.
This proves the second assertion of ANP2 for each of the four
original factors, on the full original parameter and unit domain.

Every such zero gives a finite nonzero original period $u_j=1/z_j$.
Evenness retains the companion zero $-z_j$ of the same factor;
OFM9 retains the exact conjugate-factor correspondence.
This existence proof alone does not prove that an arbitrarily chosen
zero lies in the five-orbit locus, nor that its symbol order is one.
Those stronger conclusions at the particular certified point in
FPZ4--14 remain the conclusions of that full certificate.

\section{A certified moving singularity in the original unit phase}
\label{sec:unit-phase-persistence}
The finite point FPZ4 extends to a nonconstant holomorphic curve of
simple zeros of the complete original factor. This section supplies an
explicit phase disk, the full-series bounds proving that statement,
and its exact effect on the original weighted conductor. It also
proves a singularity by varying the actual unit while keeping the
certified period fixed. The quartet remains the geometric member
$\delta=1/4$, $\gamma=3$ of FPZ1. This calculation does not identify
that quartet with arithmetic zeta zeros. Original period and weighted
coordinates are those of \cite{PCLOriginal,WCF}; the four ES marks
and their human sources remain \cite{ES488} and FSR1--24.

\subsection{The exact two-parameter family}
Use the exact rational centre $c$ in FPZ4, and put
\[
 r=10^{-9},\qquad \varepsilon=10^{-10},\qquad
 a=\alpha(1+ix),\quad \alpha\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\},
 \quad J=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,-1,1),\quad W(x)=I+ixJ.
 \tag{UPP1}
\]
For real $x$, the original matrix is
$U=\alpha W=\operatorname{diag}(a,\bar a,\bar a,a)$.
Its magnitude is $|\alpha|\sqrt{1+x^2}$ and has not been assigned
a new value. The scalar $\alpha$ cancels with its exact inverse in
the original conjugation. For $|x|<1$ define its holomorphic extension by
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 W^{-1}&=(I-ixJ)/(1+x^2),\\
 M_j(z,x)&=W^{-1}V R(z)^{-1}D_jR(z)V^{-1}W,\\
 f_j(\xi,z,x)&=Q_0(M_j(z,x)(e^{\rho_a\xi})_a),\quad
 d_j(z,x)=f_j(0,z,x),\\
 E_A(\xi,z,x)&=\prod_{j=1}^4 f_j(\xi,z,x),\quad
 \mu_n(z,x)=\partial_\xi^n E_A(0,z,x).
 \end{aligned}\tag{UPP2}
\]
Here $R,V,D_j,\rho_a$ are exactly FPZ1--3. Complex $x$ is used
for analytic continuation; the two entries $\alpha(1\pm ix)$ are
the actual conjugate unit entries precisely on the real phase axis.
No branch factor or Gamma ray factor in the original $H$ is changed.
The identity with $H^{-1}D_jH$ follows directly from PCL7--9.

There is a unique holomorphic function $z(x)$ on $|x|<\varepsilon$
with a continuous extension to its closed disk such that
\[
 |z(x)-c|<r,\quad d_1(z(x),x)=0,\quad z(0)=z_*.
 \tag{UPP3}
\]
All four factors are retained. On this entire closed phase disk,
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 m(x)&=\mu_1(z(x),x)
     =(f_1)_\xi(0,z(x),x)\prod_{j=2}^4d_j(z(x),x),
       &|m(x)|&>14.01,\\
 b(x)&=(\mu_0)_z(z(x),x)
     =(d_1)_z(z(x),x)\prod_{j=2}^4d_j(z(x),x),
       &|b(x)|&>1516,\\
 e(x)&=(\mu_0)_x(z(x),x)
     =(d_1)_x(z(x),x)\prod_{j=2}^4d_j(z(x),x),
       &|e(x)|&>53.65.
 \end{aligned}\tag{UPP4}
\]
The full enclosing proof of these numerical assertions follows.

\subsection{Every derivative and every infinite tail used in the certificate}
Put $A=R^{-1}$ and retain the indicated noncommuting matrix orders.
Twice differentiating $AR=I$ gives
$A_z=-AR_zA$ and $A_{zz}=2AR_zAR_zA-AR_{zz}A$. Therefore
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 C_j&=AD_jR,\quad (C_j)_z=AD_jR_z-AR_zAD_jR,\\
 (C_j)_{zz}&=AD_jR_{zz}-2AR_zAD_jR_z
       +2AR_zAR_zAD_jR-AR_{zz}AD_jR,\\
 (M_j)_{z^h}&=W^{-1}V(C_j)_{z^h}V^{-1}W\quad(h=0,1,2),\\
 (M_j)_x&=i[M_j,J]/(1+x^2),\quad
 (M_j)_{zx}=i[(M_j)_z,J]/(1+x^2),\\
 (M_j)_{xx}&=-\{[[M_j,J],J]+2ix[M_j,J]\}/(1+x^2)^2.
 \end{aligned}\tag{UPP5}
\]
The phase formulas follow by differentiating $W^{-1}NW$:
$W^{-1}W_x=(xI+iJ)/(1+x^2)$, whose scalar summand commutes with
$M_j$. A second differentiation gives the last formula.
Define the complex bilinear form
$\mathfrak b(v,w)=v_1w_4+v_4w_1-v_2w_3-v_3w_2$.
For $y=M_j\mathbf1$, $h=M_j(\rho_a)_a$, the complete derivatives are
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 d_j&=\mathfrak b(y,y)/2,&(d_j)_z&=\mathfrak b(y,y_z),\\
 (d_j)_{zz}&=\mathfrak b(y_z,y_z)+\mathfrak b(y,y_{zz}),&
 (d_j)_x&=\mathfrak b(y,y_x),\\
 (d_j)_{zx}&=\mathfrak b(y_x,y_z)+\mathfrak b(y,y_{zx}),&
 (d_j)_{xx}&=\mathfrak b(y_x,y_x)+\mathfrak b(y,y_{xx}),\\
 (f_j)_\xi&=\mathfrak b(y,h),&
 (f_j)_{\xi z}&=\mathfrak b(y_z,h)+\mathfrak b(y,h_z),\\
 (f_j)_{\xi x}&=\mathfrak b(y_x,h)+\mathfrak b(y,h_x).
 \end{aligned}\tag{UPP6}
\]
These identities are product rules for the original quadratic,
not Hermitian replacements. Every $\rho_a$ retains its original $1/2$.

The coefficient bound FPZ6 is used with $N=400$, $K=11/2$,
$C_R=4K^3$, $T_R=6K^5/5$. Let $\varrho$ be an outward modulus
bound on the closed rectangle
$|\Re(z-c)|,|\Im(z-c)|\le r$, and put $w=T_R\varrho$.
Besides FPZ7's $\tau_0,\tau_1$, the omitted second derivative has bound
\[
 \tau_2=
 \frac{C_R(2N+4)N(N+1)T_R^2w^{N-1}}
 {(N+1)!\{1-w(N+3)/(N(N+2))\}}.
 \tag{UPP7}
\]
Indeed its $n$th majorant is
$C_R(2n+2)T_R^2w^{n-2}/(n-2)!$; the ratio of successive terms is
$w(n+2)/((n+1)(n-1))$, bounded by $w(N+3)/(N(N+2))$ for
$n\ge N+1$. The computed denominator is positive. Geometric
summation gives UPP7, including every omitted coefficient.
All three polynomial derivatives are evaluated by simultaneous Horner
recursion $P_2\leftarrow zP_2+2P_1$,
$P_1\leftarrow zP_1+P$, $P\leftarrow zP+R_n$, in that order,
and their respective tails are added entrywise.

The certificate improves the matrix enclosure by an exact Taylor
integral, retaining the same full functions. On a rectangle centred
at $c$, let $h$ bound $|z-c|$ and let $L_{ar}$ bound $|R''_{ar}|$
from the complete derivative enclosure. Then
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 |R_{ar}(z)-R_{ar}(c)-R'_{ar}(c)(z-c)|&\le L_{ar}h^2/2,\\
 |R'_{ar}(z)-R'_{ar}(c)|&\le L_{ar}h.
 \end{aligned}\tag{UPP8}
\]
Every segment from $c$ stays inside this rectangle; this restriction
is essential to UPP8. In the rectangle, $h$ includes its diagonal
factor $\sqrt2$. The scalar zero count below instead uses the
inscribed disks $|z-c|\le r$, $|x|\le\varepsilon$.

The homotopy to $A_c(z-c)$ has no boundary zero. The argument

The refined scalar enclosures use exactly the same segment argument.
For each factor let $p_j=d_j(c,0)$ and $p_{j,z}=(d_j)_z(c,0)$.

$L_{j,zx}r+L_{j,xx}\varepsilon$.
For $(f_j)_\xi$ it is
$L_{j,\xi z}r+L_{j,\xi x}\varepsilon$.
These enclosing radii are added to both real and imaginary parts.
In particular the receipt proves
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 \Im(f_1)_\xi>3.68,\qquad
 -.230259<\Re d_2<-.230257,\\
 -2.422916<\Re d_3<-2.422904,\qquad
 -3.348013<\Re d_4<-3.348007.
 \end{gathered}\tag{UPP13}
\]
All four relevant quantities are nonzero. Multiplying the complete
complex enclosures gives UPP4, including its stronger product bounds.
Thus the symbol order is exactly one everywhere on the graph.
FPZ14's prime-five orbit proof applies at each point: a shorter
orbit would make $f_1(\xi)$ identically zero, contradicting UPP13.
All five quadrics are therefore irreducible and nonassociated there.

\subsection{The graph moves, and a fixed period gives a phase singularity}
Differentiating the exact zero identity gives
\[
 z'(x)=-\frac{(d_1)_x}{(d_1)_z}(z(x),x)
       =-\frac{e(x)}{b(x)},\qquad
 u'(x)=\frac{(d_1)_x}{z(x)^2(d_1)_z},\quad u(x)=1/z(x).
 \tag{UPP14}
\]
The disk excludes zero. UPP10--12 give $|z'(x)|<1.145$ and hence
$|z(x)-z(0)|<1.145|x|$. A second run of the same full-series
certificate, with period radius $10^{-14}$ and phase radius
$10^{-30}$, retains the same root at $x=0$. Its separate receipt
\texttt{UNIT\_PHASE\_TANGENT\_CERTIFICATE.json} gives
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 z'(0)&\in[-.03099394451\pm5.37\cdot10^{-12}]
       +i[.011074723404\pm7.11\cdot10^{-13}],\\
 e(0)&\in[21.49053615\pm2.97\cdot10^{-9}]
       +i[-49.20852959\pm2.47\cdot10^{-9}],\qquad |e(0)|>53.696.
 \end{aligned}\tag{UPP15}
\]
Both derivatives are nonzero; neither statement is a numerical
guess at an unenclosed root. Thus $\mu_0(z_*,x)=e(0)x+O(x^2)$
at the fixed exact period $z_*$. The remaining three factors remain
nonzero by UPP13.

Here is also an exact two-parameter description of the singularity.
Within the period disk the identity
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \mu_0(z,x)&=(z-z(x))\,\mathcal B(z,x),\\
 \mathcal B(z,x)&=
 \left[\int_0^1(d_1)_z(z(x)+t(z-z(x)),x)\,dt\right]
                  \prod_{j=2}^4d_j(z,x)
 \end{aligned}\tag{UPP16}
\]
has $\mathcal B(z(x),x)=b(x)$.
Every derivative in the integral differs from $A_c$ by less than
$|A_c|-426.55$, so the integral never vanishes. UPP13 excludes
zeros of the other factors. Thus $\mathcal B$ is holomorphic and
nowhere zero on this bidisk. The zero locus is precisely the graph
UPP3, and its projection to either coordinate has nonzero tangent
at the base point by UPP15.

\subsection{The full original weighted return on both transverse paths}
Keep $a_{\rm amp}=4\ell+1\ge9$, $s\in\{1,a_{\rm amp}\}$,
$c_0=a_{\rm amp}/2$, $c_1=c_0-4$, the full measure $dm_s$,
and $\rho_n=\sqrt{n!/(s/2)_n}$. Define $B_{D,s}(z,x)$ by FPZ15,
using the complete $E_A(\xi,z,x)$. Its diagonal is $\mu_0$ and
its next diagonal on the graph is $-im(x)\rho_{j+1}/\rho_j$.
Hence at every graph point it has rank $D$, kernel the constant
polynomial, image $\mathcal P_{D-1}$, and
\[
 \det B_{D,s}(z,x)=\mu_0(z,x)^{D+1}.
 \tag{UPP17}
\]
The first column and last row vanish there and the remaining
$D$ by $D$ block has nonzero diagonal, proving all those assertions.
Let $n=D+1$. For an invertible $n$ by $n$ matrix $B$, multiplying
its ordered singular values proves
$\|\bigwedge^r B^{-1}\|=\|\bigwedge^{n-r}B\|/|\det B|$.
Continuity of the forward exterior powers, UPP4, UPP15 and UPP17
therefore prove both exact limits, for every $1\le r\le D+1$:
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \lim_{z\to z(x)} |z-z(x)|^{D+1}
       \|\bigwedge^r B_{D,s}(z,x)^{-1}\|
 &=\frac{\|\bigwedge^{D+1-r}B_{D,s}(z(x),x)\|}{|b(x)|^{D+1}}>0,\\
 \lim_{x\to0} |x|^{D+1}
       \|\bigwedge^r B_{D,s}(z_*,x)^{-1}\|
 &=\frac{\|\bigwedge^{D+1-r}B_{D,s}(z_*,0)\|}{|e(0)|^{D+1}}>0.
 \end{aligned}\tag{UPP18}
\]
The second limit includes the actual real unit path
$a=\alpha(1+ix)$; it is not a newly introduced nonlinear conductor.
There is one inverse singular value with pole $D+1$, and $D$ with
finite positive limits, on both paths. In degree three every inverse
exterior rank has pole four. The numerators are the complete original
Gamma-weighted exterior norms, with no scalar coefficient omitted.
For $r=1$ their common numerator is $\rho_D|m(0)|^D$ at the base
point, as follows by multiplying the $D$ nonzero diagonal entries
of the remaining block. The original $u$-coordinate version of the
first limit has the factor $|u(x)|^{2(D+1)}$ from FPZ24.

The actual order-one quotient also remains present:
\[
 T_A:\mathcal P_{D+1}/\mathcal P_0\longrightarrow\mathcal P_D,
 \qquad \hbox{diagonal }-im(x)\rho_{j+1}/\rho_j\ne0.
 \tag{UPP19}
\]
Thus its invertibility and the fixed old space singularity are proved
in their exact respective domains. For the four-label ES return, keep
the literal $K$, $V_\rho$, and polynomial $P$ of FSR1--4. The maps
are exactly
\[
 \Phi=(V_\rho^{\mathsf T})^{-1}K^{-1},\quad
 J_x=T_{A(z(x),x)}\Phi,\quad
 \Theta_x(q)=(J_xq,\tfrac14\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}K^{-1}q),\quad
 \widehat P_x=\Theta_xP\Theta_x^{-1}.
 \tag{UPP20}
\]
The inverse in FSR12--14 uses division only by $m(x)$ and the
fixed invertible matrices, so UPP4 proves it throughout this graph.
The common kernel remains $K\mathbf1$; all four marks remain
distinct, and the exact degree-eight obstruction FSR7--10 remains
nonzero because its leading target coefficient is a nonzero fixed
constant times $m(x)$. All original moments $\mu_2,\mu_3$ and the
Gamma cross term FSR20 remain in that inverse and metric. The
actual-order identity $\Psi_1=S'J_x+T_{E_A'}\Phi$ and determinant
$24m(x)^4/(\det V_\rho\det K)$ from FSR22--24 also hold with
these actual moving moments. These are explicit continuations of
the proved four-point return, with its correction and lost scalar
retained; no descent through the unaugmented quotient is presumed.

\section{Every original unit forces a finite singularity in the fixed old conductor spaces}
The global existence result ANP2 has a direct consequence for the original
linear conductor itself, without selecting its moments independently.
Fix any original $0<\delta<1/2$, $\gamma>2$ and any nonzero original
unit $a=\alpha+i\chi$. Define the original entire function
\[
 G(z)=\mu_0(z)=E_A(0,z)=\prod_{j=1}^4F_j(z).
 \tag{GUC1}
\]
Every $F_j$ is nonconstant by ANP2, hence is not identically zero.
The identity theorem then implies that their product is not identically
zero. ANP2 supplies a nonzero finite zero $z_0$ of each chosen factor,
so in particular $G(z_0)=0$. Its multiplicity is a finite positive
integer $\nu$; write its complete local factorization as
\[
 G(z)=(z-z_0)^\nu h(z),\qquad
 h(z_0)=\frac{G^{(\nu)}(z_0)}{\nu!}\ne0.
 \tag{GUC2}
\]
This follows from the first nonzero Taylor coefficient of the nonzero
entire function. Its order equals the sum of the vanishing orders of
the four actual factors at $z_0$, with zero contribution from each
nonvanishing factor. No common factor or multiplicity is removed.

Retain every original Gamma measure, both centres and
$\rho_n=\sqrt{n!/(s/2)_n}$, with $s\in\{1,a_{\rm amp}\}$.
The fixed old $v=0$ conductor in degree $D$ is precisely FPZ15,
with $g(t,z)=e^{-4\omega(t)}E_A(\omega(t),z)$ and
$\omega(t)=-i\arctan t$. Its diagonal is $g(0,z)=G(z)$.
All entries are entire in $z$, since each required coefficient
is a finite derivative in $\xi$ of the original factors. Therefore
\[
 \begin{split}
 B_{D,s}(z)&=\operatorname{diag}(\rho_0,\ldots,\rho_D)^{-1}
              T_D(g(z))\operatorname{diag}(\rho_0,\ldots,\rho_D),\\
 \det B_{D,s}(z)&=G(z)^{D+1},\qquad
 \operatorname{Spec}B_{D,s}(z)=\{G(z)\text{ repeated }D+1\text{ times}\}.
 \end{split}\tag{GUC3}
\]
Triangularity proves both identities. In particular the original
constant polynomial is killed at $z_0$ and the full matrix is singular.
For $z\ne z_0$ sufficiently close to $z_0$, GUC2 makes the matrix
invertible. Its inverse remains triangular with diagonal $G(z)^{-1}$.
In the ordered exterior basis every diagonal of its $r$th exterior
power is therefore $G(z)^{-r}$. The operator norm is at least the
modulus of any matrix entry in the two orthonormal exterior frames:
apply it to the relevant source basis vector and project onto the
relevant target basis vector. No identification of physical centres
is required for this coordinate argument.
This proves in the exact original orthonormal Gamma coordinates
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 \|\bigwedge^r B_{D,s}(z)^{-1}\|\ge |G(z)|^{-r},
               \qquad 1\le r\le D+1,\\
 \liminf_{z\to z_0}|z-z_0|^{\nu r}
       \|\bigwedge^r B_{D,s}(z)^{-1}\|
            \ge |h(z_0)|^{-r}>0,\\
 \lim_{z\to z_0}|z-z_0|^{\nu(D+1)}
       \|\bigwedge^{D+1}B_{D,s}(z)^{-1}\|
            =|h(z_0)|^{-(D+1)}>0.
 \end{gathered}\tag{GUC4}
\]
The last equality uses the one-dimensional top exterior space and
the exact determinant GUC3. Thus every inverse exterior rank diverges
at a finite nonzero original period for every original quartet and unit.
The lower bound does not assert that the smaller exterior ranks have
exactly the lower exponent $\nu r$; UPP18 calculates their stronger
exact exponent at the certified order-one points.

There is no hidden assumption about symbol order at the guaranteed
zero. If the entire function $E_A(\xi,z_0)$ is nonzero and has order
$v\ge1$ at $\xi=0$, then $g(t,z_0)$ has the same order, since
$\omega'(0)=-i\ne0$ and $e^{-4\omega(0)}=1$.
Writing $g=t^v\widetilde g$ with $\widetilde g(0)\ne0$ shows that
$T_D(g)$ is a $v$-step shift times an invertible triangular matrix.
Consequently its rank is $\max(D+1-v,0)$ and its kernel is the
original $\mathcal P_{\min(v-1,D)}$.
If instead $E_A(\xi,z_0)$ is identically zero, every coefficient
of $g$ vanishes and $B_{D,s}(z_0)=0$. GUC3--4 hold in that case
as well, because they depend on the nonzero entire function $G(z)$
of the period parameter, not on a finite symbol order at $z_0$.
This exhausts both cases. Neither orbit admissibility nor a finite
symbol-order hypothesis was used to infer the fixed-space singularity.

Finally put $u_0=1/z_0$, retaining the original finite nonzero period.
The exact identity
$z-z_0=-(u-u_0)/(uu_0)$ gives
\[
 \begin{split}
 \liminf_{u\to u_0}|u-u_0|^{\nu r}
       \|\bigwedge^r B_{D,s}(u^{-1})^{-1}\|
       &\ge |u_0|^{2\nu r}|h(z_0)|^{-r},\\
 \lim_{u\to u_0}|u-u_0|^{\nu(D+1)}
       \|\bigwedge^{D+1}B_{D,s}(u^{-1})^{-1}\|
       &=|u_0|^{2\nu(D+1)}|h(z_0)|^{-(D+1)}.
 \end{split}\tag{GUC5}
\]
These statements locate a necessary obstruction to extending an
inverse-exterior estimate across the whole complex period family.
They do not place the guaranteed period inside any separately
restricted arithmetic period domain. UPP3--20 provides explicit
locations, actual symbol order, five-orbit admissibility and the
corrected ES return on its certified geometric region; the global
conclusion here is the proved singularity and divergence GUC1--5.
The complete original coefficient and norm sources remain
\cite{PCLOriginal,WCF}; ANP1--32 supplies the new existence input.

\section{Global finite-period degeneration of the original fixed conductor spaces}
Fix every original quartet and nonzero unit allowed in ANP1, including
its complete four-factor period matrix and all original coefficients.
The exact original norms, translations and Gamma frames below are those
of FC20--24 and WCF1--6 \cite{WCF,Cumulative,PCLOriginal}.
No five-orbit hypothesis is imposed in this section. In particular,
the symbol may vanish identically at the selected period.

Write $F_j(z)=f_j(0,z)$ for the four original functions and
\[
 E_A(\xi,z)=\prod_{j=1}^4 f_j(\xi,z),\qquad
 \mu_m(z)=\partial_\xi^mE_A(0,z),\qquad
 \mu_0(z)=\prod_{j=1}^4F_j(z).
 \tag{GFC1}
\]
ANP2 proves that each $F_j$ is nonconstant, nonzero entire and has a
nonzero finite zero. Thus $\mu_0$ is a nonzero entire function with a
nonzero finite zero $z_0$. The product cannot vanish identically:
the zeros of each nonzero entire factor are isolated, and the union
of four such zero sets cannot contain a disk.
Choose any such $z_0$, not necessarily a simple or isolated-factor zero.
For the complete four-factor multiplicities and coefficients set
\[
 \ell_j=\min\{m\ge0:F_j^{(m)}(z_0)\ne0\},\quad
 \nu=\sum_{j=1}^4\ell_j\ge1,\quad
 c=\prod_{j=1}^4\frac{F_j^{(\ell_j)}(z_0)}{\ell_j!}\ne0.
 \tag{GFC2}
\]
All four integers are finite because their factors are nonzero entire.
With $\tau=z-z_0$, multiplication of the full Taylor series gives
\[
 \mu_0(z)=c\tau^\nu+O(\tau^{\nu+1}),\qquad
 c=\frac{\mu_0^{(\nu)}(z_0)}{\nu!}.
 \tag{GFC3}
\]
An isolated-zero disk can be chosen small enough that $z\ne0$ and
$\mu_0(z)\ne0$ for $0<|\tau|<\epsilon$.

\subsection{The complete fixed-space matrix and its entire inverse-exterior consequences}
For the unchanged cutoff $D\ge0$ put $N=D+1$ and retain the original
$s\in\{1,a_{\rm amp}\}$, $M_s=(2\pi)^{s/2}$,
$\rho_n=\sqrt{n!/(s/2)_n}$, and centers
$c_0=a_{\rm amp}/2$, $c_1=a_{\rm amp}/2-4$.
The two fixed old spaces are
\[
 (\mathcal P_D,\|\cdot\|_{s,c_0})
       \longrightarrow(\mathcal P_D,\|\cdot\|_{s,c_1}),\qquad
 \|P\|_{s,c}^2=\int_{\mathbb R}|P(c+iy)|^2
 \frac{(2\pi)^{s/2}2^{s/2}}{4\pi\Gamma(s/2)}
       |\Gamma(s/4+iy/2)|^2\,dy.
 \tag{GFC4}
\]
The original orthonormal frames are
$\phi_{n,s,c}=p_{n,s}((S-c)/i)/\sqrt{M_sn!(s/2)_n}$,
with the full WCF2 recurrence for $p_{n,s}$.
Define
\[
 \omega(t)=-i\arctan t,\qquad
 g(t,z)=e^{-4\omega(t)}E_A(\omega(t),z)
       =\sum_{m\ge0}g_m(z)t^m,
 \quad
 R_D=\operatorname{diag}(\rho_0,\ldots,\rho_D).
 \tag{GFC5}
\]
All $g_m(z)$ are entire: each is a finite combination of original
moments, and every original coefficient is entire in $z$ by PCL2--10.
This is the fixed-space symbol, without a division by a symbol-order
power. It has $g_0(z)=\mu_0(z)$ at every period.
The exact matrix of the original translation conductor on GFC4 is
\[
 B_{D,s}(z)=R_D^{-1}T_D(g(\cdot,z))R_D,
 \qquad
 B_{ij}(z)=
 \begin{cases}
 g_{j-i}(z)\rho_j/\rho_i,&0\le i\le j\le D,\\
 0,&i>j.
 \end{cases}
 \tag{GFC6}
\]
The original generating identity WCF3--6 proves these entries without
requiring a nonzero symbol. The common mass cancels in the two
orthonormal-frame entries, while the norms in GFC4 retain it.
In particular every diagonal entry is the unchanged $\mu_0(z)$, so
\[
 \det B_{D,s}(z)=\mu_0(z)^N,\qquad
 B_{D,s}(z)\text{ is invertible exactly when }\mu_0(z)\ne0.
 \tag{GFC7}
\]
The coordinate matrix has characteristic polynomial
$(\lambda-\mu_0(z))^N$. This is a statement in the two specified
orthonormal coordinate frames; no identification of their physical
centers is required to use the following norm consequence.

For every $1\le r\le N$ and every $\mu_0(z)\ne0$,
\[
 \boxed{\qquad
 \|\bigwedge^r B_{D,s}(z)^{-1}\|
                \ge |\mu_0(z)|^{-r}.
 \qquad}\tag{GFC8}
\]
To prove this directly, the inverse of the upper triangular matrix
GFC6 is upper triangular with diagonal $\mu_0^{-1}$.
In the orthonormal exterior power frames, each diagonal matrix entry
of its $r$th exterior power is the corresponding principal minor,
equal to $\mu_0^{-r}$. The norm of an operator is at least the
absolute value of any one of its matrix entries in orthonormal
frames: apply it to the unit source basis vector and project onto
the unit target basis vector. This proves GFC8 with all original
Gamma weights and centers retained.
For the top exterior power the space is one-dimensional, giving
the stronger exact identity and pole:
\[
 \|\bigwedge^N B_{D,s}(z)^{-1}\|=|\mu_0(z)|^{-N},\qquad
 \lim_{z\to z_0}|z-z_0|^{\nu N}
       \|\bigwedge^N B_{D,s}(z)^{-1}\|=|c|^{-N}>0.
 \tag{GFC9}
\]
GFC8 also gives, at every exterior rank,
$\liminf_{z\to z_0}|z-z_0|^{\nu r}
\|\bigwedge^rB_{D,s}(z)^{-1}\|\ge|c|^{-r}$.

There is a complete finite test for the exact pole and coefficient at
every rank, even when the symbol vanishes identically at $z_0$.
For $0\le k\le N$ let
\[
 m_k=\min\left\{0\le m\le\nu k:
     \left.\frac1{m!}\partial_z^m\bigwedge^kB_{D,s}(z)
          \right|_{z=z_0}\ne0\right\},\qquad
 L_k=\left.\frac1{m_k!}\partial_z^{m_k}
                  \bigwedge^kB_{D,s}(z)\right|_{z=z_0}.
 \tag{GFC10}
\]
For $k=0$ these definitions mean $m_0=0,L_0=1$.
For every positive $k$ the finite test terminates: a principal minor
of $B$ equals $\mu_0^k$, whose order is exactly $\nu k$.
Thus the indicated exterior matrix has a nonzero coefficient no
later than that order. Every derivative in GFC10 is a finite
determinant expansion in the explicit original entries GFC6 and
their derivatives, so this test introduces no free matrix or norm.

For $1\le r\le N$ put $k=N-r$. The singular values of an
invertible $N$ by $N$ matrix give the exact identity
\[
 \|\bigwedge^rB^{-1}\|
       =\frac{\|\bigwedge^{N-r}B\|}{|\det B|}.
 \tag{GFC11}
\]
Indeed if the forward singular values are
$\sigma_1\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_N>0$, its numerator is
$\sigma_1\cdots\sigma_{N-r}$ and its denominator is
$\sigma_1\cdots\sigma_N$. Their quotient is the product of
the $r$ largest inverse singular values, proving the identity.
Since $\bigwedge^kB=\tau^{m_k}(L_k+O(\tau))$, continuity
of the operator norm now proves the full exact pole data
\[
 \boxed{\quad
 p_r=\nu N-m_{N-r}\ge\nu r,\qquad
 \lim_{z\to z_0}|z-z_0|^{p_r}
       \|\bigwedge^rB_{D,s}(z)^{-1}\|
       =\frac{\|L_{N-r}\|}{|c|^N}>0.
 \quad}\tag{GFC12}
\]
This gives integer pole exponents and their exact original-metric
constants at all ranks; GFC9 is the case $r=N$.

\subsection{Every possible symbol order at the selected zero}
The nine-frequency test and order bound $32$ are the earlier PZ12,
PZX and OFM results \cite{PeriodZeroOriginal}; here they are applied
at the finite zeros whose existence is newly established by ANP2.
The complete factor test does not need admissibility. Retain the nine
distinct original frequencies and full coefficients in OFM2--3,
\[
 \lambda_{uw}=1+(2u-2)\delta+i(2w-2)\gamma,
 \quad
 f_j(\xi,z_0)=\sum_{u,w=0}^2c_{j,uw}(z_0)e^{\lambda_{uw}\xi}.
 \tag{GFC13}
\]
The nine-by-nine matrix $(\lambda_{uw}^m)_{0\le m\le8}$
is invertible because all frequencies are distinct.
Thus exactly one of the following alternatives holds for each factor:
its first nonzero derivative occurs at some $n_j\in\{0,\ldots,8\}$,
or all nine derivatives vanish and the factor vanishes identically
in $\xi$. In the latter case the invertible derivative matrix forces
every coefficient in GFC13 to vanish. The test is therefore finite
and complete even outside the five-orbit locus.

If at least one factor is identically zero, $E_A(\xi,z_0)$ is
identically zero, all its moments vanish, and
\[
       g(t,z_0)=0,\qquad B_{D,s}(z_0)=0
                       \quad\text{for every }D.
 \tag{GFC14}
\]
Conversely a product of finitely many nonzero entire functions of
$\xi$ cannot vanish identically, by the same isolated-zero argument
used for GFC1. This proves that GFC14's symbol condition occurs
precisely when one of the original factors is identically zero.
It makes no assertion that $\mu_0(z)$ vanishes as a function of
the period: GFC3 has already proved its finite multiplicity there.

If all four factors are nonzero functions of $\xi$, define their
orders by the finite test above. Then at the selected period
\[
 v=n_1+n_2+n_3+n_4\in\{1,\ldots,32\},\qquad
 \mu_v(z_0)=v!\prod_{j=1}^4
                 \frac{\partial_\xi^{n_j}f_j(0,z_0)}{n_j!}\ne0,
 \quad
 g(t,z_0)=t^v\widetilde g(t),\quad
 \widetilde g(0)=\frac{(-i)^v\mu_v(z_0)}{v!}\ne0.
 \tag{GFC15}
\]
The lower bound $v\ge1$ follows from $\mu_0(z_0)=0$.
Multiplication of the four Taylor series proves the order and
coefficient, and $\omega(t)=-it+O(t^3)$ proves the displayed
coefficient of $g$.

Let $J_D$ be the upper shift with ones in positions $(i,i+1)$.
The full finite matrix at this point is
\[
 B_{D,s}(z_0)=R_D^{-1}J_D^vT_D(\widetilde g)R_D.
 \tag{GFC16}
\]
The Toeplitz factor is upper triangular with nonzero diagonal and
is invertible. It commutes with $J_D$ since both are polynomials
in that shift. Therefore, putting $v_D=\min(v,N)$,
\[
 \begin{split}
 \operatorname{rank}B_{D,s}(z_0)&=N-v_D,\\
 \ker B_{D,s}(z_0)&=\mathcal P_{v_D-1}
               \quad\text{inside its original source frame},\\
 \operatorname{im}B_{D,s}(z_0)&=\mathcal P_{D-v_D}
               \quad\text{inside its original target frame}.
 \end{split}\tag{GFC17}
\]
Here $\mathcal P_{-1}=0$. The kernel statement follows either
from the shift factor or from the exact translation formula
$T_AS^m=\sum_{n\ge v}\binom mn\mu_nS^{m-n}$; its leading
coefficient is nonzero when $m\ge v$.
If $v>D$, GFC17 correctly says that this cutoff matrix is zero
although the complete symbol is not identically zero.

For finite $v$, the actual order-adjusted map remains the distinct
isomorphism
\[
 (\mathcal P_{D+v}/\mathcal P_{v-1},\|\cdot\|_{s,c_0,\rm quot})
       \longrightarrow(\mathcal P_D,\|\cdot\|_{s,c_1}),\qquad
 \widetilde B_{D,s}=
 \operatorname{diag}(\rho_0,\ldots,\rho_D)^{-1}
 T_D(\widetilde g)
 \operatorname{diag}(\rho_v,\ldots,\rho_{v+D}).
 \tag{GFC18}
\]
Its nonzero triangular diagonal proves invertibility with the complete
quotient norm. When the symbol vanishes identically there is no
finite $v$ or such isomorphism: the original translation annihilates
every polynomial, as all its moments are zero. Thus neither possible
symbol case is replaced by an assumption of admissibility.

The rank formula sharpens GFC12 where its hypothesis is decided by
GFC13: for finite $v\le D$ and $r\ge v$, the nonzero exterior
power $\bigwedge^{N-r}B(z_0)$ gives $m_{N-r}=0$. Hence
\[
 p_r=\nu N,\qquad
 \lim_{z\to z_0}|z-z_0|^{\nu N}\|\bigwedge^rB(z)^{-1}\|
   =\frac{\|\bigwedge^{N-r}B(z_0)\|}{|c|^N}>0
              \quad(v\le r\le N).
 \tag{GFC19}
\]
For $r<v$ the minors vanish at $z_0$, and the finite test GFC10
gives their exact nonzero higher jets rather than presuming simple
rank loss. If $B(z_0)=0$, it gives $m_k\ge k$ for $k\ge1$,
since each $k$-minor is a sum of products of $k$ entries vanishing
at that point. Together with GFC10 this proves
$\nu r\le p_r\le\nu N-(N-r)$ for $1\le r<N$ in that case,
while the top exterior identity is unchanged.

\subsection{Exact original-period constants and the scope of the conclusion}
Put $u_0=1/z_0\ne0$ and use $z=1/u$ on every original logarithm
branch. The factor functions and GFC6 are independent of that branch
by the full diagonal cancellation PCL7--9. The exact coordinate identity is
\[
 z-z_0=-\frac{u-u_0}{u u_0},\qquad
 \mu_0(u^{-1})=
       c\left(-\frac1{u_0^2}\right)^\nu
                  (u-u_0)^\nu+O((u-u_0)^{\nu+1}).
 \tag{GFC20}
\]
Therefore the complete constants in the original period coordinate are
\[
 \boxed{\quad
 \lim_{u\to u_0}|u-u_0|^{p_r}
       \|\bigwedge^rB_{D,s}(u^{-1})^{-1}\|

Equations RPCJ8--10 give
\[
 g_0=c\tau^2+c_3\tau^3+O(\tau^4),\quad
 g_1=d\tau+d_2\tau^2+O(\tau^3),\quad
 g_2=e+e_1\tau+O(\tau^2),\quad g_3=f+O(\tau).
 \tag{RPCJ12}
\]
At $\tau=0$ the nonzero matrix block is
\[
 C_s=\begin{pmatrix}
 e\rho_2/\rho_0&f\rho_3/\rho_0\\
 0&e\rho_3/\rho_1
 \end{pmatrix}.
 \tag{RPCJ13}
\]
Its columns are source indices $2,3$ and its rows are target indices
$0,1$ in the displayed coordinate matrix; equivalently the original
map sends source degrees $2,3$ to target degrees $0,1$.
The matrix $C_s$ is invertible because $e\ne0$.
Thus $B_s(z_0)$ has rank two, and its two positive forward singular
values are exactly the two singular values of this complete block.

The inverse series through degree three is exactly
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 h_0=\frac1{g_0},\quad h_1=-\frac{g_1}{g_0^2},\\
 h_2=\frac{g_1^2-g_0g_2}{g_0^3},\quad
 h_3=\frac{-g_1^3+2g_0g_1g_2-g_0^2g_3}{g_0^4},\\
 B_s^{-1}=\operatorname{diag}(\rho)^{-1}T_3(h)
                               \operatorname{diag}(\rho).
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{RPCJ14}
\]
Multiplication of the two truncated series proves all entries.
Set
\[
       \Delta=d(d^2-2ce),\qquad L=\frac{d^2-ce}{c^3}.
 \tag{RPCJ15}
\]
If $\Delta\ne0$, the only inverse entry with order five is
$h_3\rho_3/\rho_0$. Its leading coefficient is
$-\Delta\rho_3/(c^4\rho_0)$.
Every other entry has order at most four by RPCJ12--14.
It follows that the largest inverse singular value has the exact
limit
\[
 \lim_{z\to z_0}|z-z_0|^5\|B_s(z)^{-1}\|
               =\frac{|\Delta|\rho_3}{c^4\rho_0}>0.
 \tag{RPCJ16}
\]

The exceptional coefficient locus $\Delta=0$ is also completely
determined. Put
\[\theta=\operatorname{Re}(A\bar B)/(|A||B|)\in[-1,1].\]
This quotient is an exact auxiliary value of the two original
derivatives; their magnitudes remain in RPCJ11 and every constant.
Then $\Delta=0$ exactly when
\[
        \theta=0\quad\hbox{or}\quad\theta^2=1/2.
 \tag{RPCJ17}
\]
Indeed $d=-2i|A||B|\theta$ and $ce=-|A|^2|B|^2$.
On this locus $d^2$ equals either $0$ or $2ce$, so
$d^2-ce$ equals $-ce$ or $ce$ and is nonzero.
Thus $L\ne0$ in all exceptional cases.
The complete next coefficient of the top-right inverse entry is
\[
 K=\frac{2cde_1+2c_3de+(2ce-3d^2)d_2-c^2f}{c^4}.
 \tag{RPCJ18}
\]
To prove it, the coefficient of $\tau^4$ in the numerator of
$h_3$ in RPCJ14 is exactly the displayed numerator, whereas its
$\tau^3$ coefficient is $-\Delta=0$. The denominator has leading
coefficient $c^4\tau^8$, so no denominator correction contributes
at order $\tau^{-4}$. Consequently the full leading inverse block is
\[
 N_s=\begin{pmatrix}
 L\rho_2/\rho_0&K\rho_3/\rho_0\\
 0&L\rho_3/\rho_1
 \end{pmatrix},\qquad
 \lim_{z\to z_0}|z-z_0|^4\|B_s(z)^{-1}\|=\|N_s\|>0
                   \quad(\Delta=0).
 \tag{RPCJ19}
\]
For this limit, multiplication by $\tau^4$ makes every other inverse
entry tend to zero, while these four block entries have the stated
limits. Continuity of the operator norm proves RPCJ19 for complex
as well as real approaches to the original real period.

\subsection{Every exterior rank and every inverse singular value}
Independently of $\Delta$, the exact complementary-exterior identity
GFC11 and $\det B_s=\mu_0^4$ prove
\[
 \begin{split}
 \lim_{z\to z_0}|z-z_0|^8\|\bigwedge^2B_s(z)^{-1}\|
   &=\frac{|e|^2\rho_2\rho_3}{c^4\rho_0\rho_1},\\
 \lim_{z\to z_0}|z-z_0|^8\|\bigwedge^3B_s(z)^{-1}\|
   &=\frac{\|C_s\|}{c^4},\\
 \lim_{z\to z_0}|z-z_0|^8\|\bigwedge^4B_s(z)^{-1}\|
   &=c^{-4}.
 \end{split}\tag{RPCJ20}
\]
The first numerator is $|\det C_s|$, because the only nonzero
second exterior singular value of the rank-two limiting matrix is
the product of its two positive singular values. The next numerator
is its largest singular value $\|C_s\|$.
All displayed constants are strictly positive.

For an explicit evaluation of either block norm, if
$T=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}u&v\\0&w\end{smallmatrix}\right)$,
put $S_T=|u|^2+|v|^2+|w|^2$ and $P_T=|uw|^2$.
The two singular values are
\[
 \sigma_\pm(T)=
 \left(\frac{S_T\pm\sqrt{S_T^2-4P_T}}2\right)^{1/2},
 \qquad\|T\|=\sigma_+(T).
 \tag{RPCJ21}
\]
This follows from the trace and determinant of $T^*T$ and keeps
both exact off-diagonal coefficients in RPCJ13 and RPCJ19.

Let the inverse singular values be in descending order.
For $\Delta\ne0$, their pole exponents and leading constants are
\[
 \begin{gathered}
       (5,3,0,0),\\
 \left(
 \frac{|\Delta|\rho_3}{c^4\rho_0},\quad
 \frac{|e|^2\rho_2}{|\Delta|\rho_1},\quad
 \frac1{\sigma_-(C_s)},\quad\frac1{\sigma_+(C_s)}
 \right).
 \end{gathered}\tag{RPCJ22}
\]
The first two constants follow by dividing the first line of RPCJ20
by RPCJ16. The last two follow from the convergence of the two
nonzero forward singular values to $\sigma_\pm(C_s)$.
For $\Delta=0$, the complete answer is instead
\[
       (4,4,0,0),\qquad
 \left(\sigma_+(N_s),\sigma_-(N_s),
       \frac1{\sigma_-(C_s)},\frac1{\sigma_+(C_s)}\right).
 \tag{RPCJ23}
\]
The limiting rank-two inverse block in RPCJ19 is invertible, so both
first constants are nonzero. As a check retaining all weights,
on this locus $|L|=|e|/c^2$ and hence
$|\det N_s|=|\det C_s|/c^4$, exactly RPCJ20's first coefficient.
Thus the exterior exponents are $(5,8,8,8)$ or $(4,8,8,8)$,
respectively. Nonzero first $z$ and $\xi$ derivatives alone do not
select between these two calculated possibilities.

At the collision the order-adjusted map is the exact $v=2$ map
$\mathcal P_5/\mathcal P_1\to\mathcal P_3$ with its original
Gamma quotient norm and diagonal
$(-i)^2\mu_2\rho_{j+2}/(2\rho_j)$, $0\le j\le3$.
It is invertible because $\mu_2=2|B|^2>0$.
This distinct domain is retained alongside the singular fixed old
map; no quotient change is used to erase the fixed-space poles.

Finally $u_0=1/z_0$ is real and nonzero, and
$z-z_0=-(u-u_0)/(uu_0)$ exactly.
Each singular or exterior pole of exponent $p$ above therefore has
the same exponent in the original $u$ coordinate and its displayed
constant multiplied by $|u_0|^{2p}$. This specifies every original
coordinate constant without selecting a candidate real period.

\section{The certified positive real period: complete four-label return and correction}
This section applies the full RPCJ calculation to the actual original
real-period point established by the accompanying contraction proof.
The ordered ES--Fable labels and polynomial retain FC5--6, FC15a and
FC31--35 and the original 488-page reader's provenance
\cite{ES488,Cumulative}; the conductor and every norm retain WCF1--6
\cite{WCF}. The conjugation and real-axis positivity used here are
the existing OFM8--11 and earlier PCL15--16 identities
\cite{PCLOriginal,Cumulative}, not a new parity or positivity theorem.

The exact point $(z_*,x_*)$ is the unique real solution of
$f_1(0,z,x)=0$ in the closed rectangle of radius $10^{-15}$ in
each coordinate about the exact rational center
\[
 \begin{split}
 z_c&=0.02211947780866184513200791639903555836071244787217846841,\\
 x_c&=-1.466817440463494183975448871845763045856183562396293859.
 \end{split}\tag{RPE1}
\]
The original parameters are
$\delta=1/4$, $\gamma=3$, $\beta=143/8$, $\eta=21025/256$;
the exact unit is $a=\alpha(1+ix_*)$ for its retained real nonzero
scale $\alpha$, and the original period is $u_*=1/z_*>0$.
The scale cancels with its inverse only in the original conjugated
operator, as in PCL9. Every remaining unit entry is kept there.
The full-series certificate proves $f_1=f_4=0$,
$f_2,f_3\ne0$, and nonzero $z$ and $\xi$ derivatives of $f_1$.
Thus RPCJ8 gives exactly $\nu=2$ and $v=2$ at this point.
The same certificate proves the five-orbit property at this point.
The two vanishing factors are nonzero functions of $\xi$ because
their first $\xi$ derivatives are nonzero; the other two factors
have nonzero value. If a nontrivial conjugated quadric were associated
to $Q_0$, its restriction to the original exponential curve would
vanish identically, contrary to those statements. Association of two
distinct orbit members would reduce to such an association by their
inverse group action. Hence all five original quadrics are distinct.

All moments used below are the actual ones at this certified point.
For a completely explicit finite expression, let $M_j=M_j(z_*,x_*)$
be the original matrix, $v_{j,n}=M_j(\rho_a^n)_a$, and use the
literal polar form
$\mathcal B(v,w)=v_1w_4+v_4w_1-v_2w_3-v_3w_2$.
Then
\[
 a_{j,n}=\frac12\sum_{r=0}^n\binom nr
            \mathcal B(v_{j,r},v_{j,n-r}),\quad
 G_n=\sum_{r=0}^n\binom nr a_{1,r}a_{2,n-r},\quad
 \mu_n=\sum_{r=0}^n\binom nrG_r\bar G_{n-r}.
 \tag{RPE2}
\]
The factor $1/2$ retains the original $Q_0(v)=\mathcal B(v,v)/2$.
These formulas evaluate every needed derivative of the full original
period and factor matrices, including all four multiplicities through
their exact conjugation. The certificate supplies the real enclosures
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 \mu_0=\mu_1=0,\qquad
 \mu_2\in[69.926906\mathbin\pm8.99\,10^{-7}],\\
 \mu_3\in[-11161.6109\mathbin\pm8.96\,10^{-5}],\quad
 \mu_4\in[576883.78\mathbin\pm6.81\,10^{-3}],\quad
 \mu_5\in[5.254785\,10^6\mathbin\pm0.252].
 \end{gathered}\tag{RPE3}
\]
The zero values here are exact consequences of the certified root
and RPCJ3, not the rounding of an interval through zero.
The real parts of the other enclosures are valid because RPCJ4
proves the exact moments real at this real period.

\subsection{All four original labels on the old and corrected source spaces}

The rank is exactly two and the kernel on that original source is

In the original ES coordinates the kernel of

For its proof use the complete original Taylor translation formula

There is also an exact operator identity giving every correction to
