\subsection{The two lost scalars, their complete metric, and the total return}
The rank-two old receiver has four distinct marked outputs. Indeed,
in the ordered pair list $(\mathrm{MN},\mathrm{MT},\mathrm{ME},
\mathrm{NT},\mathrm{NE},\mathrm{TE})$, RPE11 gives
\[
 \lambda_{3a}-\lambda_{3b}
  =\frac1{435}(-4i,-48,-48-4i,-48+4i,-48,-4i)_{ab}.
 \tag{RPE19}
\]
The coefficient of $S'$ in $y_a^{\rm old}-y_b^{\rm old}$ is
$3\mu_2(\lambda_{3a}-\lambda_{3b})\ne0$. This proves all six
distinctions without identifying a label with a conjugate label.
For the exact metric statement, put $b=s/2$, $M=(2\pi)^{s/2}$,
$c=a_{\rm amp}/2$ and $c'=c-4$. If this difference is $d_0+d_1S'$,
its original squared norm is
$M(|d_0+c'd_1|^2+b|d_1|^2)>0$.

Let $\Phi_0q=\sum_a(K^{-1}q)_a\ell_a(S)$ and
$J_0=T_A\Phi_0$. Retain the literal two coefficient functionals
$t_r(q)=[S^r]\Phi_0q$, $r=0,1$. Define the complete linear map
\[
 \Theta_2:\mathbb C^4\longrightarrow\mathcal P_1\oplus\mathbb C^2,
 \qquad \Theta_2q=(J_0q,t_0(q),t_1(q)).
 \tag{RPE20}
\]
Here the first $\mathcal P_1$ uses the original target variable $S'$;
the two scalar coordinates are the coefficients lost by the original
degree-three conductor. For $Y=Y_0+Y_1S'$, put
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 c_3=\frac{Y_1}{3\mu_2},\qquad
 c_2=\frac{Y_0-\mu_3c_3}{\mu_2},\qquad
 p_Y(S)=c_2S^2+c_3S^3,\\
 \Theta_2^{-1}(Y,t_0,t_1)
       =K\bigl(p_Y(\rho_a)+t_0+t_1\rho_a\bigr)_a.
 \end{gathered}\tag{RPE21}
\]
The two coefficients of $T_Ap_Y$ are precisely $Y_0,Y_1$ by
RPE12, whereas $p_Y$ itself has zero constant and linear coefficients.
These identities prove $\Theta_2\Theta_2^{-1}=I$.
Conversely any polynomial in the old source differs from its
corresponding $p_Y$ by exactly its original constant and linear
terms; interpolation proves the other composition. In coefficient
bases the determinant of $\Theta_2$ is
$3\mu_2^2/((\det V_\rho^{\mathsf T})(\det K))\ne0$.
Thus both lost scalars, including their original ES coordinates,
are recovered by finite displayed formulas.

Every cross term of the original source metric is as follows. Set
$m_4=b(3b+2)$ and $m_6=b(15b^2+30b+16)$, and define
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 Q=\begin{pmatrix}1&c\\c&c^2+b\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 U=\begin{pmatrix}
 c^2-b&c^3-3cb\\c^3+cb&c^4-m_4
 \end{pmatrix},\\
 H=\begin{pmatrix}
 c^4+2c^2b+m_4&c(c^4+2c^2b+m_4)\\
 c(c^4+2c^2b+m_4)&c^6+3c^4b+3c^2m_4+m_6
 \end{pmatrix}.
 \end{gathered}\tag{RPE22}
\]
With $v=(c_2,c_3)^{\mathsf T}$ and $t=(t_0,t_1)^{\mathsf T}$,
direct integration against the unchanged WCF2 measure gives
\[
 \begin{split}
 \|p_Y+t_0+t_1S\|_{s,c}^2
 &=M\{v^*Hv+2\operatorname{Re}(t^*Uv)+t^*Qt\}\\
 &=M v^*(H-U^*Q^{-1}U)v
       +M(t+Q^{-1}Uv)^*Q(t+Q^{-1}Uv),\\
 Q^{-1}Uv
 &=\begin{pmatrix}
 -(c^2+b)c_2+(-2c^3+2c)c_3\\
 2cc_2+(3c^2-3b-2)c_3
 \end{pmatrix},\\
 H-U^*Q^{-1}U
 &=\begin{pmatrix}
 2b(b+1)&6cb(b+1)\\
 6cb(b+1)&18c^2b(b+1)+6b(b+1)(b+2)
 \end{pmatrix}.
 \end{split}\tag{RPE23}
\]
For completeness, WCF2's recurrence gives the unchanged measure's
moments $M$, $Mb$, $Mm_4$, $Mm_6$ in even degrees zero through six.
One may verify them from
$p_2=y^2-b$, $p_3=y^3-(3b+2)y$ and their exact WCF2 norms.
Odd moments vanish. Substitution of $S=c+iy$ then gives every
entry of RPE22; for example
$M^{-1}\langle S,S^3\rangle=c^4-m_4$ and
$M^{-1}\langle S^2,S^3\rangle=c(c^4+2c^2b+m_4)$.
The inverse of $Q$ is
$b^{-1}\left(\begin{smallmatrix}c^2+b&-c\\-c&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$.
Multiplication gives the last two expressions in RPE23 and proves
the completed square. The original quotient norm is its first term,
attained at the exact two-scalar value $t=-Q^{-1}Uv$.
No source mass, center, kernel direction or cross term is omitted.

For a full Gram directly in the displayed augmented coordinates,
define
\[
 D_Y=\begin{pmatrix}
 1/\mu_2&-\mu_3/(3\mu_2^2)\\0&1/(3\mu_2)
 \end{pmatrix},\qquad
 G_{\Theta_2}=M\begin{pmatrix}
 D_Y^*HD_Y&D_Y^*U^*\\UD_Y&Q
 \end{pmatrix}.
 \tag{RPE24}
\]
Thus $v=D_Y(Y_0,Y_1)^{\mathsf T}$ and RPE24 is exactly the
original source metric transported by RPE21, in the order
$(Y_0,Y_1,t_0,t_1)$. Its quotient block is
$M D_Y^*(H-U^*Q^{-1}U)D_Y$.
The target norm stays
$\|Y\|_{s,c'}^2=M(|Y_0+c'Y_1|^2+b|Y_1|^2)$; it is not
replaced by that source quotient metric.

The four marked total states and their full common images retain
both scalars:
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 \Theta_2(Ke_a)=(y_a^{\rm old},\lambda_{0a},\lambda_{1a}),\\
 \Theta_2P(Ke_a)
   =(2i y_{\mathrm M}^{\rm old},
          2i\lambda_{0\mathrm M},2i\lambda_{1\mathrm M}).
 \end{gathered}\tag{RPE25}
\]
All constants on the right are RPE11--12's exact original values.
Finally the entire polynomial return is
\[
 \widehat P_2(Y,t_0,t_1)
  =\Theta_2P\!\left(K(p_Y(\rho_a)+t_0+t_1\rho_a)_a\right),
 \quad \Theta_2P=\widehat P_2\Theta_2,
 \quad\det D\widehat P_2=-2.
 \tag{RPE26}
\]
The full original $P$ is FC31, so these are explicit finite
polynomial expressions with inverse coordinate map RPE21.
The chain rule proves the determinant because the two constant
determinants of $\Theta_2$ and its inverse cancel. This uses the
existing FC31 Jacobian identity with its ES--Fable provenance; it
asserts no new counterexample beyond that source polynomial.
Equations RPE20--26 retain the old map with both lost scalars;
RPE13--18 separately give the actual order-two conductor on its
correct quotient. The exact morphisms and their different original
metrics have both been computed.
No assertion places the chosen geometric quartet or unit on the
arithmetic Riemann-zeta locus.

\section{Every original cutoff: the complete two-pole law and its exact resonance}
This section calculates every cutoff of the same original conductor
at the real pair of RPZ1--19. It also identifies the entire resonance
locus of the RPCJ simple real-pair family. No moment, original weight
or higher coefficient is removed. The full geometric family and
Gamma dictionary retain \cite{PCLOriginal,WCF,DLMF18Source}.

Retain RPCJ5--12's actual constants $c>0$, $d=-iR$, $e<0$,
$c_3,d_2,e_1,f$. For each integer $D\ge1$ set $N=D+1$ and
\[
 B_{D,s}(z)=\operatorname{diag}(\rho_0,\ldots,\rho_D)^{-1}
          T_D(g(\cdot,z))\operatorname{diag}(\rho_0,\ldots,\rho_D),
 \qquad \rho_j=\sqrt{j!/(s/2)_j}.
 \tag{RPAC1}
\]
Here $T_D(g)_{ij}=g_{j-i}$ for $j\ge i$, and is zero otherwise;
$g(t,z)=e^{-4\omega(t)}E_A(\omega(t),z)$ and
$\omega(t)=-i\arctan t$, exactly RPCJ9. Both original values
$s\in\{1,a_{\rm amp}\}$ retain their full mass
$(2\pi)^{s/2}$ and centers $a_{\rm amp}/2$, $a_{\rm amp}/2-4$.
The displayed matrix uses their orthonormal frames.

Put $\tau=z-z_*$. Since $g_0=c\tau^2+O(\tau^3)$, it is
nonzero in a sufficiently small punctured neighborhood of zero.
There the exact inverse is the weighted triangular matrix of the
coefficients $h_n=[t^n]g(t,z)^{-1}$, $0\le n\le D$.
Define the finite expressions
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 H_n&=\sum_{j=0}^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}
    (-1)^{n-j}\binom{n-j}{j}
           \frac{d^{n-2j}e^j}{c^{n-j+1}},\qquad H_{-1}=0,\\
 K_n&=-[y^n]\frac{c_3+d_2y+e_1y^2+fy^3}{(c+dy+ey^2)^2}.
 \end{aligned}\tag{RPAC2}
\]
Coefficient extraction in the second line is finite: explicitly it is
$-\sum_{j=0}^{\min(3,n)}a_j\sum_{k=0}^{n-j}H_kH_{n-j-k}$,
where $(a_0,a_1,a_2,a_3)=(c_3,d_2,e_1,f)$.
Every constant on the right is an original derivative in RPCJ5--11.
They are not independently prescribed values.

The complete inverse entries have the Laurent expansions
\[
 h_n(\tau)=\tau^{-n-2}\{H_n+\tau K_n+O(\tau^2)\},\qquad
 cH_0=1,\quad cH_n+dH_{n-1}+eH_{n-2}=0\quad(n\ge1),
 \tag{RPAC3}
\]
where $H_{-2}=0$. To prove both claims, substitute $t=\tau y$
as an exact auxiliary coefficient identity, retaining the inverse
substitution and all powers:
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 g(\tau y,z_*+\tau)
 &=\tau^2(c+dy+ey^2)
   +\tau^3(c_3+d_2y+e_1y^2+fy^3)+O(\tau^4),\\
 \tau^2g(\tau y,z_*+\tau)^{-1}
 &=\frac1{c+dy+ey^2}
 -\tau\frac{c_3+d_2y+e_1y^2+fy^3}{(c+dy+ey^2)^2}
 +O(\tau^2).
 \end{aligned}\tag{RPAC4}
\]
These identities hold coefficientwise through each fixed degree $D$;
analyticity gives the stated remainder for every such finite set.
Terms $g_jt^j$ with $j\ge4$ first contribute at order at least four
in the first line. They are retained in the remainder and in the
exact inverse. Taking $[y^n]$ in the second line multiplies the
original $h_n$ by exactly $\tau^{n+2}$, proving RPAC3.
Expanding the reciprocal geometric series proves RPAC2, and
multiplying it by $c+dy+ey^2$ proves the recurrence.

\subsection{Exact resonance and the impossibility of consecutive zeros}
In terms of the actual derivatives $A=G_z$ and $B=G_\xi$, put
\[
 \lambda=\frac{|B|}{|A|}>0,\qquad
 \theta=\frac{\Re(A\bar B)}{|A||B|}\in[-1,1].\tag{RPAC5}
\]
Their magnitudes remain in every formula through $c=|A|^2$,
$d=-2ic\lambda\theta$, $e=-c\lambda^2$.
Define $U_0(X)=1$, $U_1(X)=2X$ and
$U_n(X)=2XU_{n-1}(X)-U_{n-2}(X)$. These are the explicitly
defined polynomials; the familiar Chebyshev notation introduces
no external bound. Induction in RPAC3 proves
\[
 H_n=\frac{(i\lambda)^n}{c}U_n(\theta),\qquad
 H_{n-1}^2-H_nH_{n-2}=\frac{e^{n-1}}{c^{n+1}}
                      \quad(n\ge1).\tag{RPAC6}
\]
For the second identity, its left side at $n=1$ is $c^{-2}$.
Substitution of the recurrence makes the left side at $n+1$
equal to $e/c$ times its value at $n$, proving it for all $n$.
In particular $H_D$ and $H_{D-1}$ cannot vanish together.

The angle addition formula for sine verifies the same recurrence
for $\sin((n+1)\phi)/\sin\phi$, with the same initial terms.
The endpoints give $U_n(1)=n+1$ and
$U_n(-1)=(-1)^n(n+1)$ by the recurrence. It follows that the
complete zero set is
\[
 H_D=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \theta=\cos\frac{k\pi}{D+1}\text{ for some }k=1,\ldots,D.
 \tag{RPAC7}
\]
Indeed these are $D$ distinct roots of the degree-$D$ polynomial,
whose leading coefficient is $2^D$, so there are no other roots.
This characterizes all exceptional cutoffs without discarding any
original derivative or asserting that a finite interval decides
infinitely many equalities.

\subsection{The entire limiting forward block and all exterior constants}
For $D\ge2$ the limiting matrix has nonzero block $C_{D,s}$
with rows $0,\ldots,D-2$ and columns $2,\ldots,D$:
\[
 (C_{D,s})_{ij}=
 \begin{cases}g_{j+2-i}(z_*)\rho_{j+2}/\rho_i,&j\ge i,\\
 0,&j<i,
 \end{cases}\quad 0\le i,j\le D-2 .\tag{RPAC8}
\]
Its diagonal is $e\rho_{i+2}/\rho_i$, so it is invertible.
All higher coefficients $g_3,\ldots,g_D$, with their actual
moments and center corrections, remain in this block.
For $D=1$ use the empty block, whose zeroth exterior norm and
determinant are one. The limiting forward rank is exactly $N-2$.
For $2\le r\le N$ set
\[
 L_{r,D,s}=\frac{\|\bigwedge^{N-r}C_{D,s}\|}{c^N}>0.
 \tag{RPAC9}
\]
The norms in RPAC9 are completely specified finite matrix norms
of RPAC8 in the original orthonormal frames. In particular
\[
 L_{2,D,s}=\frac{|e|^{D-1}\rho_{D-1}\rho_D}
                    {c^{D+1}\rho_0\rho_1},\qquad
 L_{N,D,s}=c^{-N}.\tag{RPAC10}
\]
The first formula follows by multiplying the diagonal of RPAC8;
its weight product telescopes to the displayed original ratios.
It also gives $c^{-2}$ at $D=1$.

For every original cutoff and every $2\le r\le N$ one has
\[
 \lim_{z\to z_*}|z-z_*|^{2N}
       \|\bigwedge^rB_{D,s}(z)^{-1}\|=L_{r,D,s}.
 \tag{RPAC11}
\]
To prove this identity, let the forward singular values of an
invertible $N$-dimensional matrix be
$\sigma_1\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_N>0$. The product of the largest
$r$ inverse singular values is
$\sigma_1\cdots\sigma_{N-r}/|\det B|$.
Thus its $r$th inverse exterior norm equals
$\|\bigwedge^{N-r}B\|/|\det B|$.
Here $\det B=g_0^N$ and $g_0=c\tau^2+O(\tau^3)$.
The limiting numerator is the strictly positive numerator in
RPAC9. Continuity gives RPAC11, for complex as well as real
approaches. This proves the exponent $2N$ at every exterior rank
from two through $N$, without a resonance restriction.

\subsection{Both complete inverse spectra}
When $H_D\ne0$, RPAC3 shows that the only entry of pole order
$D+2$ is the top-right entry, with coefficient
$H_D\rho_D/\rho_0$. All other entries have lower pole order.
Consequently, with
$A_{D,s}=|H_D|\rho_D/\rho_0>0$, the two divergent inverse
singular values have exact exponents and leading constants
\[
 (D+2,D),\qquad (A_{D,s},L_{2,D,s}/A_{D,s}).\tag{RPAC12}
\]
The first constant follows by taking the norm after multiplication
by $\tau^{D+2}$. The second follows by dividing RPAC11 at rank
two by the first singular asymptotic. Every other inverse singular
value has a finite positive limit, the reciprocal of the nonzero
forward singular values of $C_{D,s}$ in reverse order.

When $H_D=0$, RPAC6 gives $H_{D-1}\ne0$. The entire leading
inverse matrix at order $D+1$ has the block
\[
 N_{D,s}=\begin{pmatrix}
 H_{D-1}\rho_{D-1}/\rho_0&K_D\rho_D/\rho_0\\
 0&H_{D-1}\rho_D/\rho_1
 \end{pmatrix}.\tag{RPAC13}
\]
It occupies rows $0,1$ and columns $D-1,D$.
All other entries vanish after multiplication by $\tau^{D+1}$.
For $D=1$ this is the full matrix, with diagonal entries
$H_0=1/c$; hence the statement also covers the endpoint.
The block is invertible. Its two positive singular values are
the exact leading constants of the two divergent inverse
singular values, both of exponent $D+1$.
For an explicit finite formula write its entries as
$\left(\begin{smallmatrix}a&b\\0&d_0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$,
set $S=|a|^2+|b|^2+|d_0|^2$ and $Q=|ad_0|^2$, and obtain
\[
 \sigma_\pm(N_{D,s})=
   \left(\frac{S\pm\sqrt{S^2-4Q}}2\right)^{1/2}.
 \tag{RPAC14}
\]
This follows from the trace and determinant of $N_{D,s}^*N_{D,s}$.
The full $K_D$ in RPAC2 retains every next-jet correction.
Furthermore RPAC6 at $n=D$ gives
$|H_{D-1}|^2=|e|^{D-1}/c^{D+1}$, so
$|\det N_{D,s}|=L_{2,D,s}$, consistently with RPAC11.

These calculations exhaust the alternatives. The inverse exterior
exponents are
\[
 \begin{cases}
 (D+2,2N,\ldots,2N),&H_D\ne0,\\
 (D+1,2N,\ldots,2N),&H_D=0.
 \end{cases}
\]
The first exterior constants are
$A_{D,s}$ and $\sigma_+(N_{D,s})$, respectively; all remaining
constants are RPAC9. At cutoff $D=0$ the single matrix entry is
$g_0$, so its sole inverse pole has exponent two and constant
$c^{-1}$. In the original coordinate $u$, every constant at pole
exponent $p$ is multiplied by $|u_*|^{2p}$, by the exact identity
$z-z_*=-(u-u_*)/(uu_*)$.

\subsection{An actual finite range on the certified original pair}
The companion \nolinkurl{check_real_pair_all_cutoffs.py} first
checks the finite coefficient and reciprocal identities exactly,
then propagates the complete RPZ certificate's outward enclosures
for $c$, $|B|^2$ and $R$ to the actual
$\theta=R/(2\sqrt{c|B|^2})$. For every $D=1,\ldots,100$ it
encloses each of the $D$ values $\cos(k\pi/(D+1))$ and verifies
strict separation from that same interval for $\theta$.
Every one of these 5050 comparisons is with an enclosing interval;
no decimal equality test is used. The full receipt records the
minimum gap and the source-certificate hash. It verifies
\[
 \left|\theta-\cos\frac{k\pi}{D+1}\right|>1.95\,10^{-5}
 \quad(1\le k\le D\le100).\tag{RPAC15}
\]
This strict bound proves $H_D\ne0$ throughout those one hundred
cutoffs. Therefore the actual original pair has the singular poles
$(D+2,D,0,\ldots,0)$ and exterior poles
$(D+2,2D+2,\ldots,2D+2)$ for every $1\le D\le100$,
with every constant given by RPAC9--12. For larger cutoffs,
RPAC2 and RPAC7--14 remain the exact complete formulas; a finite
interval check does not assert nonresonance at every integer cutoff.
The arithmetic underlying the outward comparisons is Johansson's
Arb \cite{human:arb2016}; the polynomial recurrence, full pole law
and its original-metric constants have been proved above.

\section{The complete real directional geometry at the certified pair}
\label{sec:real-pair-directional}

This continuation uses the exact point proved in RPZ1--19
\cite{RPZ005}, not a
numerically selected substitute.  It calculates the original two real

\cite[PCL1--10]{PCLOriginal}; its

\subsection{Original functions and the exact derivative isomorphism}

Write $p=(z,x)$ and $p_*=(z_*,x_*)$, the unique real zero in RPZ4's
specified rational rectangle.  Retain $u=1/z$,
$a=\alpha(1+ix)$ with its original nonzero real $\alpha$,
$\delta=1/4$, $\gamma=3$, $\beta=143/8$, $\eta=21025/256$,
$w=(\delta+i\gamma,\delta-i\gamma,-\delta+i\gamma,-\delta-i\gamma)$,
$\rho_a^{\rm prim}=1/2+w_a$, and $V_{ar}=w_a^r$.
The superscript distinguishes these four primary exponents from the
Gamma weights below.  With $J_d=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,-1,1)$,
$W(x)=I+ixJ_d$, $\zeta=e^{2\pi i/5}$, the full original functions are
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \mathcal R(z)&=\sum_{n\ge0}R_nz^n,\\
 (R_n)_{ar}&=\sum_{2h+4k=5n+r+1-a}
 \frac{(\beta/3)^h\eta^k(-5)^{h+k-n}(a/5)_{h+k-n}}{h!k!},\\
 M_j(p)&=W(x)^{-1}V\mathcal R(z)^{-1}D_j\mathcal R(z)V^{-1}W(x),\\
 D_j&=\operatorname{diag}(\zeta^{-j},\ldots,\zeta^{-4j}),\\
 f_j(\xi,p)&=Q_0\bigl(M_j(p)(e^{\rho_a^{\rm prim}\xi})_a\bigr),\\
 Q_0(y)&=y_1y_4-y_2y_3,\\
 G(\xi,p)&=f_1(\xi,p)f_2(\xi,p),\\
 E_A(\xi,p)&=\prod_{j=1}^4f_j(\xi,p).
\end{aligned}\tag{RPD1}
\]
Here $1\le a\le4$, $0\le r\le3$, and the sum has $h,k\ge0$;
empty sums are zero.  These are the same coefficients as RPZ2,
with summation letters changed to avoid the parameter $p$.
RPZ5--9 prove convergence and all differentiation used below and
prove invertibility of the matrices on a neighborhood of $p_*$.
The common $\alpha$ cancels only in its matrix conjugation.
Conjugating the original matrices exactly as in RPCJ2, now with
both real parameters varying, gives
\[
 f_{5-j}(\xi,p)=-\overline{f_j(\bar\xi,p)},\qquad
 E_A(\xi,p)=G(\xi,p)\overline{G(\bar\xi,p)}
 \quad(p\in\mathbb R^2).\tag{RPD2}
\]
Indeed the real series $\mathcal R$, the conjugate-paired $V$, and
$\overline{W(x)}=J_cW(x)J_c$ obey the identical products for every
real $x$; $J_c$ exchanges indices $1,2$ and $3,4$, and
$Q_0(J_cy)=-Q_0(y)$.  Thus RPD2 retains both minus signs, and
$E_A(\xi,p)=|G(\xi,p)|^2$ for real $\xi,p$.
Write $\mu_n(p)=\partial_\xi^nE_A(0,p)$.  All path limits below
are real; fractional powers use $\tau>0$ explicitly.

All derivatives in the following definitions are at $(0,p_*)$:
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 b_*=f_2\ne0,\quad f_1=0,\quad B=G_\xi=b_*f_{1,\xi}\ne0,\\
 A_z=G_z=b_*f_{1,z},\qquad A_x=G_x=b_*f_{1,x},\\
 \Lambda:\mathbb R^2\longrightarrow\mathbb C,\qquad
 \Lambda(v)=A_zv_z+A_xv_x,\qquad
 \mathcal J=\begin{pmatrix}\Re A_z&\Re A_x\\\Im A_z&\Im A_x\end{pmatrix}.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{RPD3}
\]
Here $\mathbb C$ is a two-dimensional real vector space.  RPZ10--13
give an invertible exact real $P$ and
$\|I-PJ\|_r<1$, where
$J=D_p(\Re f_1,\Im f_1)|_{p_*}$.
The geometric series in $I-PJ$ inverts $PJ$, so $J$ is invertible.
Multiplication by $b_*$ has real matrix
$\left(\begin{smallmatrix}\Re b_*&-\Im b_*\\\Im b_*&\Re b_*\end{smallmatrix}\right)$
and determinant $|b_*|^2>0$.  The product rule and $f_1=0$ give
$\mathcal J=\operatorname{Mat}_{\mathbb R}(b_*)J$.
Consequently
\[
 \Delta=\det\mathcal J=\Im(\overline{A_z}A_x)
       =|b_*|^2\det J\ne0,\qquad
 \Lambda^{-1}(q)=\frac1\Delta
 \begin{pmatrix}\Im(A_x\bar q)\\\Im(\overline{A_z}q)\end{pmatrix}.
 \tag{RPD4}
\]
Multiplying this vector by the two rows of $\mathcal J$ proves the
inverse formula, including both signs.  This is an exact morphism,
not an identification of two coordinate presentations by assertion.
It also proves $A_v:=\Lambda(v)\ne0$ for every real $v\ne0$.
For reference its orientation is negative: the real continuous
matrices $I-t(I-PJ)$ are invertible for $0\le t\le1$, so
$\det(PJ)>0$, whereas RPZ11 proves $\det P<0$.

\subsection{The full quadratic form and the real spectral zero curve}

For $h=(h_z,h_x)$ the original zeroth moment has the expansion
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \mu_0(p_*+h)&=h^{\mathsf T}\mathcal Qh+O(\|h\|^3),\\
 \mathcal Q&=\mathcal J^{\mathsf T}\mathcal J
 =\begin{pmatrix}|A_z|^2&\Re(A_z\overline{A_x})\\
                 \Re(A_z\overline{A_x})&|A_x|^2\end{pmatrix},\\
 \det\mathcal Q&=\Delta^2>0,
 \qquad D_p^2\mu_0(p_*)=2\mathcal Q.
 \end{aligned}\tag{RPD5}
\]
This follows by Taylor expanding $G(0,p_*+h)=\Lambda(h)+O(\|h\|^2)$
and multiplying by its conjugate.  Thus the quadratic form is positive
definite in the unchanged two original parameters.  On RPZ4's
rectangle, $f_2$ never vanishes and $f_1$ has its unique zero at $p_*$;
hence $\mu_0>0$ at every other real point of that rectangle.
The joint real expansion, retaining the spectral coordinate, is
\[
 E_A(\xi,p_*+h)=|B\xi+\Lambda(h)|^2
                 +O((|\xi|+\|h\|)^3).\tag{RPD6}
\]
Its real quadratic form has rank two and its exact null line is
$\{(\xi,-\xi\Lambda^{-1}(B)):\xi\in\mathbb R\}$.
The actual zero set is a smooth curve, not this tangent line alone.

Here is a construction of that curve without substituting a formal
tangent for the actual equation.  Let
$\mathcal H_\xi(h)=h-\Lambda^{-1}G(\xi,p_*+h)$, with complex outputs
interpreted as real vectors.  At $(\xi,h)=(0,0)$ its derivative in
$h$ is zero.  Choose a closed sufficiently small real ball on which
its derivative norm is at most $1/2$, and then restrict $|\xi|$ so
$\|\mathcal H_\xi(0)\|$ is at most half the radius.  Continuity of
the complete derivatives in RPD1 guarantees these two strict
inequalities after reducing the radius and interval.  The map
preserves the ball and contracts it.  Iteration from zero converges
by the geometric difference estimate in RPZ14 and gives its unique
fixed point $h(\xi)$.  Each fixed point is precisely a zero of $G$.
The same contraction estimate gives continuous, locally Lipschitz
dependence on $\xi$; Taylor subtraction of the two zero equations
then gives differentiability with the invertible parameter derivative.
Repeated differentiation gives every derivative because the full
functions are smooth.  Every real zero nearby is this fixed point.
Writing $p(\xi)=p_*+h(\xi)$, its first two derivatives are exactly
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 v_0=p'(0)&=-\Lambda^{-1}(B),\\
 p''(0)&=-\Lambda^{-1}\left(F+2\mathcal H(v_0)+\mathcal C(v_0,v_0)\right),\\
 F&=G_{\xi\xi},\quad
 \mathcal H(v)=G_{\xi z}v_z+G_{\xi x}v_x,\quad
 \mathcal C(v,w)=\sum_{i,j\in\{z,x\}}G_{ij}v_iw_j.
 \end{aligned}\tag{RPD7}
\]
Differentiating $G(\xi,p(\xi))=0$ twice proves the formula.  Because
$E_A=|G|^2$, its zero set on this real neighborhood is exactly the
same curve.

\subsection{Full original jets along each nonzero direction}

Fix an arbitrary nonzero $v\in\mathbb R^2$ and use the literal path
$p=p_*+\tau v$.  Put
$A_v=\Lambda(v)$, $C_v=\mathcal C(v,v)$ and $H_v=\mathcal H(v)$.
Every derivative here is determined by the original factors:
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 C_v&=b_*\partial_v^2f_1+2(\partial_v f_1)(\partial_vf_2),\\
 H_v&=b_*\partial_v\partial_\xi f_1
          +(\partial_vf_1)\partial_\xi f_2
          +(\partial_\xi f_1)\partial_v f_2,\\
 F&=b_*\partial_\xi^2 f_1+2(\partial_\xi f_1)(\partial_\xi f_2),\\
 \partial_v^m\mu_n(p_*)&=\sum_{r=0}^n\sum_{j=0}^m
 \binom nr\binom mj(\partial_\xi^r\partial_v^jG)
       \overline{\partial_\xi^{n-r}\partial_v^{m-j}G}.
 \end{aligned}\tag{RPD8}
\]
The first three identities are the product rule with $f_1=0$;
the last differentiates RPD2 and therefore includes every moment.
Define the exact directional constants
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 c_v&=|A_v|^2>0,& R_v&=2\Re(A_v\bar B),& b&=|B|^2>0,\\
 d_v&=-iR_v,& e&=-b,& c_{3,v}&=\Re(C_v\overline{A_v}),\\
 d_{2,v}&=-i\{\Re(B\overline{C_v})+2\Re(H_v\overline{A_v})-4c_v\},\\
 e_{1,v}&=-\Re(F\overline{A_v})-2\Re(H_v\bar B)+4R_v,\\
 f&=i\{\Re(F\bar B)-4b\}.
 \end{aligned}\tag{RPD9}
\]
These constants are not independent choices of jets.  For the complete
original symbol
$g(t,p)=e^{-4\omega(t)}E_A(\omega(t),p)$,
$\omega(t)=-i\arctan t$, coefficient differentiation gives
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 g_0(p_*+\tau v)&=c_v\tau^2+c_{3,v}\tau^3+O(\tau^4),\\
 g_1(p_*+\tau v)&=d_v\tau+d_{2,v}\tau^2+O(\tau^3),\\
 g_2(p_*+\tau v)&=e+e_{1,v}\tau+O(\tau^2),\qquad
 g_3(p_*+\tau v)=f+O(\tau).
 \end{aligned}\tag{RPD10}
\]
For clarity the identities before taking these jets are
$g_0=\mu_0$, $g_1=-i(\mu_1-4\mu_0)$,
$g_2=-\mu_2/2+4\mu_1-8\mu_0$, and
$g_3=i(\mu_3/6-2\mu_2+25\mu_1/3-12\mu_0)$.
They follow by expanding the exact $\omega$ and exponential through
the stated degree; RPD8 supplies their complete parameter jets.

\subsection{Every cutoff and its full metric constants}

Retain $s\in\{1,a_{\rm amp}\}$ and the original centers
$a_{\rm amp}/2$ and $a_{\rm amp}/2-4$.  The physical measure and
weights, with no removal of mass or center, are
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 dm_s(y)=\frac{(2\pi)^{s/2}2^{s/2}}{4\pi\Gamma(s/2)}
       |\Gamma(s/4+iy/2)|^2\,dy,\quad M_s=(2\pi)^{s/2},\\
 \rho_j=\sqrt{j!/(s/2)_j},\quad N=D+1,\quad
 B_{D,s}(p)=\operatorname{diag}(\rho)^{-1}T_D(g(\cdot,p))
                                  \operatorname{diag}(\rho),\\
 T_D(g)_{ij}=g_{j-i}\ (j\ge i),\qquad T_D(g)_{ij}=0\ (j<i).
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{RPD11}
\]
These are the original orthonormal frames of WCF2--6.  Its two mass
factors cancel only in the displayed matrix representation.
In particular the fixed old map has domain and codomain
\[
(\mathcal P_D,\|\cdot\|_{s,a_{\rm amp}/2})\quad\text{and}\quad
(\mathcal P_D,\|\cdot\|_{s,a_{\rm amp}/2-4}),
\]
where
$\mathcal P_D=\mathbb C[S]_{\le D}$ and
$\|P\|_{s,c}^2=\int_{\mathbb R}|P(c+iy)|^2dm_s(y)$.
At $p_*$ the fixed old matrix has rank $N-2$ for $D\ge1$.
For $D\ge2$ its full nonzero block $C_{D,s}$ has rows $0,\ldots,D-2$
and columns $2,\ldots,D$, with entries
\[
 (C_{D,s})_{ij}=g_{j+2-i}(p_*)\rho_{j+2}/\rho_i\quad(j\ge i),
 \qquad (C_{D,s})_{ij}=0\quad(j<i).\tag{RPD12}
\]
The diagonal $e\rho_{i+2}/\rho_i$ never vanishes.  All higher
coefficients $g_j(p_*)$ remain in this block.  For $D=1$ it is empty,
with zeroth exterior norm and determinant equal to one.
The actual order-two quotient at the point retains a different
domain, and its exact original matrix is
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 \mathcal A_{D,s}:\mathcal P_{D+2}/\mathcal P_1\longrightarrow\mathcal P_D,
 \qquad (\mathcal A_{D,s})_{ij}=
       g_{j-i+2}(p_*)\rho_{j+2}/\rho_i\quad(j\ge i),\\
 (\mathcal A_{D,s})_{ij}=0\quad(j<i),\qquad
 (\mathcal A_{D,s})_{ii}=e\rho_{i+2}/\rho_i\ne0.
 \end{gathered}\tag{RPD12a}
\]
The source has the original quotient norm at center
$a_{\rm amp}/2$, and the target has its original norm at center
$a_{\rm amp}/2-4$.  WCF4--6 applied to the complete symbol gives
RPD12a: the original polynomial map sends
$S^n$ to $\sum_j\binom nj\mu_jS'^{n-j}$, its first nonzero moment
is $\mu_2=2|B|^2$, and its quotient symbol is $t^{-2}g(t,p_*)$.
The nonzero diagonal proves this quotient map invertible.  Changing
its domain does not remove the poles of the fixed old map just
specified in RPD11.

For $n\ge0$ define finite expressions
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 H_n(v)&=\sum_{j=0}^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}(-1)^{n-j}\binom{n-j}{j}
      \frac{d_v^{n-2j}e^j}{c_v^{n-j+1}},\quad H_{-1}=H_{-2}=0,\\
 K_n(v)&=-[y^n]\frac{c_{3,v}+d_{2,v}y+e_{1,v}y^2+fy^3}
                            {(c_v+d_vy+ey^2)^2}\\
 &=-\sum_{j=0}^{\min(3,n)}a_{j,v}\sum_{k=0}^{n-j}H_k(v)H_{n-j-k}(v),\quad
 (a_{0,v},a_{1,v},a_{2,v},a_{3,v})=(c_{3,v},d_{2,v},e_{1,v},f).
 \end{aligned}\tag{RPD13}
\]
All higher original coefficients remain in $g$.  The exact inverse
entries, for $0\le n\le D$, satisfy
\[
 [t^n]g(t,p_*+\tau v)^{-1}
   =\tau^{-n-2}\{H_n(v)+\tau K_n(v)+O(\tau^2)\}.\tag{RPD14}
\]
To prove this, the exact coefficient substitution $t=\tau y$ gives
$g(\tau y,p_*+\tau v)=\tau^2q_v(y)+\tau^3a_v(y)+O(\tau^4)$,
where $q_v=c_v+d_vy+ey^2$ and $a_v$ is the numerator in RPD13.
Reciprocation gives $q_v^{-1}-\tau a_vq_v^{-2}+O(\tau^2)$ after
the exact factor $\tau^2$ is retained.  Coefficient extraction
proves RPD14 and geometric expansion proves RPD13.  This is a
coefficient identity for each finite cutoff, not deletion of higher
moments.

Put $\lambda_v=|B|/|A_v|$ and
$\theta_v=\Re(A_v\bar B)/(|A_v||B|)$.  Multiplication by $q_v$
gives $c_vH_n+d_vH_{n-1}+eH_{n-2}=\boldsymbol1_{n=0}$.
Defining $U_0=1$, $U_1=2X$, $U_n=2XU_{n-1}-U_{n-2}$, induction
and the sine addition identity prove
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 H_n(v)=\frac{(i\lambda_v)^n}{c_v}U_n(\theta_v),\qquad
 H_{n-1}(v)^2-H_n(v)H_{n-2}(v)=\frac{e^{n-1}}{c_v^{n+1}}
          \quad(n\ge1),\\
 H_D(v)=0\ \Longleftrightarrow\
 \theta_v=\cos\frac{k\pi}{D+1}\quad\text{for some }1\le k\le D.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{RPD15}
\]
The first identity holds for every $n\ge0$.
For the second identity the initial value is $c_v^{-2}$ and the
recurrence multiplies it by $e/c_v$ at each step.  For the last,
$U_D(\cos\phi)=\sin((D+1)\phi)/\sin\phi$; the $D$ displayed
roots are distinct, and $U_D$ has degree $D$ and leading coefficient
$2^D$.  These arguments prove all degrees, with no finite-degree
test standing in for the proof.

For $2\le r\le N$ define the positive constants
\[
 L_{r,D,s}(v)=\frac{\|\bigwedge^{N-r}C_{D,s}\|}{c_v^N},\qquad
 L_{2,D,s}(v)=\frac{|e|^{D-1}\rho_{D-1}\rho_D}
                       {c_v^{D+1}\rho_0\rho_1}.\tag{RPD16}
\]
The second equality multiplies the complete block diagonal and
telescopes its weights.  The exact singular-value identity
$\|\bigwedge^rB^{-1}\|=\|\bigwedge^{N-r}B\|/|\det B|$ follows
by multiplying the corresponding singular values.  Here
$\det B=g_0^N$, so continuity and RPD10 prove
\[
 \lim_{\tau\to0}|\tau|^{2N}
  \|\bigwedge^rB_{D,s}(p_*+\tau v)^{-1}\|=L_{r,D,s}(v)
  \quad(2\le r\le N).\tag{RPD17}
\]
When $H_D(v)\ne0$, the sole entry at pole $D+2$ is the top right.
The two divergent inverse singular values, in decreasing order,
have poles and constants
\[
 (D+2,D),\qquad
 \left(a_{D,s}(v),\frac{L_{2,D,s}(v)}{a_{D,s}(v)}\right),\qquad
 a_{D,s}(v)=|H_D(v)|\rho_D/\rho_0.\tag{RPD18}
\]
Indeed RPD14 gives the first limit; division of RPD17 at $r=2$
gives the second.  When $H_D(v)=0$, RPD15 forces $H_{D-1}(v)\ne0$.
The full leading block of $\tau^{D+1}B_{D,s}^{-1}$ is
\[
 N_{D,s}(v)=\begin{pmatrix}
 H_{D-1}(v)\rho_{D-1}/\rho_0&K_D(v)\rho_D/\rho_0\\
 0&H_{D-1}(v)\rho_D/\rho_1
 \end{pmatrix}.\tag{RPD19}
\]
It occupies rows $0,1$ and columns $D-1,D$, and is invertible.
Every remaining entry tends to zero.  Therefore both divergent
inverse singular values have pole $D+1$, with constants
$\sigma_+(N_{D,s})$ and $\sigma_-(N_{D,s})$.
For entries $(u,w;0,v_1)$ these constants equal
$\{(S\pm\sqrt{S^2-4|uv_1|^2})/2\}^{1/2}$,
$S=|u|^2+|w|^2+|v_1|^2$, retaining the complete upper-right term.
In both cases all other inverse singular values tend to reciprocals
of the positive singular values of $C_{D,s}$ in reverse order.
For $D=1$ the block RPD19 is the full matrix; for $D=0$ the only
inverse pole is two with constant $c_v^{-1}$.

\subsection{All resonance rays in the original coordinates}

For $D\ge1$, $1\le k\le D$, $\varepsilon\in\{1,-1\}$ and $r>0$
put $\phi_k=k\pi/(D+1)$ and define the exact real vectors
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 v_{D,k,\varepsilon}(r)
 &=\Lambda^{-1}(rB e^{i\varepsilon\phi_k})\\
 &=\frac r\Delta
 \begin{pmatrix}
 \Im(A_x\bar B e^{-i\varepsilon\phi_k})\\
 \Im(\overline{A_z}B e^{i\varepsilon\phi_k})
 \end{pmatrix}.
 \end{aligned}\tag{RPD20}
\]
Their actual values satisfy $A_v=rB e^{i\varepsilon\phi_k}$,
$c_v=r^2|B|^2$, $R_v=2r|B|^2\cos\phi_k$ and
$\lambda_v=1/r$.  No magnitude is discarded: $r$ remains arbitrary
and all its powers remain in RPD9--19.
They give every resonant direction.  In fact for any nonzero $v$
the number $A_v/B$ is nonzero, and the equality
$\Re(A_v/B)/|A_v/B|=\cos\phi_k$ forces
$A_v/B=r e^{i\phi_k}$ or $r e^{-i\phi_k}$ for its actual $r>0$.
Applying the inverse in RPD4 proves exhaustiveness.

For positive rays there are exactly $2D$ distinct choices, since
their image arguments $\pm\phi_k$ are distinct modulo $2\pi$.
The exact duplication upon forgetting orientation is
\[
 v_{D,D+1-k,-\varepsilon}(r)=-v_{D,k,\varepsilon}(r).
 \tag{RPD21}
\]
Thus there are exactly $D$ unoriented real lines.  There is one
line with $\theta=0$ precisely when $D$ is odd; it corresponds to
$k=(D+1)/2$.  All remaining values of $\theta$ are paired with
$-\theta$.  Under any real scaling $\ell\ne0$, direct substitution
in RPD9 and RPD13 gives
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 \theta_{\ell v}=\operatorname{sgn}(\ell)\theta_v,\quad
 H_n(\ell v)=\ell^{-n-2}H_n(v),\quad
 K_n(\ell v)=\ell^{-n-1}K_n(v),\\
 c_{\ell v}=\ell^2c_v,\ d_{\ell v}=\ell d_v,\
 c_{3,\ell v}=\ell^3c_{3,v},\ d_{2,\ell v}=\ell^2d_{2,v},\
 e_{1,\ell v}=\ell e_{1,v}.
 \end{gathered}
 \tag{RPD22}
\]
The constants $e,f$ stay fixed.  This proves resonance invariance
under every nonzero real scaling, including the signs of $H_n,K_n$.
An inverse pole of exponent $p$ has its norm constant multiplied by
$|\ell|^{-p}$, exactly as follows also from the literal reparameterization
$p_*+\tau\ell v=p_*+(\ell\tau)v$.

These formulas also classify repetitions across all cutoffs.  An
unoriented direction has a unique image argument
$\phi\in[0,\pi)$ for the line $\mathbb R(A_v/B)$.
It is resonant for some cutoff precisely when
$\phi/\pi=m/q$ is rational with $0<m<q$ and $\gcd(m,q)=1$;
its resonant cutoffs are exactly $D=jq-1$, $j\ge1$.
The line $\phi=0$ and every irrational argument are nonresonant at
every cutoff.  Two cutoffs $D,E$ share exactly
$\gcd(D+1,E+1)-1$ resonance lines: the common fractions strictly
between zero and one are the multiples of the reciprocal of that
greatest common divisor.  This follows by reducing the fractions
in RPD20; it is an exact classification, not an interval test for
an infinite list of equalities.

\subsection{Curvature correction and the complete resonance transition}

Let a real path have
$p(\tau)=p_*+\tau v+\tfrac12\tau^2a+O(\tau^3)$, $v\ne0$.
Twice differentiating $G(\xi,p(\tau))$ shows that RPD9--14 still
hold with
\[
 C_v\longmapsto C_v+\Lambda(a),\qquad
 K_n^{\rm path}=K_n(v)+\tfrac12 DH_n(v)[a].\tag{RPD23}
\]
Here $H_v,F,B$ are unchanged to the orders in question.
To verify the second equality directly, the increments are
$\delta c_3=\Re(\Lambda(a)\overline{A_v})$
and $\delta d_2=-i\Re(B\overline{\Lambda(a)})$, with no increment
in $e_1,f$.  They equal $\tfrac12 Dc_v[a]$ and
$\tfrac12 Dd_v[a]$.  Differentiating $q_v^{-1}$ in RPD13 therefore
gives exactly the additional half derivative.  The full resonant
block uses this corrected upper-right coefficient; a tangent
direction alone does not specify that coefficient.

We now prove a uniform transition formula rather than apply a
fixed nonresonant asymptotic at changing directions.  Fix any
resonant nonzero $v$ for cutoff $D$ and any real $w$ transverse to
its line.  The derivative
$\kappa_D=DH_D(v)[w]$ is nonzero.  To see this, use the exact
transverse vector $w_0=\Lambda^{-1}(iA_v)$.
It has $Dc_v[w_0]=0$ and
$D\theta_v[w_0]=-\Im(A_v\bar B)/(|A_v||B|)\ne0$ at each
interior root in RPD15.  Those polynomial roots are simple, so
$DH_D(v)[w_0]\ne0$.  Homogeneity in RPD22 gives
$DH_D(v)[v]=-(D+2)H_D(v)=0$.
Every real $w$ is a unique real combination of $v,w_0$ because
their images are $A_v,iA_v$; transversality means its $w_0$
coefficient is nonzero.  This proves the assertion and also gives
the exact derivative
\[
 DH_D(v)[w_0]=\frac{(i\lambda_v)^D}{c_v}
 U_D'(\theta_v)\frac{-\Im(A_v\bar B)}{|A_v||B|}.\tag{RPD24}
\]

For real $\tau>0$ and $\epsilon\to0$, write
$v_\epsilon=v+\epsilon w$ and evaluate the literal point
$p_*+\tau v_\epsilon$.  On a fixed compact neighborhood of $v$,
$c_{v'}$ is bounded away from zero.  The complete analytic
coefficient expansion proving RPD14 has uniformly bounded
remainders there.  It follows entry by entry that
\[
 \tau^{D+1}B_{D,s}(p_*+\tau v_\epsilon)^{-1}
 =\iota\begin{pmatrix}
 H_{D-1}(v_\epsilon)\rho_{D-1}/\rho_0&
 \{H_D(v_\epsilon)/\tau+K_D(v_\epsilon)\}\rho_D/\rho_0\\
 0&H_{D-1}(v_\epsilon)\rho_D/\rho_1
 \end{pmatrix}+O(\tau).
 \tag{RPD25}
\]
Here $\iota$ inserts the $2\times2$ corner at rows $0,1$ and columns
$D-1,D$.  For $D=1$ it is the identity insertion.  The error is in
the original matrix norm and is uniform for these $v_\epsilon$.
The two diagonal corner errors are $O(\tau)$ by RPD14 at degree
$D-1$; the top-right error is $O(\tau)$ at degree $D$; every other
entry has degree at most $D-2$ and hence is $O(\tau)$ or smaller.
This proves the formula, including its uniformity and all weights.

If $\epsilon(\tau)/\tau\to L\in\mathbb R$, the two divergent
inverse singular values both have pole $D+1$, with constants the
two singular values of
\[
 N_{D,s}(v;L,w)=\begin{pmatrix}
 H_{D-1}(v)\rho_{D-1}/\rho_0&
 \{K_D(v)+L\kappa_D\}\rho_D/\rho_0\\
 0&H_{D-1}(v)\rho_D/\rho_1
 \end{pmatrix}.\tag{RPD26}
\]
Indeed $H_D(v+\epsilon w)=\kappa_D\epsilon+O(\epsilon^2)$,
so RPD25 converges to the displayed invertible block.  Its
determinant modulus is $L_{2,D,s}(v)$ by RPD15--16, independent
of $L$.  All remaining inverse singular values have the same
finite positive limits as before.  If instead
$|\epsilon(\tau)|/\tau\to\infty$ while $\epsilon(\tau)\to0$,
RPD25's single growing entry and the same determinant identity give
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \sigma_1(B_{D,s}^{-1})&\sim
     |\kappa_D|\frac{\rho_D}{\rho_0}
                   |\epsilon(\tau)|\tau^{-D-2},\\
 \sigma_2(B_{D,s}^{-1})&\sim
     \frac{L_{2,D,s}(v)\rho_0}{|\kappa_D|\rho_D}
                   |\epsilon(\tau)|^{-1}\tau^{-D}.
 \end{aligned}\tag{RPD27}
\]
For every $2\le r\le N$ the exterior asymptotic is always
$L_{r,D,s}(v)\tau^{-2N}$, since the direction tends to $v$ and
$g_0/\tau^2\to c_v$.  Thus no divergent crossover coefficient is
hidden inside a falsely uniform fixed-direction estimate.

In particular take $\epsilon(\tau)=q_0\tau^q$, $q_0\ne0$, $q>0$.
For $0<q<1$ the two pole exponents are
$(D+2-q,D+q)$, with constants
$|q_0\kappa_D|\rho_D/\rho_0$ and its quotient into
$L_{2,D,s}(v)$.  These paths are differentiable at zero, but are
not asserted to be twice differentiable.  For $q=1$ both poles are
$D+1$ and RPD26 uses $L=q_0$; the path has acceleration $2q_0w$,
so the result agrees exactly with RPD23.  For $q>1$ both poles
remain $D+1$ and the block is $N_{D,s}(v;0,w)$.

For the original degree-three equation, the fully explicit
specialization retains $b=|B|^2$, $c=c_v$, $R=R_v$:
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 H_3(v)&=iR(2cb-R^2)/c^4,\\
 DH_3(v)[w]&=\frac{i\{(2cb-3R^2)DR[w]+2bR\,Dc[w]\}}{c^4}
                    \quad\text{on }H_3(v)=0,\\
 Dc[w]&=2\Re(\Lambda(w)\overline{A_v}),\qquad
 DR[w]=2\Re(\Lambda(w)\bar B),\\
 H_2(v)&=(d_v^2-c_ve)/c_v^3,\\
 K_3(v)&=\frac{2c_vd_ve_{1,v}+2c_{3,v}d_ve
               +(2c_ve-3d_v^2)d_{2,v}-c_v^2f}{c_v^4}
                         \quad\text{on }H_3(v)=0.
 \end{aligned}\tag{RPD28}
\]
The three unoriented lines have $\theta_v=0$ or
$\theta_v^2=1/2$, with representatives RPD20 at
$\phi=\pi/4,\pi/2,3\pi/4$.  The two singular poles are $(5,3)$
off these lines and $(4,4)$ on straight approaches along them.
The full transition gives $(5-q,3+q)$ for $0<q<1$ and $(4,4)$
for $q\ge1$; all exterior ranks $2,3,4$ have pole eight with
constants RPD16.  RPD28 follows by differentiating its displayed
$H_3$ at a zero and by extracting the next reciprocal coefficient;
it includes the $-4$ center terms through RPD9.

\subsection{Exact return to the positive original period and actual unit}

The period inversion is an exact coordinate map, not a constant
rescaling of a curved two-parameter path:
\[
 (z,x)\longmapsto(u,x)=(1/z,x),\qquad
 (v_z,v_x)\longmapsto(-u_*^2v_z,v_x),\qquad
 da(v)=i\alpha v_x.\tag{RPD29}
\]
Its differential is invertible because $z_*>0$.
Thus every resonance vector in original $(u,x)$ coordinates is
$(-u_*^2v_z,v_x)$ with $v$ given in RPD20, and the actual unit
is always $\alpha(1+ix)$.
For a straight original-period path
$(u,x)=(u_*,x_*)+\tau(\nu_u,\nu_x)$, the exact expansion is
\[
 v=(-z_*^2\nu_u,\nu_x),\qquad
 a=(2z_*^3\nu_u^2,0),\qquad
 K_D^{(u,x)}=K_D(v)+\tfrac12DH_D(v)[a].\tag{RPD30}
\]
This follows by differentiating $z=1/u$ twice and applying RPD23.
The directional zeroth coefficient is $c_v$, all weights remain
RPD11, and the resonant leading block uses the full RPD30 term.
When only the period varies with $\nu_u=1$, this reproduces the original
$|u_*|^{2p}$ factor at pole exponent $p$.  For arbitrary nonzero
$\nu_u$ there is also the factor $|\nu_u|^{-p}$.
At resonance the curvature
vector is parallel to $v$ and its derivative term vanishes by
RPD22.  For a mixed direction there is no general license to drop
that term.  The isolated real singular point, its exact resonance
lines, and every crossover above concern the full geometric family
defined in RPD1.  No step puts an arithmetic zeta quartet on this
family's singular point or supplies that unconstructed arithmetic map.
